# BOOK I

### D 2

If a Pedestal is placed under Ionic columns, as shown in the drawing of the Arches, it shall be made as high as half the width of the opening of the Arch. It shall be divided into seven and a half parts: two parts shall form the Base, one the Cymatium <term>the crowning molding of a pedestal or cornice</term>, and four and a half shall remain for the Die <term>the central block of a pedestal, also called a dado</term>; that is, the flat middle surface. 

The base of the Ionic order is half a module thick and is divided into three parts: one is given to the Plinth <note>original: "Zocco"; the lowest square member of a base</note>, and its projection is one-fourth plus one-eighth of a module. The other two parts are divided into seven: three parts form the torus <term>a large convex, semi-circular molding</term>, and the remaining four are again divided into two—one is given to the upper scotia <term>a concave molding, here called a "cavetto"</term> and the other to the lower one, which should have more projection than the upper. The astragals <term>small convex moldings, often bead-like</term> should be one-eighth of the scotia. The fillet <term>a small, flat surface separating moldings; here called "cimbia"</term> of the column is one-third of the torus of the base. However, if the base is made joined with a part of the column shaft, the fillet shall be made thinner, as I also mentioned regarding the Doric order. The projection of this fillet is half of the projection previously mentioned. 

These are the measurements of the Ionic base according to Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura,' whose work was the foundation for Renaissance theory</note>. But because in many Ancient buildings one sees Attic bases used for this order, and they please me more, I have drawn the Attic base above the pedestal with that small torus under the fillet. Nevertheless, I have not omitted the drawing of the one taught to us by Vitruvius. The drawings marked **L** are two different profiles <note>original: "sacome"; templates used to cut stone moldings</note> for making the imposts of the Arches; on each, the measurements are noted in numbers which signify the Minutes of the Module, as has been done in all the other drawings. These imposts <term>the projecting block resting on a pillar from which an arch springs</term> are half again as high as the thickness of the pillar that supports the Arch.

*   **B**, Bead with the Fillet, which are members of the column.

<page-num>33</page-num>

<header>BOOK FIRST.</header>

To fashion the **capital**, the foot of the column is divided into eighteen parts, and nineteen of these parts comprise the width and length of the **Abacus**: and half [of nineteen] is the height of the capital including the volutes; thus it comes to be nine and a half parts high. One and a half parts are given to the **Abacus** with its **Cymatium** <note>a decorative molding at the top of the abacus</note>: the other eight remain for the **Volute** <note>the characteristic spiral scroll of the Ionic capital</note>: which is made in this manner. From the outer edge of the **Cymatium** toward the inside, one of the nineteen parts is placed, and from that point, a line is dropped straight down; this divides the **Volute** through the middle and is called the **Cathetus** <note>original: "Catheto"; a vertical line used as a geometric reference</note>. At the point on this line that separates the upper four and a half parts from the lower three and a half parts, the center of the **eye of the Volute** is placed: the diameter of which is one of the eight parts. From said point, a line is drawn which crosses the **cathetus** at right angles, dividing the volute into four parts. Within the eye, a square is then formed, the size of which is the semi-diameter of said eye; after drawing the diagonal lines, the points are marked upon them where the fixed foot of the compass must be placed to draw the **Volute**. Including the center of the eye, there are thirteen centers; the order in which these must be used appears by the numbers placed in the drawing. The **Astragal** <note>a small, rounded molding</note> of the column is level with the eye of the **Volute**. The **Volutes** are as thick in the middle as the projection of the **Ovolo** <note>original: "Ouolo"; a convex molding often carved with egg-and-dart patterns</note>, which extends beyond the **Abacus** as far as the eye of the **Volute**. The channel of the **Volute** is flush with the naked shaft of the column. The **Astragal** of the column circles beneath the **Volute** and is always visible, as appears in the plan; it is natural that a soft thing, such as the **Volute** is feigned to be, should give way to a hard thing, such as the **Astragal**; and the **Volute** always remains at an equal distance from it. At the corners of colonnades or porches of the Ionic order, it is customary to make capitals that have **Volutes** not only on the front but also on the side which, if the capital were made in the usual way, would be the flank; thus they come to have a front on two sides. These are called **angular capitals**, and I will demonstrate how they are made in my book on Temples.

**A**, **Abacus**.
**B**, Channel, or the hollow of the **Volute**.
**C**, **Ovolo**.
**D**, **Bead** <note>original: "Tondino"</note> below the **Ovolo**.
**E**, **Fillet** <note>original: "Cimbia"; a small flat band</note>.
**F**, The naked shaft of the **Column**.
**G**, The line called the **Cathetus**.

The **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice** are (as I have said) <note>referring to the general rules of proportion established earlier in the treatise</note> equal to one-fifth of the height of the column, and the whole is divided into twelve parts. The Architrave is four parts; the Frieze is three; and the Cornice is five. 

The Architrave is divided into five parts: one part forms its **Cymatium** <term>a crowning molding, often decorated</term>, and the remainder is divided into twelve: three are given to the first **fascia** <term>a plain, horizontal band</term> and its **Astragal** <term>a small, ring-like convex molding</term>; four to the second fascia and its astragal; and five to the third fascia. 

The cornice is divided into seven and three-quarter parts: two are given to the **Cavetto** <term>a concave, hollow molding</term> and **Ovolo** <term>a convex, egg-shaped molding</term>; two to the **modillion** <term>an ornamental bracket or block under the cornice</term>; and three and three-quarters to the **corona** <term>the flat, vertical face of the cornice</term> and the **cyma** <term>an S-shaped wave molding; original: "gola"</term>. It projects outward by the same amount as its thickness. I have drawn the front, the side, and the plan of the **Capital**, along with the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice with the carvings that are appropriate for them.

### ON THE CORINTHIAN ORDER.
### CHAPTER XVII.

In **Corinth**, a most noble city of the **Peloponnese**, the order that is called **Corinthian** was first discovered; it is more adorned and slender than those mentioned above. The columns are similar to the **Ionic**, and with the base and the capital added, they are nine and a half **modules** <note>A module is a standard unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually derived from the diameter or semi-diameter of the column base, used to ensure all parts of a building are in proportion</note> long. If they are fluted, they should have twenty-four **channels** <note>flutes</note>, which should be deep by half of their width. The <term>fillets</term> <note>original: "pianuzzi"; the flat vertical strips between the flutes of a column</note>, or spaces between one channel and another, shall be one-third of the width of the said channels. The **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice** are one-fifth of the height of the columns. In the drawing of the simple colonnade, the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>original: "intercolunnij"; the clear space between two adjacent columns</note> are two diameters, as is the Portico of **Santa Maria Ritonda** <note>The Pantheon in Rome, which was consecrated as a church and known by this name during the Renaissance</note> in Rome; and this manner of colonnades is called by **Vitruvius** <term>systyle</term> <note>original: "Siftilos"; from the Greek "systylos," describing a temple where the columns are spaced relatively close together—specifically two diameters apart</note>. And in the design of the **Arches**, the pilasters are two parts out of five of the opening of the arch, and the arch's opening is two and a half squares in height, including the thickness of the arch itself.

In Corinth, a most noble city of the Peloponnese, the order that is called Corinthian was first discovered. It is more ornate and slender than those mentioned previously. The columns are similar to the Ionic, and including the base and the capital, they are nine and a half **modules** <note>A module is a standard unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually based on the radius of the column at its base</note> long. 

If they are to be fluted <note>original: "incanellate"</note>, they must have twenty-four channels, which should be deep by half of their width. The <term>fillets</term> <note>original: "pianuzzi"; the flat strips between the grooves</note>, or spaces between one channel and the other, shall be one-third of the width of the said channels. The **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice** are one-fifth of the height of the columns. 

In the design of the simple colonnade, the **intercolumniations** <note>the clear space between two adjacent columns</note> are two diameters, as seen in the Portico of **Santa Maria Ritonda** <note>The Roman temple now known as the Pantheon</note> in Rome; this manner of spacing colonnades is called **Systyle** <note>original: "Sístilos"; a Greek-derived term used by the Roman architect Vitruvius to describe columns spaced exactly two diameters apart</note> by Vitruvius. And in the design with arches, the pilasters <note>the rectangular piers supporting the arches</note> are two parts out of five of the **opening** <note>original: "luce"; literally "light," referring to the clear width of the archway</note> of the arch, and the arch's height is two and a half squares, including the thickness of the arch itself.

In Corinth, a most noble city of the Peloponnese, the order that is called Corinthian was first discovered. It is more ornate and slender than those mentioned previously. The columns are similar to the Ionic, and including the base and the capital, they are nine and a half **modules** <note>A module is a standard unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually based on the radius of the column at its base</note> long. 

If they are to be fluted <note>original: "incanellate"</note>, they must have twenty-four channels, which should be deep by half of their width. The <term>fillets</term> <note>original: "pianuzzi"; the flat strips between the grooves</note>, or spaces between one channel and the other, shall be one-third of the width of the said channels. The **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice** are one-fifth of the height of the columns. 

In the design of the simple column <note>original: "collona"</note>, the measurements are distributed as follows to ensure the grace and strength characteristic of this Greek style. As shown in the accompanying diagram, the spacing between the columns—the intercolumniation—is carefully calculated using the module system to maintain harmony when these elements are repeated in an arcade.

### Proportions of the Corinthian Capital and Entablature

The **Corinthian Capital** must be as high as the thickness of the column at its base, plus an additional sixth part, which is assigned to the **Abacus** <note>The flat slab forming the top of the capital</note>. The remaining height is divided into three equal parts. The first part is given to the first row of leaves; the second to the second row; and the third part is divided again into two. From the part closest to the Abacus, the **cauliculi** <term>cauliculi: small stalks or stems that branch out to support the volutes of the capital</term> are formed, along with the leaves that appear to support them and from which they sprout. Therefore, the stems from which they emerge should be thick, and as they wind around, they should gradually taper, following the example of plants, which are thicker at their base than at their ends.

The **bell** <note>original: "campana"; the solid, vase-shaped core of the capital</note>—that is, the main body of the capital beneath the leaves—should align vertically with the depth of the column's fluting. To create an Abacus with the proper **projection** <note>original: "sporto"; the distance a molding extends outward from the central axis</note>, one forms a square where each side is one and a half modules long. Diagonal lines are drawn across it, and where they intersect in the middle, the stationary foot of the compass is placed. A distance of one module is marked toward each corner of the square. At these points, lines are drawn to intersect the diagonals at right angles and touch the sides of the square; these define the limit of the projection, and their length determines the width of the "horns" <note>The pointed corners of the Corinthian abacus</note>. The curvature, or recession of the sides, is created by stretching a string from one horn to the other and finding the point that forms a triangle, the base of which is the recession.

One then draws a line from the tips of these horns to the edge of the **astragal** <term>astragal: a small, rounded molding at the top of the column shaft</term> (or torus) of the column, ensuring that the tips of the leaves touch this line or extend slightly beyond it; this constitutes their projection. The **Rosette** <note>The carved flower at the center of each side of the abacus</note> must be as wide as one-fourth of the column's diameter at the base.

The **Architrave**, **Frieze**, and **Cornice** are, as I have mentioned, one-fifth of the column's height. The total height of these three elements is divided into twelve parts, as in the Ionic order, but with this difference: the Cornice is divided into eight and a half parts. One part is for the cymatium <note>original: "intauolato"; the uppermost molding of the cornice</note>, another for the **dentils** <term>dentils: small, tooth-like rectangular blocks used as a decorative molding</term>, the third for the **ovolo** <note>An egg-and-dart molding</note>, the fourth and fifth for the **modillions** <term>modillions: ornamental brackets or blocks placed under the corona</term>, and the remaining three and a half parts for the **corona** <note>The flat, projecting face of the cornice</note> and the **cyma** <note>original: "Gola" (literally 'throat'); a molding with an S-shaped profile</note>.

The projection of the cornice is equal to its height. The recessed compartments for the Rosettes that sit between the modillions should be square, and the modillions themselves should be as thick as half the width of the space holding those Rosettes. The members of this order have not been labeled with letters as in previous examples, because they can easily be identified by comparing them to the previous orders.

# ON THE COMPOSITE ORDER.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

The Composite order, which is also called the Latin order because it was an invention of the ancient Romans, is so named because it shares the characteristics of two of the orders mentioned previously. The most regular and beautiful version is that which is composed of the Ionic and the Corinthian. It is made more slender than the Corinthian, and can be made similar to it in all its parts, except for the capital. The columns must be ten <term>modules</term> <note>a unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually equal to the radius of the column shaft at its base</note> long. In the design for a simple colonnade, the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the clear space between two adjacent columns</note> are one and a half diameters wide; this arrangement is called <term>Pycnostyle</term> <note>original: "Picnostilos"; a Greek term meaning "thick-columned," used by the Roman architect Vitruvius to describe close spacing</note> by Vitruvius. In the design using arches, the <term>piers</term> <note>original: "pilastri"; the rectangular supports for the arches</note> are half the width of the arch's opening, and the arches themselves are two and a half squares high, measured to the underside of the vault.

# THE PROPORTIONS OF THE COLONNADE

<note>This page features an architectural plate illustrating the mathematical relationship between columns and their spacing.</note>

This diagram establishes the standard unit of measurement, the <term>Module</term> <note>original Latin: "Modulus," abbreviated as "M O" in the drawing; a unit derived from the diameter or radius of the column shaft used to ensure all parts of a building are in proportion</note>, and applies it to a series of columns.

### The Dimensional Scale

The following measurements are indicated on the architectural drawing to guide the builder:

*   **The Entablature:** The total height of the upper horizontal section <note>comprising the architrave, frieze, and cornice</note> is designated as **2 Modules**.
*   **Column Diameter:** The width of each individual column shaft is consistently **1 Module**.
*   **Intercolumniation:** The clear space between the columns is set at **1 ½ Modules** <note>in classical architecture, the distance between columns is as important as the columns themselves for creating a sense of balance and strength</note>.
*   **The Base:** The supporting structure beneath the columns is also measured at **1 Module** in height.

Below the columns, four circles illustrate the "footprint" or ground plan of the shafts. The labels reinforce the rhythm of the architecture: each circle has a diameter of **1 Module**, separated by a gap of **1 ½ Modules**.

# PROPORTIONS OF THE PEDESTAL AND BASE

And because (as I have said) this order must be made more slender than the Corinthian, its pedestal is one-third of the column's height; it is divided into eight and a half parts. One part is used for the <term>Cymatium</term> <note>the decorative crowning molding at the top of a pedestal</note>, one for the Base, and five and a half remain for the <term>Die</term> <note>original: "Dado"; the square, central block of the pedestal</note>. The Base of the pedestal is divided into three parts: two are given to the <term>Plinth</term> <note>original: "Zocco"; the solid, flat square block at the very bottom</note>, and one to its <term>Torus</term> <note>original: "Bastoni"; the rounded, convex moldings</note> along with its <term>Cyma</term> <note>original: "Gola"; literally "throat," an S-shaped molding</note>.

The base of the column can be made in the <term>Attic</term> <note>a classical base composed of two large rounded moldings separated by a hollow groove</note> style, as in the Corinthian, and can also be made as a composite of the Attic and the <term>Ionic</term> style, as shown in the drawing.

The <term>Profile</term> <note>original: "Sacoma"; a cross-section or template of the moldings</note> of the arch <term>Impost</term> <note>the structural molding on a pier from which an arch springs</note> is located next to the surface of the pedestal: and its height is equal to the thickness of the <term>Small Member</term> <note>original: "Membretto"; refers to the narrow vertical element or pilaster-strip that frames the archway</note>.

<meta>Considerable bleed-through from the preceding page is visible, particularly at the top and bottom. A line of text at the bottom of the block is extremely faint as it overlaps with the border of the illustration.</meta>

The ***Composite*** Capital has those same measurements that the ***Corinthian*** has: but it differs from that one in its ***Volute*** <note>a spiral, scroll-like ornament</note>, ***Ovolo*** <note>a convex molding, often decorated with an egg-and-dart pattern</note>, and ***Bead-and-Reel***; which are members attributed to the ***Ionic***; and the method of making it is this. From the ***Abacus*** <note>the flat slab forming the top of a capital</note> downwards, the capital is divided into three parts, as in the ***Corinthian***. The first part is given to the first leaf, the second to the second leaf, and the third to the ***Volute***; which is made in that same manner, and with those same points, with which it was said that the ***Ionic*** is made; and it occupies as much of the ***Abacus*** as is necessary so that it appears to grow out of the ***Ovolo*** near the flower, which is placed in the middle of the curvature of the said ***Abacus***: and it is as thick at the front as the curvature made upon the corners of the abacus, or slightly more. The ***Ovolo*** is three parts thick out of the five parts of the ***Abacus***: its lower part begins level with the lower part of the eye of the ***Volute***: it has a projection of three parts out of the four of its height: and its projection comes level with the curvature of the ***Abacus***, or slightly further out. The ***Bead-and-Reel*** <note>original: "Fusarolo"</note> is one-third the height of the ***Ovolo***, and has a projection slightly more than half of its thickness, and circles around the capital under the ***Volute***, and is always visible. The ***Fillet*** <note>original: "Gradetto"</note>, which goes under the ***Bead-and-Reel*** and forms the rim of the bell of the Capital, is half the size of the ***Bead-and-Reel***. The solid face of the bell aligns with the depth of the channels <note>fluting</note> of the column. I have seen one of this sort in Rome, from which I have taken these measurements, because it seemed to me very beautiful and extremely well-conceived. One also sees capitals made in other ways that can be called ***Composite***: of which more will be said, and the figures will be placed in my books of antiquities. The ***Architrave***, the ***Frieze***, and the ***Cornice*** are one-fifth of the height of the column, and according to what has been said above in the <unclear>other orders, and as</unclear> can be clearly recognized in the drawing by their proportions.

The ***Composite Capital*** is of no other measure than the ***Corinthian***: its ***abacus*** <note>the flat slab forming the top of a capital</note> is of that same shape and size: but its upper members are like those of the ***Ionic***; and the head of the Capital is in everything similar to that of the ***Corinthian***; thus the method of drawing it should be taken from there: and its height is one ***module*** <note>the standard unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually the radius or diameter of the column shaft at its base</note> and a half. It is divided into three parts: the first is for the first leaves; the second for the second leaves; and the third for the other parts; which is entirely similar to the head of the ***Corinthian***, except that the ***volutes*** <note>spiral, scroll-like ornaments</note> are larger and similar to those of the ***Ionic***; and its face is entirely flat, and the eye of the ***Volute*** <note>the circular center of the spiral</note> is on the line of the bottom of the column channels <note>the fluting or grooves carved into the column shaft</note>. The flat surface of this ***abacus*** is as thick as the ***module*** at the front, as is the shaft: and the upper shaft is a little more than half the eye of the ***Volute***: and these parts of its height are marked with numbers. The other carvings that are on the outside and continue around the capital are ***Volutes***, and they are marked like the others, except that these wrap around the ***bell*** <note>original: "campana"; the core of the capital around which the acanthus leaves are arranged</note> of the capital: and to be similar to the ***Ionic***, the line of the column channels corresponds to the inside of the bottom of the ***Volute*** channel: and the eye of the ***Volute*** is seen from the front, which I have derived from these measurements because it seemed to me to be the most beautiful that is seen in ***Rome***. And if there are also capitals made in other ways, which are shown in the figures in my books of antiquities, etc., those should be followed, according to the use of the beauty of the column, and their height and width shall be set, etc.

<summary>This page describes the proportions of the Composite capital, explaining how it blends the height and foliage of the Corinthian order with the larger volutes of the Ionic order. The author, Sebastiano Serlio, bases these specific measurements on the most beautiful examples he observed in Rome.</summary>
<keywords>Composite order, capital, abacus, volute, module, acanthus leaves, architectural proportions, Rome, Sebastiano Serlio, classical orders</keywords>

# ON PEDESTALS. Chapter XIX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'F' featuring a seated figure in a classical landscape with ruins.</image-desc>
Until now I have said as much as seemed necessary regarding simple walls and their ornaments, and touched particularly on the ***Pedestals*** <note>the support or base upon which a column stands</note> that can be assigned to each order. But because it appears that the ancients did not follow a strict rule of making a ***Pedestal*** of one size for one order more than another—and nonetheless this member greatly increases beauty and ornament when it is made with reason and in proportion to the other parts—so that one may have perfect knowledge of them and the Architect may use them according to the occasion, it should be known that they sometimes made them square; that is, as long as they were wide, as in the ***Arch of the Lions*** in Verona: and these I have given to the ***Doric*** order, because its solidity requires it. Sometimes they made them by taking the measurement from the opening of the voids <note>the "light" or clear width of an archway</note>, as in the ***Arch of Titus*** at ***Santa Maria Nova*** in Rome, and in that of ***Trajan*** at the port of Ancona: where the ***Pedestal*** is half the height of the opening of the ***Arch***: and such types of pedestals I have placed in the ***Ionic*** order. And sometimes they took the measurement from the height of the column, as is seen at Susa, a city located at the foot of the mountains that divide Italy from France, in an ***Arch*** made in honor of ***Augustus Caesar***; and in the ***Arch of Pola***, a city of Dalmatia; and in the ***Amphitheater of Rome*** <note>the Colosseum</note>, in the ***Ionic*** and ***Corinthian*** orders, in which buildings the pedestal is a fourth part of the height of the columns, as I have done in the ***Corinthian*** order. In Verona, in the ***Arch of Castel Vecchio***, which is very beautiful, the pedestal is a third of the height of the columns, as I have placed in the ***Composite*** order. And these are very beautiful forms of ***Pedestals***, and they have a beautiful proportion to the other parts. And when ***Vitruvius*** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura'</note> in the sixth book, speaking of ***Theaters***, makes mention of the ***poggio*** <note>podium</note>, it should be known that the ***poggio*** is the same as the pedestal, which is a third of the length of the columns placed as ornament for the scene. But of the pedestals that exceed a third of the column, one sees them in Rome in the ***Arch of Constantine***, where the pedestals are two and a half parts of the height of the columns <note>original: "per le due parti e meza"; this refers to a ratio where the pedestal is 2.5 parts relative to the column's total height divisions</note>. And in almost all ancient pedestals, one sees that it was observed to make the base twice as thick as the ***Cymatium*** <note>the molding at the very top of the pedestal</note>, as will be seen in my book on ***Arches***.

# ON ABUSES. Chapter XX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' featuring a seated figure, likely an architect or scholar, holding a compass and looking at a landscape with buildings.</image-desc>
Having set down the ornaments of Architecture—that is, the five orders—and taught how they should be made, and provided the profiles <note>original: "sagome"; the sectional outlines of moldings</note> of each of their parts as I have found the ancients observed them, it does not seem out of place here to warn the Reader of many abuses which, having been introduced by the Barbarians, are still observed; so that students of this art may guard against them in their own works and recognize them in the works of others. I say, then, that since Architecture (as are also all other arts) is an imitator of Nature, it suffers nothing that is foreign or distant from that which Nature herself allows. Whence we see that those ancient Architects, who began to make out of stone those Buildings that were once made of wood, established that columns should be less thick at their top than at the bottom, taking the example from trees, which are all thinner at the top than in the trunk and near the roots. Likewise, because it is very fitting that those things upon which a great load is placed should appear to be squeezed <note>original: "schizzino"; referring to the visual spreading or compression of a base under weight</note>, they placed bases under the columns, which with those rings and hollows <note>the torus and cavetto moldings</note> seem to be squeezed by the weight placed above them. So also in the cornices they introduced ***Triglyphs***, ***Modillions***, and ***Dentils*** <note>decorative rhythmic blocks in a classical cornice</note>, which represent the ends of those beams that are placed in ceilings and for the support of roofs. The same will be recognized in every other part if one gives it consideration. This being so, one cannot but blame that manner of building which, departing from what the Nature of things teaches us and from that simplicity which is seen in the things created by her, makes itself almost into another nature and departs from the true, good, and beautiful way of building. For this reason, one should not, instead of columns or pillars that have to take up some weight, place scrolls <note>original: "cartelle" or "cartocci"; decorative scroll-like brackets or cartouches</note>, which to the learned are a very ugly sight, and to those who do not understand them bring confusion rather than pleasure, nor do they produce any other effect than to increase the expense for the builders. Likewise, one should not have any of these scrolls spring out from the cornices; for since it is necessary that all parts of the cornice be made for some purpose, and be as indicators of what would be seen if the work were made of wood; and besides this, being fitting that to support a load, a thing is required...

<meta>catchword: thing</meta>

<summary>Palladio discusses the varying proportions of pedestals in ancient Roman architecture and introduces a critique of 'abuses,' arguing that architectural forms must logically imitate natural structures and wooden origins.</summary>
<keywords>pedestals, classical orders, Vitruvius, architectural theory, imitation of nature, cartouches, moldings, Roman arches, Verona, Rome</keywords>

--- Page 56 ---
<meta>This page continues Palladio's critique of architectural "abuses" or errors in judgment, specifically focusing on structural logic and the misuse of decorative elements, before transitioning into Chapter XXI regarding the layout and proportions of rooms within a house.</meta>

<page-num>52</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

something hard and capable of resisting weight; there is no doubt that these such ***cartouches*** <note>original: *cartocci*; decorative scroll-like brackets or corbels</note> are not entirely superfluous, because it is impossible that any beam or wood could produce the effect they represent: and being fashioned to look tender and soft, I do not know by what reason they can be placed under something hard and heavy.
But that which, in my opinion, matters greatly, is the abuse of making the ***pediments*** <note>original: *frontespici*; the triangular or curved gables above doors and windows</note> of doors, windows, and loggias broken in the middle; seeing as they are made to signify and indicate the shedding of rain from the buildings—which the first builders, taught by necessity itself, made peaked in the middle. I do not know what could be more contrary to natural reason than to break that part which is intended to defend the inhabitants and those entering the house from rain, snow, and hail. And although variety and new things should please everyone, one must not, however, do this against the precepts of art and against what reason shows us. Hence we see that even the Ancients varied their designs, yet they never departed from certain universal and necessary rules of Art, as will be seen in my books on Antiquity. Regarding also the projections of ***cornices*** <note>the decorative trim at the top of a wall or above a window</note> and other ornaments, it is no small abuse to make them project very far out; because when they exceed what is reasonably appropriate for them—besides the fact that if they are in an enclosed space, they make it narrow and awkward—they strike fear into those who stand beneath them, because they always threaten to fall. No less should one avoid making cornices that have no proportion to the columns; for if large cornices are placed upon small columns, or small cornices upon large columns, who can doubt that such a building must result in a most ugly appearance? In addition to this, the practice of faking ***broken columns*** by placing certain rings and garlands around them to make them appear held together and firm should be avoided as much as possible; because the more whole and strong the columns appear, the better they seem to achieve the effect for which they are placed, which is to make the work above secure and stable. Many other similar abuses I could relate, such as certain members in the cornices being made without proportion to the others, which, by what I have shown above and by those already mentioned, will be easily recognized. It remains now to come to the arrangement of the particular and principal places of the buildings.

---

### OF LOGGIAS, ENTRIES, HALLS,
### and rooms: and of their form. Chap. XXI.

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure amidst foliage and classical elements.</image-desc>

***Loggias*** <note>open-air galleries or porches supported by columns</note> are usually made mostly on the front and back faces of the house: and they are made in the middle, if making only one, or at the sides, if making two. These loggias serve many conveniences, such as for walking, eating, and other recreations: and they are made larger or smaller as the size and convenience of the building requires; but for the most part, they should not be made less than ten feet wide, nor more than twenty. Besides this, all well-ordered houses have certain places in the middle and in their most beautiful part, into which all the others correspond and open. These, on the lower floor, are commonly called ***entries*** <note>original: *entrate*; vestibules or entrance halls</note>, and on the upper floor, ***Halls*** <note>original: *Sale*; grand reception rooms</note>. They are like public places, and the entries serve as a place where those who wait for the master to come out of the house may stay to greet him and conduct business with him; and they are the first part (beyond the loggias) offered to one entering the house. The Halls serve for feasts, banquets, sets for performing plays, weddings, and similar entertainments: and therefore these places must be much larger than the others, and have that form which is most capacious, so that many people may comfortably stay there and see what is being done. I am accustomed not to exceed two squares in the length of the Halls, measured by the width; but the closer they approach a square, the more praiseworthy and convenient they will be.

The ***Rooms*** <note>original: *Stanze*</note> must be divided on both sides of the entry and the Hall; and one must take care that those on the right side correspond and are equal to those on the left, so that the building is the same in one part as in the other, and the walls feel the load of the roof equally. Because if large rooms are made on one side and small ones on the other, the latter will be more capable of resisting the weight due to the thickness of the walls, and the former will be weaker; from which, in time, very great inconveniences will arise to the ruin of the whole work. The most beautiful and proportionate manners of rooms, and those that turn out best, are seven: for they are either made round (though these rarely); or square; or their length will be the diagonal line of the square of the width; or a square and a third; or a square and a half; or a square and two-thirds; or two squares.

### ON FLOORS AND CEILINGS. Cap. XXII.

HAVING seen the forms of Loggias, Halls, and rooms, it is appropriate to speak of their **Floors** and **Ceilings**. Floors are usually made either of ***terrazzo*** <note>original: *terrazzo*; a flooring material made of stone chips set in lime, common in Venice</note>, as is the custom in Venice, or of fired stones <note>original: *pietre cotte*; likely terracotta tiles or bricks</note>, or of natural stones. Those *terrazzi* are excellent which are made of crushed tiles and fine gravel, mixed with lime made from river pebbles or from Padua, and are well beaten; they should be made in the Spring or Summer so that they may dry well. Floors of fired stones—because the stones can be made in different shapes and colors due to the diversity of the clays—will turn out very beautiful and pleasing to the eye because of the variety of colors. Those made of natural stone are very rarely used in rooms, because in the Winter they become extremely cold; however, in Loggias and public places they serve very well. One should take care that rooms located one behind the other all have the same floor level, so that not even the **thresholds** <note>original: *sottolimitari*</note> of the doors are higher than the rest of the floor plane. And if some small chamber does not reach that height, a ***mezzanine*** <note>original: *mezato*; a low-ceilinged intermediate floor</note> or a false ceiling should be constructed above it. Ceilings are also made in different ways; many delight in having them with beautiful and well-worked beams. Here one must note that these beams should be distant from one another by one and a half times the thickness of a beam. In this way, the ceilings appear beautiful to the eye, and enough wall remains between the heads of the beams to support the wall above. But if they are placed further apart, they will not look good; and if they are closer, it will almost create a division between the wall above and the wall below, so that if the beams rot or burn, the upper wall will be forced to collapse. Others prefer compartments of stucco or wood in which paintings are placed; thus they are adorned according to various inventions. Therefore, no certain and determined rule can be given in this matter.

### ON THE HEIGHT OF ROOMS. Cap. XXIII.

Rooms are made either with a ***vault*** <note>original: *volto*</note> or with a flat ceiling <note>original: *solaro*</note>. If with a flat ceiling: the height from the floor to the beams will be equal to their width, and the rooms above will be one-sixth less in height than those below. If vaulted (as those of the first order <note>the ground floor or main floor</note> are usually made, because they turn out more beautiful and are less exposed to fire), the heights of the vaults in square rooms will be the width of the room plus one-third. But in rooms longer than they are wide, it will be necessary to find the height from the length and width so that they have a proportional relationship. This height will be found by placing the width next to the length and dividing the total into two equal parts; for one of those halves will be the height of the vault. For example, let *b, c* be the place to be vaulted: add the width *a, c* to the length *a, b*, and make the line *c, b*, which is divided into two equal parts at point *f*. We shall say *f, b* is the height we seek. Or, let the room to be vaulted be 12 feet long and 6 wide; adding 6 to 12 results in 18, half of which is nine; therefore, the vault should be nine feet high.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram illustrating the first geometric method for determining the height of a vault. A room is shown in section with an arched ceiling. Above the room, a construction line is marked with points a, f, and b, demonstrating how the average of the length and width (the midpoint f) determines the proportional height of the vault.</image-desc>

Another height may also be found that will be in proportion to the length and width of the room in this manner. Given the place to be vaulted *c, b*: we will add the width to the length and make the line *b, f*; then we will divide it into two equal parts at point *e*. Using that point as the center, we will make the semi-circle *b, g, f*, and extend *a, c* until it touches the circumference at point *g*; then *a, g* will be the height of the vault of *c, b*. In numbers, it will be found in this way: knowing how many feet wide and how many feet long the room is, we will find a number that has the same proportion to the width as the length has to it. We will find it by multiplying the smaller extreme by the larger; the square root of what results from said multiplication will be the height we seek. For example, if the place we want to vault is 9 feet long and 4 wide, the height of the vault will be six feet; and that proportion which 9 has to 6, 6 also has to 4—that is, the ***sesquialtera*** <note>original: *sesquialtera*; a ratio of 3:2 where the larger number contains the smaller plus its half</note>. But it should be noted that it will not always be possible to find this height using numbers.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram showing a second geometric construction for vault height based on proportional means. A semi-circle is drawn with center 'e' on a base line extending from 'b' to 'f'. A vertical line segment 'ag' rises from the base to intersect the arc at point 'g'. The height 'ag' represents the geometric mean between the length and width of the room.</image-desc>

<meta>catchword: It can [Si può]</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of calculating room heights. Having established the arithmetic mean (the first method) on the previous page, Palladio now introduces a second method (the harmonic mean) to determine a lower, yet still proportional, height for a room's vault.</meta>

<page-num>54</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

Another height can also be found, which will be lower, but nonetheless proportionate to the room, in this manner. Having drawn the lines a-b, a-c, c-d, and b-d—which show the width and length of the room—one finds the height as in the first method <note>The arithmetic mean described on the previous page</note>, which will be c-e. This is then added to a-c; then the line e-d-f is made, and a-b is extended until b touches the line e-d-f at point f. The height of the vault will then be the line b-f. But this can also be found using numbers in this manner. Having found the height according to the first method from the length and width of the room—which, following the example used above, is 9—one places the length, width, and height as shown in the figure. Then, multiply the 9 by the 12 and by the 6. Place the result of the 12 [108] under the 12, and the result of the 6 [54] under the 6. Next, multiply the 6 by the 12, and place the result under the 9; this makes 72. Then, find a number which, when multiplied by 9, reaches the sum of 72—which in our case would be 8. We would then say that 8 feet is the height of the vault.

| 12 | 9 | 6 |
|---|---|---|
| 108 | 72 | 54 |
| | 8 | |

These heights relate to one another in such a way that the first is greater than the second, and the second is greater than the third <note>Palladio is describing the three architectural "means": Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic. Each provides a different aesthetic "weight" to a room.</note>. However, we shall make use of each of these heights according to what works best to ensure that several rooms of different sizes have vaults of equal height, and yet said vaults remain proportionate to them. From this, there results both beauty for the eye and convenience for the floor or pavement that will go above them, because it will all come out level. There are also other heights for vaults which do not fall under a specific rule, and the Architect must make use of these according to his own judgment and according to necessity.

### OF THE TYPES OF VAULTS. Cap. XXIIII.

There are six types of vaults: namely, the <term>cross vault</term> <note>original: *crociera*; formed by the intersection of two barrel vaults</note>, the <term>barrel vault</term> <note>original: *fascia*; a simple continuous arched ceiling</note>, the <term>segmental vault</term> <note>original: *remenato*; vaults that are a portion of a circle but do not reach a full <term>semicircle</term></note>, round vaults, <term>lunette</term> vaults <note>original: *lunette*; small vaults intersecting a larger one, often containing windows</note>, and <term>conch</term> vaults <note>original: *conca*; often used for apses or niches</note>. These have a <term>rise</term> <note>original: *frezza*; the vertical distance between the base and the highest point of the arch</note> equal to one-third of the room's width. These last two types were discovered by the Moderns; the first four were also used by the Ancients. Round vaults are made in square rooms, and the method of making them is as follows: in the corners of the room, one leaves certain <term>squinches</term> <note>original: *smuffi*; diagonal masonry structures that support a dome over a square room</note> that take up the half-round of the vault; this vault becomes a segmental vault in the middle, and the closer it gets to the corners, the more rounded it becomes. There is one of this sort in Rome in the <term>Baths of Titus</term> <note>original: *Terme di Tito*; the 1st-century Roman public baths</note>, and when I saw it, it was partially ruined. I have placed below the figures of all these types applied to the shapes of rooms.

FIRST BOOK

# ON THE MEASUREMENTS OF DOORS AND WINDOWS. Chapter XXV.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' with foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

**There can be no certain and fixed rule** regarding the heights and widths of the principal doors of buildings, nor for the doors and windows of individual rooms. This is because, in making the principal doors, the Architect must adapt to the size of the building, the status of the owner, and the types of things that must be led or carried through them. It seems to me appropriate to divide the space from the floor to the surface of the ceiling beams into three and a half parts <note>original: "tre parti, e meza"</note> (as Vitruvius says in Book IV, Chapter 6). Of these, two parts should be given to the height of the clear opening <note>The "clear opening" or "light" refers to the actual open space within the frame.</note>, and one part to its width, minus one-twelfth of the height. The ancients used to make their doors narrower at the top than at the bottom—as can be seen in a temple at Tivoli <note>Likely the Temple of the Sibyl or the Temple of Vesta, famous for its tapered "Tuscan" doors.</note> and as Vitruvius teaches us—perhaps for greater structural strength. The location for the principal doors should be chosen so that one may easily travel to them from the entire house.

The doors of the rooms should not be made wider than three feet and six and a half feet high; nor less than two feet in width and five in height. In making the windows, one must take care that they take in neither more nor less light than is needed, and that they are neither more sparse nor more frequent than necessity requires. Therefore, great regard must be had for the size of the rooms that must receive light from them. For it is manifest that a large room needs much more light to be bright and clear than a small one. If the windows are made smaller or fewer than is appropriate, they will make the places dark; if they exceed in size, they will make them almost uninhabitable, because the air will bring in both cold and heat. This will make those places extremely hot or cold depending on the seasons, unless the "reason of the heavens" <note>The orientation of the building relative to the sun and prevailing winds.</note> to which they face provides some relief.

For this reason, windows should not be wider than one-fourth of the width of the rooms, nor narrower than one-fifth. They should be made two squares high, plus one-sixth of their width. And because in houses there are large, medium, and small rooms, and yet the windows must all be equal within the same row or floor <note>original: "ordine, ò solaro"</note>, I find it very helpful to take the measurement of said windows from those rooms where the length is two-thirds greater than the width—that is, if the width is 18 feet, the length is 30. I divide the width into four and a half parts. One of these I use for the width of the window opening, and two for the height, adding one-sixth of the width; according to the size of these, I make all the windows of the other rooms.

The windows above—that is, those of the second story—must be one-sixth smaller than the length of the opening of those below; and if further windows are made even higher, they should likewise be diminished by one-sixth. The windows on the right side must correspond to those on the left, and those above must be directly over those below. Similarly, the doors should all be directly one over the other, so that **void is over void, and solid is over solid** <note>This is a fundamental rule of classical architecture to ensure that the weight of the walls is supported by the solid parts of the floor below, rather than pushing down on the empty space of a window or door.</note>. They should also align with one another so that, standing at one end of the house, one can see through to the other side; this brings beauty, a breeze in the summer, and other conveniences.

For greater strength, so that the lintels <note>original: "sopracigli, ò sopraliminari"</note> of the doors and windows are not burdened by weight, it is customary to make certain arches which are commonly called **segmental arches** <term>remenati <gloss>arches that are less than a full semicircle, used to divert weight</gloss></term>, which are of great utility for the permanence of the building. Windows should be kept away from the corners of the building, as was said above, because that part which must hold the entire structure upright and together must not be opened and weakened. The jambs <note>original: "Pilastrate, ouero Erte"</note> of the doors and windows should be no less thick than one-sixth of the width of the opening, and no more than one-fifth. It remains for us to look at their ornaments.

---

# ON THE ORNAMENTS OF DOORS AND WINDOWS. Chapter XXVI.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' with scrolling foliate designs.</image-desc>

**How the ornaments of the principal doors** of buildings ought to be made can easily be learned from what Vitruvius teaches us in Chapter 6 of Book IV, adding what the Most Reverend Barbaro <note>Daniele Barbaro (1514–1570), a scholar and patron of Palladio who published a famous commentary on Vitruvius.</note> says and shows in drawings in that place, and from what I have said and drawn above regarding all five orders. Therefore, leaving these aside, I will set down only some profiles <note>original: "sagome"</note> of the ornaments for the doors and windows of rooms, according to how they may be diversely made, and I will demonstrate how to mark each individual member so that it has grace and its proper projection. The ornaments given to doors and windows are the **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice**. The Architrave wraps around the door and must be as thick as the jambs or side-posts;

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence. The catchword "le quali" (the which) indicates the next page will continue describing the proportions or characteristics of these architectural members.</meta>

He introduces the aesthetic and practical importance of vertical alignment (void over void) and the use of relief arches to protect lintels.</summary>

which I have said should be made no less than one-sixth of the width of the clear opening <note>The "light" or clear opening refers to the empty space within the frame.</note>, and no more than one-fifth. From the width of this frame, the **Frieze** and the **Cornice** derive their own thickness. Of the two designs <note>original: "inuentioni"</note> that follow, the first—that is, the one shown above—has these measurements: The **Architrave** <term>Architrave: The primary beam or lowest part of the entablature that rests directly on the columns or door frame.</term> is divided into four parts: three of these parts determine the height of the **Frieze**, and five determine the height of the **Cornice**. The Architrave is then further divided into ten parts: three go to the first band <note>original: "fascia"</note>, four to the second; and the remaining three are divided into five: two are given to the fillet <note>original: "regolo, ouer' orlo"</note>, and the remaining three to the ogee molding <term>Intauolato: Also known as a cyma reversa, an S-shaped molding with the convex part at the top.</term>. Its projection is equal to its height; the fillet projects outward less than half of its thickness. The ogee molding is marked in this way: draw a straight line ending at the points below the fillet and above the second band; divide it in the middle, and make each of those halves the base of an equilateral triangle. Place the stationary foot of the compass on the angle opposite the base and draw the curved lines that form the said ogee. The Frieze is three-fourths the height of the Architrave and is marked with a portion of a circle smaller than a semi-circle, and its swell <note>original: "gonfiezza"</note> comes level with the molding <note>original: "cimacio"</note> of the Architrave. The five parts given to the cornice are attributed to its members in this way: one is given to the **cavetto** <term>Cavetto: A concave molding with a regular curve.</term> with its listel <note>a small flat strip</note>, which is one-fifth of the Cavetto. The cavetto projects two-thirds of its height; to mark it, form an equilateral triangle and make the center at angle C, so that the cavetto becomes the base of the triangle. Another of the said five parts is given to the **Ovolo** <term>Ovolo: A convex molding, usually egg-shaped in profile.</term>. It projects two-thirds of its height and is marked by making an equilateral triangle with the center at point H. The other three parts are divided into seventeen: eight are given to the **corona** <note>original: "gocciolatoio," literally the drip-edge</note> with its listels, of which the top one is one of those eight parts, and the bottom one—which forms the hollow of the drip-edge—is one-sixth of the ovolo. The other nine parts are given to the **cyma recta** <note>original: "Gola diritta"</note> and its fillet, which is one-third of the cyma itself. To form it so that it stands well and has grace, draw the straight line A, B, and divide it into two equal parts at point C. One of these halves is divided into seven parts; take six of them at point D, then form two triangles A, E, C and C, B, F. Place the stationary foot of the compass at points E and F and draw the circular arcs A, C and C, B, which form the Cyma.

Similarly, in the second design, the Architrave is divided into four parts: three form the height of the Frieze and five that of the Cornice. The Architrave is then divided into three parts: two of those are divided into seven, with three given to the first band and four to the second. The third part is divided into nine: two form the bead molding <note>original: "tondino"</note>; the other seven are divided into five: three make the ogee and two make the fillet. The height of the cornice is divided into five and three-quarter parts: one of these is divided into six parts; five make the ogee above the frieze, and one makes the listel. The ogee projects as much as its height, as does the listel. Another part is given to the ovolo, which projects three-fourths of its height. The small step <note>original: "gradetto"</note> above the ovolo is one-sixth of the ovolo and has the same projection. The other three parts are divided into seventeen, and eight of those are given to the **Corona**: which projects four-thirds of its height. The other nine are divided into four: three are given to the **Cyma**, and one to the fillet. The remaining three-quarters are divided into five and a half parts: one makes the small step, and four and a half make its ogee above the Corona. This cornice projects outward as much as its thickness.

...portion of a circle whose center is found by constructing an equilateral triangle <note>original: "triangolo di tre lati vguali," a triangle with three equal sides.</note> using the height of the frieze as the base; the third point of the triangle provides the center where the foot of the compass is placed to draw the curve. <note>This describes the "pulvinated frieze," a decorative element that bulges outward in a convex shape, common in the Ionic and Composite orders of architecture.</note>

The **Cornice**, which I have stated should be five parts of the height of the Architrave, is divided into six equal portions.
*   The first portion is divided into four parts: one is for the **listello** <term>a small, flat, ribbon-like molding</term>, and the other three are for the **cyma reversa** <term>an S-shaped molding that curves outward at the top</term>.
*   The second portion is designated for the **dentils** <term>a series of small, rectangular blocks resembling teeth</term>.
*   The third portion is divided into four parts: one for the **listello** and three for the **ovolo** <term>a convex molding with a profile like a quarter-section of an egg</term>.
*   The fourth portion is for the **corona** <note>original: "gocciolatoio," literally "the dripper."</note> <term>the flat, vertical face of the cornice that projects out to shed rainwater</term>.
*   The fifth and sixth portions together are divided into five parts: one is for the **listello** and the remaining four are for the **cyma recta** <term>a double-curved molding that is concave at the top and convex at the bottom</term>.

<margin>The total projection of the cornice must be equal to its total height.</margin>

The projection of the entire **Cornice** is made equal to its height. To determine the correct projection of each individual member <note>In this context, a "member" is any single molding or part of the architectural whole.</note>, one uses the geometric method shown in the diagram. A square is formed where point **A** represents the outer upper corner and point **B** the inner lower corner. By drawing the diagonal line **AB** and finding the intersection at point **D**, the architect can ensure that every molding projects forward in the correct mathematical proportion to its height.

Of these two other designs, the **Architrave** of the first—which is marked **F**—is similarly divided into four parts: three and one-quarter of these parts form the height of the **Frieze**, and five parts form the height of the **Cornice**. The **Architrave** is divided into eight parts: five are assigned to the face <note>original: "piano," the flat vertical surface of the molding.</note>, and three to the **cymatium** <term>the crowning molding of an architrave</term>. This cymatium is further divided into eight parts: three are given to the **intavolato** <term>a specific molding, often a cyma or waved profile</term>, three to the **cavetto** <term>a concave, hollow molding</term>, and two to the **fillet** <note>original: "orlo," the narrow flat band at the very top.</note>. The height of the **Cornice** is partitioned into six parts: two form the **cyma recta** <term>an S-shaped molding that is concave at the top and convex at the bottom</term> with its fillet, and one forms the **intavolato**. This **cyma** is then divided into nine parts: eight of those form the **corona** <note>original: "gocciolatoio," or drip-edge.</note> and the **fillet** <note>original: "gradetto," a small step or molding.</note>. The **astragal** <term>a small semi-circular molding</term> or **roundel** above the **Frieze** takes up one-third of one of the aforementioned six parts, and whatever remains between the **corona** and the **roundel** is left for the **cavetto**.

In the other design, the **Architrave** marked **H** is divided into four parts: three and a half parts form the height of the **frieze**, and five parts form the height of the **cornice**. The **Architrave** is divided into eight parts; five go to the face and three to the **cymatium**. The **cymatium** is divided into seven parts: one forms the **astragal**, and the remainder is divided again into eight parts; three are given to the **cyma reversa** <term>an S-shaped molding that is convex at the top and concave at the bottom</term>, three to the **cavetto**, and two to the **fillet**. The height of the **cornice** is divided into six and three-quarter parts. Three parts are used for the **intavolato**, the **dentils** <term>small rectangular blocks used as decoration</term>, and the **ovolo** <term>a convex molding shaped like an egg</term>. The **intavolato** projects out as much as it is thick; the **dentils** take up two of the three parts of their height; and the **ovolo** takes up three of the four parts. Of the remaining three-quarters of a part, the **intavolato** is made between the **cyma** and the **corona**; and the other three parts are divided into seventeen: nine make the **cyma** and the **fillet**, and eight make the **corona**. This **Cornice** comes to have a projection <note>original: "sporto."</note> equal to its thickness, just like those mentioned above.

# BOOK OF CHIMNEYS, Chapter XXVII.

THE Ancients used to heat their rooms in this way. They made the chimneys in the middle with columns, or <term>modillions</term> <note>ornamental brackets</note>, which supported the <term>architraves</term>; above which was the pyramid <note>the hood</note> of the chimney, from where the smoke exited, as one could be seen at Baia near the Pool of Nero; and one not very far from Civitavecchia. And when they did not want chimneys, they made within the thickness of the wall some pipes, or tubes, through which the heat of the fire, which was beneath those rooms, rose up and exited through certain vents or mouths made at the top of those pipes.

In almost the same way, the Trento gentlemen of Vicenza at their villa in Costoza refresh their rooms in the Summer. For within the mountains of said villa are some very large caves, which the inhabitants of those places call *couali*, and were anciently <term>quarries</term>, which I believe <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the famous Roman author of 'De architectura'</note> means when, in the second book where he treats of stones, he says that in the Treviso Marches a kind of stone is quarried that is cut with a saw, like wood. In these caves certain very cool winds are born; these Gentlemen, through certain subterranean vaults which they call <term>wind-ducts</term> <note>original: "Ventidotti"</note>, lead them to their houses, and with pipes similar to those mentioned above, they then conduct that cool wind through all the rooms, closing and opening them at their pleasure to take more or less cool air according to the seasons. And although this place is marvelous for this great convenience, it is rendered much more worthy of being enjoyed and seen by the "Prison of the Winds," which is a subterranean room made by the Most Excellent Signor Francesco Trento, and called by him **AEOLIA** <note>named after Aeolia, the mythical home of the winds</note>; where many of the said wind-ducts empty. To ensure it is ornate, beautiful, and consistent with the name, he has spared neither diligence nor any expense.

But returning to chimneys: we make them within the thickness of the walls and raise their flues until they are outside the roof, so that they carry the smoke into the air. Here it must be noted that the flues should be made neither too wide nor too narrow; because if they are made wide, the air wandering through them will drive the smoke downward and not let it ascend and exit freely; and in those that are too narrow, the smoke, not having a free exit, will become choked and turn back. Therefore, in chimneys for rooms, the flues shall be made no less wide than half a foot, and no more than nine inches, and two and a half feet long; and the mouth of the pyramid where it joins the flue shall be made somewhat narrower, so that if the smoke returns downward, it finds that impediment and cannot enter the room. Some make the flues curved, so that through that tortuosity and the fire that pushes it upward, the smoke cannot turn back. The chimney-pots—that is, the holes through which the smoke must exit—must be wide and far from any material liable to catch fire. The <term>mantels</term> <note>original: "Nappe"</note>, above which the pyramid of the chimney is made, must be worked very delicately, and entirely far from the <term>Rustic</term> style; because rustic work is not suitable except for very large buildings for the reasons already stated.

# OF STAIRS, AND VARIOUS MANNERS OF THEM,
->and of the number and size of steps. Chapter XXVIII.<-

GREAT care must be taken in the placement of stairs; for it is no small difficulty to find a site that suits them and does not impede the rest of the building. Therefore, a proper place shall be assigned to them principally so that they do not obstruct other areas, nor are they obstructed by them. Three openings are required in stairs: the first is the door through which one ascends the stairs, which is more to be praised the less it is hidden from those entering the house; and it will please me much if it is in a place where, before reaching it, one sees the most beautiful part of the house, because even if the house were small, it will appear very large; but let it nonetheless be manifest and easy to find. The second opening is the windows, which are necessary to give light to the steps; they should be in the middle and high up, so that the light spreads equally everywhere. The third is the opening through which one enters the floor above. This must lead us into ample, beautiful, and ornate places.

Stairs will be praiseworthy if they are bright, ample, and comfortable for climbing, so that they almost invite people to ascend. They will be bright if they have clear light and if, as I have said, the light spreads equally everywhere. They will be ample enough if they do not seem narrow and cramped in relation to the size and quality of the building; but they shall never be made less than four feet wide, so that if two people meet on them, they can comfortably give way to each other. They will be comfortable for the whole building if the arches beneath them can

P R I M O. 61

serve to store some necessary things: and as for men, so long as their access is not difficult and steep. Therefore, their length shall be made double the height. The steps <note>original: "i gradi"</note> should not be made higher than six inches <note>The Venetian inch was slightly different from the modern English inch, but the proportions remain standard for the era.</note> of a foot, and if they are made lower, especially in continuous and long staircases, they will make them easier: because in climbing, the foot will tire less; but they shall never be made less than four inches high. The width of the steps must not be made less than one foot, nor more than one foot and a half. The Ancients observed to make the steps odd in number so that, beginning to climb with the right foot, one would finish with the same: which they took as a good omen, and of greater religious significance, when they entered the Temples. Therefore, one shall not exceed the number of eleven, or thirteen at the most: and having reached this point, if one must climb higher, a level floor shall be made, which is called a **Rest** <note>original: "Requie"</note>: so that the weak and weary may find where to rest themselves: and if it happens that something falls from above, it has a place to stop. Staircases are made either straight or like a **Spiral** <note>original: "Lumaca," literally "snail."</note>. The straight ones are either extended in two branches, or square; which turn in four branches. To make these, one divides the whole space into four parts: two are given to the steps, and two to the void in the middle: from which, if it were left uncovered, the stairs would have light. They can be made with an inner wall, and then within the two parts given to the steps: that number is also enclosed; and they can also be made without it. These two methods of Stairs were discovered by the happy memory of the Magnificent Signor **Luigi Cornaro**, a Gentleman of excellent judgment, as is known from the most beautiful loggia, and from the most ornate rooms built by him for his residence in **Padua** <note>Cornaro was a celebrated writer on the "sober life" and a significant patron of architecture.</note>. Spiral stairs, which are also called **Snail-shell** <note>original: "Chiocciola"</note>; are made in some places round, and in others oval: sometimes with the column in the middle, and sometimes hollow; they are used especially in narrow places because they occupy less space than the straight ones: but they are somewhat more difficult to climb. Those that are hollow in the middle turn out very well: because they can have light from above: and those who are at the top of the Stair see all those who are climbing or beginning to climb, and similarly they are seen by them. Those that have the column in the middle are made in this way: the diameter being divided into three parts, two are left for the steps, and one is given to the column, as in drawing **A**: or the diameter will be divided into seven parts, and three will be given to the middle column, and four to the steps: and in this exact way the Stair of the **Trajan Column** <note>The famous Roman triumphal column dedicated to Emperor Trajan, featuring a spiral internal staircase.</note> is made: and if the steps were made winding, as in drawing **B**, they would be very beautiful to see, and would turn out longer than if they were made straight. But in the hollow ones, the diameter is divided into four parts: two are given to the steps, and two remain for the space in the middle. Beyond the usual manners of Stairs, one was also found in a Spiral form by the Most Illustrious Signor **Marc' Antonio Barbaro**, a Venetian Gentleman of most beautiful genius, which serves very well in very narrow places. It has no column in the middle, and the steps, being winding, turn out very long, and it is divided like the one mentioned above. The oval ones also are divided in the same way as the round ones. They are very graceful and beautiful to see: because all the windows and doors come at the head of the oval, and in the middle, and they are quite comfortable. I have made one hollow in the middle in the **Monastery of the Charity** <note>original: "Monasterio della Carità," now the Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice.</note> in Venice, which turns out admirably.

64

Another beautiful manner of **spiral staircases** <note>Original: "Scale a lumaca," literally "snail-shell stairs."</note> was once commissioned at **Chambord** <note>Original: "Sciambur." This refers to the famous Château de Chambord in the Loire Valley, France, renowned for its double-helix staircase often attributed to Leonardo da Vinci.</note>, a place in France, by the magnanimous **King Francis** <note>King Francis I of France (reigned 1515–1547), a great patron of the Renaissance.</note> for a palace he built in a forest, and it is designed in this way: there are four staircases, which have four separate entrances; that is, each has its own, and they ascend one above the other in such a way that, being placed in the center of the building, they can serve four different apartments. This allows those who live in one apartment to use their own stairs without encountering those from another. Because the center is hollow, everyone can see each other ascending and descending without causing the slightest obstruction to one another. Because this is a most beautiful and novel invention, I have included it here, marking the stairs with letters in the plan and the elevation so that one may see where they begin and how they rise.

There were also very laudable designs for spiral staircases in the **Porticoes of Pompey**, which are in Rome, used to go into the **Piazza Giudea** <note>The area of the Roman Ghetto or Jewish Quarter.</note>. Since these were placed in the middle of the structure where they could not receive light except from above, they were built upon columns so that the light might spread equally throughout. Following the example of these, **Bramante** <note>Donato Bramante (1444–1514), the first architect of St. Peter's Basilica.</note>—a most singular architect of his time—built one in the **Belvedere** <note>The Cortile del Belvedere in the Vatican.</note>. He designed it without steps <note>A ramp intended for horses and people to ascend easily.</note> and utilized the four orders of columns: namely, the **Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite**. To build such stairs, the entire space is divided into four parts: two are given to the central void, and one part on each side is given to the steps and columns.

Many other styles of staircases are seen in ancient buildings, such as **triangular** ones; of this sort are the stairs in Rome that lead above the dome of **Santa Maria Rotonda** <note>The Pantheon, which was consecrated as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres (St. Mary and the Martyrs), colloquially "the Round."</note>; these are hollow in the middle and receive light from above. Also very magnificent were those at **Santi Apostoli** in the same city, which lead up to **Monte Cavallo** <note>Now known as the Quirinal Hill, the highest of the seven hills of Rome.</note>. These were double staircases, from which many have since taken the example, and they led to a Temple situated at the top of the hill, as I show in my book on Temples. The last drawing provided here is of this type of staircase.

# THE FIRST [BOOK]

## ON ROOFS. Chapter XXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and an architectural motif within a square border.</image-desc>

**ONCE** the walls have been raised to their full height, the vaults completed, the floor timbers laid, the staircases installed, and all those things of which we have spoken above have been settled; it becomes necessary to construct the roof. Because it embraces every part of the building and presses down with its weight equally upon the walls, the roof acts as a bond for the entire work. Beyond protecting the inhabitants from rain, snow, the burning sun, and the dampness of the night, it provides no small benefit to the structure itself by casting rainwater far from the walls; for although such water may seem to do little harm, in the course of time it is the cause of the greatest damage.

The first men, as one reads in **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio was a Roman architect whose 1st-century BC treatise *De Architectura* was the "bible" for Renaissance builders like Palladio.</note>, made the roofs of their dwellings flat. However, realizing they were not defended from the rains, they were driven by necessity to begin making them gabled—that is, peaked in the middle. These peaks must be made higher or lower according to the regions where one builds. Thus, in **Germany**, because of the great quantity of snow that falls there, the roofs are made very acute <note>Meaning very steep or sharp-angled.</note> and are covered with <term>shingles <note>original: "scandole"; small flat pieces of wood used like tiles.</note></term> or very thin tiles. If they were made otherwise, they would be ruined by the heaviness of the snow. 

But we, who live in a temperate region, ought to choose that height which makes the roof graceful in appearance, beautiful in form, and allows the rain to run off easily. Therefore, one should divide the width of the space to be covered into nine parts, and two of those parts shall be the height of the <term>ridge <note>original: "colmo"; the highest horizontal point of the roof.</note></term>. If the height were made a quarter of the width, the roof would be too steep, and the <term>curved tiles <note>original: "coppi"; semi-cylindrical clay tiles common in Italy.</note></term> would stay in place with difficulty. If it were made a fifth of the width, it would be too flat, and the tiles, the boards, and the snow (when it comes) would weigh upon it too heavily.

It is customary to make <term>gutters <note>original: "gorne".</note></term> around the houses, into which the water falls from the tiles and is then cast far from the walls by means of pipes. These gutters ought to have a foot and a half of wall above them; this, besides holding them firm, will protect the roof timbers from water should the gutters fail in any part. There are various ways of arranging the roof timbers, but when the interior walls are used to support the beams, they are easily accommodated. This method pleases me greatly, because the exterior walls do not feel too much of the load, and if the end of a single beam should rot, the roof is not in immediate danger of collapse.

---

->THE END OF THE FIRST BOOK.<-
