# ON ROOFS.
### Chapter XXIX.

**NOW THAT** all the walls have reached their summit, the openings have been vaulted, the floors put into execution, and the staircases arranged; it is time to cover the building. This must be done quickly, as we have discussed elsewhere, because the weight of the roof unites the structure and presses it down. It acts almost as a bond for the entire work, protecting the inhabitants from rain, snow, the burning sun, and the humidity of the night. It brings no small benefit to the structures by casting the water that falls upon them far from the walls, so that they have less power to harm, and so the walls do not crumble over time—which would be a cause of great damage.

The first men, therefore, who made for themselves such light huts, covered their solid dwellings with a flat roof. Realizing later that this did not provide order against the rains, they developed roofs in the shape of a <term>donkey's back <note>original: "schiena d'asino"; a common term for a gabled or double-pitched roof.</note></term>. This is truly the case: either they are made of two planes with two slopes, or when the calculations that form the roofs are taken in four parts by <term>plumb-line <note>original: "scandaglio"; a measurement of verticality or depth.</note></term>, taking half of the span that will be there. From this come the roofs which rise higher in height, such as those made of <term>shingles <note>original: "scandolo" (OCR error for *scandola*); small wooden tiles.</note></term>, which consist of a single face of wood, or a single <term>slope <note>original: "falda"; the inclined surface of a roof.</note></term>, which is excellent for the whole building. Or perhaps a single flat roof for the chimneys to the air, not like those on donkey-back roofs, nor those at an angle, which serve for public places, streets, planes, or slopes.

Therefore, the height of the <term>ridge <note>original: "culmine"; the highest point or peak of the roof.</note></term> and the width of the space must be managed so that the rafters of the roofs are exactly half the space; for these roofs, one makes the height a quarter of the width. One cannot do more for the whole, just as for <term>curved tiles <note>original: "coppa"; likely referring to *coppi*, the traditional clay tiles used in Italy.</note></term> they shall be made a third of the width. For the fifth parts, a double of the plane, where the tiles and further roofs come to join the mass of the walls. One places around it a sixth of the plane, so that the rains and the waters, wherever they fall, are cast far from the walls. These are also called the "leaves" or eaves of the roofs, which fold halfway to the wall, and which with their projection defend the building from the "tears" or runoff of the cover. Furthermore, in some other facade of the order, there are various ways of binding the design of the covering, as we shall show again. The rafters of their roofs are transported and arranged into one; the limits of the fiber move, and not only do they have much load, but through moderation in the space of some place, one could not cover it better.

---

->THE END OF THE FIRST BOOK.<-

# THE SECOND BOOK OF ARCHITECTURE
## BY ANDREA PALLADIO.
### ON DECORUM, OR PROPRIETY, WHICH MUST BE observed in private buildings. Chapter One.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'H' set within a square frame featuring architectural elements and floral scrolls.</image-desc>
I have set forth in the previous book all those things that seemed to me most worthy of consideration for the construction of public edifices and private houses, so that the work might turn out beautiful, graceful, and lasting. I also spoke, regarding private houses, of certain matters pertaining to convenience, toward which this second book will be principally directed. For a house ought to be called convenient if it is suitable to the status of the person who is to inhabit it, and if its parts correspond to the whole and to each other. Therefore, the Architect must above all take care that (as Vitruvius says in the first and sixth books) for great Gentlemen, and especially those of a Republic, houses with loggias and spacious, decorated halls will be required, so that in such places those who wait for the master to greet him or to beg some help or favor may pass the time with pleasure. And for lesser Gentlemen, smaller buildings will be appropriate, of less expense and fewer ornaments. For Pleaders and Lawyers <note>original: "Causidici, & Auocati"</note>, it will likewise be necessary to build so that in their houses there are beautiful places to walk and decorated spaces, so that their clients may stay there without boredom. The houses of merchants shall have places where merchandise is stored, facing North and arranged in such a way that the owners need not fear thieves. Decorum <note>original: "Decoro"; in classical architecture, this refers to the suitability of a building's style to its function and the status of its owner.</note> shall also be preserved regarding the workmanship if the parts correspond to the whole, so that in large buildings there are large members; in small ones, small; and in mediocre ones, mediocre. For it would certainly be a structural and unseemly thing if in a very large building there were small halls and rooms, and on the contrary, in a small one, there were two or three rooms that occupied the whole. One must therefore (as I have said), as much as possible, have regard both for those who wish to build, and not so much for what they are able to do, as for what quality of building is suitable for them. Once the choice has been made, the parts shall be arranged in a way that they suit the whole and each other, and those ornaments that appear fitting shall be applied. But many times the Architect must accommodate himself more to the will of those who pay the expense than to that which ought to be observed.

---

### ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF ROOMS, and of other places. Chapter Two.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring a seated figure in a landscape with foliage and a circular architectural element in the background.</image-desc>
In order that houses may be convenient for the use of the family—without which convenience they would be worthy of the greatest blame, far from being praised—one must take great care not only regarding the principal parts, such as the loggias, halls, courtyards, magnificent rooms, and wide, bright, and easy-to-climb stairs; but also that the smallest and less attractive parts are in places adapted for the service of the larger and more noble ones. For just as in the human body there are some noble and beautiful parts, and some rather ignoble and ugly ones, and yet we see that the former have a great need for the latter and could not exist without them; so too in buildings there must be some parts that are remarkable and honored, and some less elegant, without which the aforementioned could not remain free, and thus would lose part of their dignity and beauty. But just as Blessed God has ordered our members so that the most beautiful are in places more exposed to being seen, and the less honorable in hidden places; so too in building, we shall place the principal and remarkable parts in open places, and the less beautiful in places as hidden from our eyes as possible; because in those will be placed all the ugliness of the house, and all those things that might cause hindrance or in part make the most beautiful parts appear ugly. Therefore, I recommend that in the lowest part of the building, which I make somewhat underground, there should be arranged the cellars, the wood stores, the pantries, the kitchens, the servants' dining rooms <note>original: "tinelli"</note>, the places for laundry <note>original: "liscia, o bucata"</note>, the ovens, and other similar things necessary for daily use. From this, two conveniences are derived: one, that the upper part remains entirely free; and the other, which is no less important, is that the said upper floor becomes healthy for habitation, its floor being far

<summary>Palladio introduces the concept of architectural decorum and convenience, arguing that a building's design must reflect the social status of its owner. He also explains the functional necessity of hiding service areas, like kitchens and cellars, in the basement to maintain the beauty and health of the primary living quarters.</summary>

from the dampness of the earth; furthermore, by being raised, it possesses a more beautiful grace to be looked upon, and for looking out. One shall then take care in the rest of the building that there be large, medium, and small rooms: and all placed one beside the other, so that they may mutually serve each other. The small rooms shall be divided by mezzanines <note>original: "amezzeranno"; creating low-ceilinged intermediate floors between main stories</note> to carve out small chambers <note>original: "camerini"</note>, where one may place studies, or libraries, riding gear, and other bundles of which we have daily need; for it is not well that they remain in the rooms where one sleeps, eats, and receives foreigners. It also pertains to convenience that the rooms for the summer be ample and spacious, and turned toward the North; and those for the winter toward the South <note>original: "Meriggie"</note> and the West <note>original: "Ponente"</note>, and be rather small than otherwise: because in the summer we seek the shade and the winds, and in the winter the sun, and small rooms will heat more easily than large ones. But those which we would wish to use in the Spring and the Autumn shall be turned toward the East, and shall look out over gardens and greenery. In this same part shall also be the studies or libraries: because they are used in the morning more than at any other time. But the large rooms with the medium ones, and these with the small ones, must be partitioned in such a manner that (as I have said elsewhere) one part of the building corresponds to the other, and thus the entire body of the edifice has within itself a certain suitability of members <note>referring to "symmetria" or the proportional relationship of parts</note> that renders it all beautiful and gracious. But because in cities almost always either the walls of neighbors, or the streets and public squares assign certain limits beyond which the Architect cannot extend; it is necessary to accommodate oneself according to the occasion of the sites: to which the plans and elevations that follow will give great light <note>meaning "clarity" or "insight"</note> (if I am not mistaken): which will serve as examples of the things said also in the past book.

# OF THE DESIGNS OF CITY HOUSES Cap. III.

I make myself certain that among those who shall see the buildings placed below, and who know how difficult a thing it is to introduce a new custom, especially in building—of which profession everyone persuades himself to know his part—I shall be held very fortunate, having found gentlemen of such noble and generous spirit, and excellent judgment, who have believed my reasons, and have departed from that aged custom of building without grace and without any beauty; and in truth I cannot but supremely thank God (as in all our actions one must do) that He has lent me so much of His favor, that I have been able to practice many of those things which I have learned with my greatest labors through the long journeys I have made, and with much of my study. And because, although some of the buildings designed are not entirely finished; one may nonetheless from what is done understand what the finished work ought to be; I have placed on each the name of the builder <note>the patron or client</note> and the place where they are, so that anyone wishing to do so may see in effect how they turn out. And in this part the reader shall be warned that in placing the said designs, I have had no respect for the ranks or the dignity of the gentlemen who shall be named: but I have placed them in the spot that came best to me: since they are all most honored. But let us come now to the buildings, of which the one placed below is in Udine, the Metropolis of Friuli, and was built from the foundations by Signor Floriano Antonini, a gentleman of that City. The first order of the facade is of rusticated work <note>original: "opera rustica"; masonry with roughened surfaces and recessed joints</note>: the columns of the facade, of the entry, and of the loggia behind are of the Ionic order. The first rooms are vaulted: the larger ones have the height of the vaults according to the first method set down above regarding the height of vaults in places longer than they are wide. The rooms above have flat ceilings <note>original: "in solaro"</note>, and are as much larger than those below as the contractions or thinnings of the walls <note>the reduction in wall thickness as the building rises</note> allow, and they have ceilings as high as they are wide. Above these, there are other rooms which can serve as a granary. The hall <note>original: "la sala"</note> reaches with its height up to the roof. The kitchen is outside the house, but nevertheless most convenient. The latrines <note>original: "i cessi"</note> are beside the stairs, and although they are within the body of the building, they do not give off any bad odor: because they are placed in locations far from the Sun, and they have some vent-holes from the bottom of the pit through the thickness of the wall, which exit at the top of the house.

The floor plan illustrates a harmonious and symmetrical arrangement for a town house. ## SECOND BOOK

In Vicenza, overlooking the square commonly called the Island <note>original: "l’Isola." This area was so named because it was surrounded by the Retrone and Bacchiglione rivers and was frequently subject to flooding.</note>; Count Valerio Chiericati, a Knight and honored gentleman of that city, has built according to the design that follows. This building has a loggia <term>Loggia: a covered gallery or porch open on at least one side, supported by columns</term> in the lower part of the front which spans the entire facade. The floor of the first order <note>The "first order" refers to the ground floor level.</note> is raised five feet from the ground; this was done partly to place the cellars and other rooms intended for the convenience of the house beneath it—which would not have been successful if they had been built entirely underground, as the river is not far away—and also so that the upper orders might better enjoy the beautiful view in front. 

The larger rooms have their vaults <term>Vault: an arched ceiling made of stone, brick, or plaster</term> high according to the first method of vault heights <note>Palladio refers here to his mathematical rules for determining ceiling heights based on room dimensions, which he detailed in the First Book.</note>; the medium-sized rooms are vaulted with lunettes <term>Lunette: a crescent-shaped space or window in a vaulted ceiling</term> and have vaults as high as those of the larger rooms. The small studies <note>original: "camerini"</note> are also vaulted and are divided by mezzanines <term>Mezzanine: a low-ceilinged floor between two main stories, often used for storage or service</term>. All these vaults are decorated with most excellent stucco compartments by the hand of Master Bartolameo Ridolfi, a Veronese sculptor; and with paintings by the hand of Master Domenico Rizzo <note>Likely referring to Domenico Campagnola.</note> and Master Battista Venetiano <note>Likely referring to Battista Zelotti.</note>, men who are singular in these professions. 

The hall is located upstairs in the middle of the facade and occupies the central portion of the loggia below. Its height extends all the way to the roof; and because it projects somewhat forward, it has double columns at the corners. On either side of this hall, there are two loggias—one on each side—which have their ceilings or coffered panels <term>Lacunari: recessed panels in a ceiling, often highly decorated</term> adorned with beautiful paintings, creating a magnificent sight. The first order of the facade is **Doric**, and the second is **Ionic**.

-># SECOND BOOK<-

The drawings that follow are of the house of Count Iseppo da Porto <note>original: "Iseppo de' Porti"</note>, a most noble family of the said city [Vicenza]. This house faces onto two public streets; and therefore it has two entrances, each of which has four columns that support the vault and make the space above secure. The rooms on the first floor are vaulted <term>involto: a masonry ceiling construction, typically arched</term>. The height of those rooms which are beside the said entrances follows the final method for the height of vaults <note>Palladio is referring to the mathematical rules for vault height he established in Book I, Chapter 24</note>. The rooms of the second story—that is, the second order—have flat ceilings <term>in solaro: a ceiling supported by wooden beams or joists</term>. Both the first and second floor rooms of the part of the building already completed are decorated with beautiful paintings and stuccos by the hands of the aforementioned talented men <note>Referencing the artists mentioned on the previous page: Domenico Brusasorci, Battista Farinato, and Battista Veneziano</note>, and by Master Paolo Veronese, a most excellent painter.

The courtyard, surrounded by porticos, which is reached from the said entrances through a corridor <term>andito: a passage or hallway</term>, will have columns thirty-six and a half feet high; that is, as high as the first and second orders combined. Behind these columns there are pilasters one and three-quarter feet wide and one foot two inches thick, which will support the floor of the loggia above. This courtyard divides the whole house into two parts: the front part will serve the master and his ladies, and the rear part will be for hosting guests. Thus, the household and the guests will remain free from any mutual interference <note>original: "liberi da ogni rispetto"</note>—a consideration the ancients, and especially the Greeks, held in very high regard. Furthermore, this division will also serve in case the descendants of the aforementioned gentleman wish to have their apartments separated. I chose to place the main staircases under the portico, corresponding to the middle of the courtyard, so that those who wish to go upstairs are almost compelled to see the most beautiful parts of the building; and also so that, being in the middle, they can serve both parts. The cellars and similar service areas are underground. The stables are outside the main square of the house and have their entrance from under the stairs. Of the large-scale drawings, the first shows part of the facade, and the second shows part of the courtyard.

# SECOND [BOOK]

->### [THE RESIDENCE OF THE DALLA TORRE FAMILY]<-

The following building is located in Verona and was begun by Count Giovanni Battista dalla Torre, a gentleman of that city. Because he was overtaken by death, he was unable to finish it; however, a significant portion of it has been completed. One enters this house from the sides, where there are passageways ten feet wide. From these, one reaches the courtyards, each of which is fifty feet long, and from there, one enters an open hall. This hall features four columns to provide greater structural stability <note>original: "sicurezza"</note> for the hall located directly above it. From this hall, one enters the staircases, which are oval in shape and hollow in the center. The aforementioned courtyards are surrounded by corridors or balconies <term>Poggiuoli: raised walkways or galleries, often overlooking a courtyard</term> at the same level as the floor of the second-story rooms. The additional staircases are included for the greater convenience of the entire household. This layout <note>original: "compartimento"</note> is very successful for this particular site, which is long and narrow and faces the main street along one of its shorter facades.

# BOOK [TWO]

The drawings that follow are of a building in Vicenza belonging to Count Ottavio de’ Thiene, which previously belonged to Count Marc’ Antonio, who began its construction. This house is situated in the center of the city, near the main square, and therefore I thought it appropriate to arrange some shops in the part facing said square. This is because an architect must also consider the profit <note>original: "vtile"</note> of the builder, which can be done conveniently when the site is sufficiently large. Each shop has a mezzanine <term>mezato: a low-ceilinged floor situated between two main stories</term> above it for the use of the shopkeepers, and above those are the rooms for the master of the house. This house is an island block <term>Isola: a building completely surrounded by four streets, common in planned urban developments</term>; that is, it is surrounded by four streets.

The main entrance, or what we might call the master door, has a loggia in front of it and is located on the busiest street in the city. Above it, the Great Hall <term>Sala maggiore: the primary reception room for entertaining guests</term> will be located, which will project outward even with the loggia. There are two other entrances on the sides, which have columns in the middle; these are placed there not so much for ornament as to make the space above secure and to proportion the width to the height. From these entrances, one enters the courtyard, which is surrounded by loggias of pillars—the first order being rustic <term>ordine rustico: a style of masonry characterized by rough-hewn or "unfinished" stone surfaces</term>, and the second being of the Composite order. In the corners, there are octagonal rooms, which turn out well both because of their shape and because of the various uses to which they can be adapted.

The rooms of this building that are now finished have been decorated with beautiful stuccoes by Master <note>original: "Messer"</note> Alessandro Vittoria and Master Bartolomeo Ridolfi, and with paintings by Master Anselmo Canera and Master Bernardino India of Verona, who are second to none in our times. The cellars and similar spaces are underground because this building is in the highest part of the city, where there is no danger that water will cause an obstruction <note>original: "dia impaccio", likely referring to flooding or dampness</note>.

->**DETAIL OF THE FACADE**<-

*This architectural drawing illustrates a section of the building’s exterior wall, showing the precise proportions of the windows and masonry.*

### THE UPPER STORY
The upper floor is designed with a sophisticated <term>Attic</term> style. It features:
*   A grand <term>cornice</term> <note>the projecting top section of the wall</note> and an ornate **frieze** decorated with flowing leaves and carved masks.
*   The wall is made of **ashlar masonry** <note>finely cut and squared stones</note>.
*   Two distinct window styles are shown: the left window is crowned by a **triangular pediment**, while the right features an **arched pediment**.
*   Each window is framed by <term>pilasters</term> <note>flat rectangular columns attached to the wall</note> and sits above a small **balustrade**.

**Measurements for the Upper Story:**
*   The height and width of the window openings are marked with **2 Feet** <note>original: "P" for *Piedi*</note> and **2 Ounces** <note>original: "o" for *Oncie*</note>.
*   The spacing between the windows is indicated as **1 Foot** and **4 Feet** in various sections of the vertical margin.

### THE LOWER STORY
The ground floor presents a stark contrast with its **rusticated masonry** <note>blocks with deep joints and rough faces to suggest strength</note>.
*   It features two large arched openings.
*   Inside the arches, the letter **M** is visible. <note>original: "M" likely referring to *Modulo* (Module), the standard unit of measurement derived from the radius of a column, or *Mezzo* (Half).</note>
*   The horizontal bands above the arches are marked with **P** <note>original: "P" for *Piedi* (Feet)</note>, indicating the height of the stone courses.

<margin>The numbers along the margins (1, 4, 2, P) provide the master builders with the exact scale required to recreate these classical proportions in stone.</margin>

<note>Palladio's use of alternating triangular and arched pediments is a hallmark of the High Renaissance style, inspired by ancient Roman temples.</note>

# THE SECOND BOOK

<note>This plate illustrates the courtyard facade of Palazzo Thiene in Vicenza. Palladio’s design is famous for its "Mannerist" qualities—specifically the contrast between the rough, powerful ground floor and the refined, statue-filled upper stories.</note>

->**ELEVATION OF THE COURTYARD FACADE**<-

*This drawing provides a precise guide to the proportions and ornamental features of the palace exterior, showcasing the transition from heavy masonry to delicate classical sculpture.*

### THE ATTIC STORY
The building is topped by an <term>Attic</term> <note>a low story or wall above the main cornice of a building</note> that serves to balance the height of the structure.
*   **Statues:** Three standing classical figures are placed on pedestals along the roofline, aligned with the columns below to draw the eye upward.
*   **Panels:** The wall of the attic is decorated with simple rectangular panels that echo the rhythm of the windows.

### THE PRINCIPAL FLOOR (PIANO NOBILE)
The middle level, or <term>Piano Nobile</term> <note>literally the "noble floor," the primary living and reception area for the aristocracy</note>, is the most decorative.
*   **Arches and Columns:** The facade features large arched openings supported by columns with elaborate capitals. 
*   **Pilasters:** Flat, decorative <term>pilasters</term> <note>rectangular columns attached to the wall</note> provide additional vertical structure between the bays.
*   **Niches:** To the right, a statue is housed within a semi-circular <term>niche</term> <note>a decorative recess in a wall designed to hold a statue or urn</note>.
*   **Balustrade:** A continuous **balustrade** <note>a railing composed of small posts called balusters</note> runs along the base of this floor, separating it from the level below.

**Measurements for the Principal Floor:**
| Architectural Element | Measurement in Feet | Measurement in Ounces |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Left Arch Opening | 2 Feet | 3/4 Foot |
| Central Arch Opening | 4 Feet | — |
| Column Bases | 2 to 4 Feet | — |
| Niche Section | 2 Feet | 2 Ounces |
<note>In the original text, "P" stands for *Piedi* (Feet) and "o" stands for *Oncie* (Ounces).</note>

### THE GROUND FLOOR
The lowest level is defined by its **rusticated masonry** <note>stonework with a rough, unfinished surface and deep-cut joints to create a sense of strength and age</note>.
*   **Entrance Arches:** Two massive arches serve as the primary openings, their rugged stones contrasting with the smooth carvings above.
*   **Lower Niche:** A niche on the far right mirrors the one on the floor above, containing a statue to maintain symmetry across the entire height of the wall.

**Measurements for the Ground Floor:**
*   The interior of the arches is marked with the number **8** and **4 Feet** <note>original: "8, P. 4"</note>.
*   The base of the left section is measured at **7 Feet, 2 Ounces** <note>original: "P. 7, 2"</note>.
*   The vertical wall sections carry the ratio of **6/10**, likely referring to the modular proportion used to determine the thickness of the masonry.

<summary>This page provides a detailed architectural elevation of the Palazzo Thiene courtyard, illustrating the measurements and stylistic differences between the rusticated ground floor, the ornate Piano Nobile, and the statue-adorned Attic.</summary>

# THE SECOND BOOK

->**VILLA ALMERICO (LA ROTONDA)**<-

AMONG many honored Vicentine gentlemen is **Monsignor Paolo Almerico**, a man of the Church and a <term>Referendary</term> <note>An official in the Roman Curia responsible for reviewing petitions and judicial matters</note> to two Supreme Pontiffs, Pius IV and V, who for his merit deserved to be made a Roman Citizen with all his household. This gentleman, after having traveled for many years in search of honor, finally—all his relatives having died—returned to his homeland. For his leisure, he retired to one of his suburban estates on a hill, less than a quarter of a mile from the city, where he has built according to the design that follows. It did not seem right to me to place this among the <term>villa buildings</term> <note>original: "fabriche di Villa"; typically rural agricultural estates</note> because of its proximity to the city; indeed, one might say it is in the city itself.

The site is one of the most pleasant and delightful that can be found, situated atop a small hill of very easy ascent. It is bathed on one side by the **Bacchiglione**, a navigable river, and on the other is surrounded by other most pleasant hills that create the appearance of a vast **Theater**. These hills are all cultivated and abundant with excellent fruits and very fine vines. Because the house enjoys beautiful views from every side—some nearby, some more distant, and others reaching the horizon—**loggias** have been built on all four facades. 

Under the floor of these loggias and the central Hall are the rooms for the convenience and use of the household staff <note>original: "famiglia"; in this context, it refers to the domestic servants and assistants</note>. The **Hall** <note>original: "Sala"</note> is in the middle; it is circular and receives light from above. The small chambers are <term>mezzanines</term> <note>low-ceilinged intermediate floors; original: "amezati"</note>. Above the large rooms, which have high <term>vaults</term> <note>arched ceilings</note> built according to the first method <note>referring to a specific construction technique described earlier in the treatise</note>, there is a walkway around the Hall fifteen and a half feet wide. At the ends of the pedestals that support the stairs of the loggias, there are statues by the hand of **Master Lorenzo Vicentino**, a most excellent sculptor.

I CREATED the following design for Count Montano Barbarano for a site of his in Vicenza. In this design, because of the constraints of the site, I did not initially maintain the same arrangement on one side as on the other. Now, however, this Gentleman has purchased the neighboring site; therefore, the same order is maintained on both sides. Just as on one side there are the stables and quarters for servants (as can be seen in the drawing), so on the other side there will be rooms that will serve as the kitchen, the women's quarters <note>In Renaissance palaces, specific suites were often designated for the women of the household for privacy and domestic management</note>, and for other conveniences. Construction has already begun, and the facade <term>facciata</term> is being built according to the drawing that follows in a larger size. I have not yet included the drawing of the floor plan <term>pianta</term> according to how it was ultimately decided and how the foundations have by now been laid, because I was not able to have it engraved in time for printing. 

The entrance of this design has several columns that support the vault <note>Palladio often used columns in the entryway to mimic the "Egyptian Atrium" described by the Roman architect Vitruvius</note> for the reasons already stated. On the right and left sides, there are two rooms that are one and a half squares long, and next to them two other square ones, and beyond these, two small rooms <term>camerini</term>. Opposite the entrance is a passage, from which one enters a loggia overlooking the courtyard. This passage has a small room on each side, and above them are mezzanines <term>mezzati</term> <note>Lower-ceilinged intermediate floors often used for storage or servant quarters</note>, which are served by the greater and principal staircase of the house. 

In all these places, the vaults are twenty-one and a half feet high. The upper Hall <term>Sala</term> and all the other rooms have flat timber ceilings <term>solaro</term>; only the small rooms have vaults at the same height as the ceilings of the larger rooms. The columns of the facade have pedestals <term>piedestili</term> beneath them and support a balcony <term>poggiuolo</term>, which is entered through the attic <term>soffitta</term>. However, the facade is not being built in this manner (as I have said), but according to the drawing that follows in a larger size.

-># BOOK TWO<-

**I designed** the present invention for **Count Montano Barbarano** for a site of his in **Vicenza**. Due to the nature of the site, the order of one part did not originally match the other. However, this **Gentleman** has since purchased the neighboring site; therefore, the same order is now observed in both parts. Just as on one side there are the stables and quarters for servants (as seen in the drawing), so on the other side there are rooms that will serve as the kitchen, the **women's quarters** <note>In 16th-century Italian architecture, 'luoghi da donne' referred to semi-private apartments reserved for the mistress of the house and her female attendants</note>, and for other conveniences. Construction has already begun, and the **facade** <term>facciata</term> is being built according to the large-scale drawing that follows. I have not yet included the drawing of the **floor plan** <term>pianta</term> as it was ultimately decided upon and as the foundations have now been laid, because I was unable to have it engraved in time for printing. 

The entrance of this invention has several columns that support the **vault** <note>An arched ceiling or roof, usually made of stone or brick</note> for the reasons already mentioned. To the right and left sides, there are two rooms a square and a half in length, and next to them two other square rooms, and beyond these, two small studies. Opposite the entrance is a passage, from which one enters a **loggia** <term>loggia</term> <note>A gallery or corridor open to the air on one side, supported by columns</note> overlooking the courtyard. This passage has a small room on each side, one for the steward <note>original: "massaro," the person responsible for managing the household's supplies and staff</note> and the other for the servant who attends the gate. The courtyard has a loggia all around it, and the columns of this loggia support the balconies that give access to the upper rooms. The stairs are placed in the corners of the courtyard and serve the entire house.

The following **facade** <term>facciata</term> is of the same house; it features two orders of columns. The first is **Ionic** <note>A classical order of architecture characterized by capitals with spiral, scroll-like ornaments called volutes</note>, and the second is **Corinthian** <note>The most decorative of the classical orders, featuring capitals adorned with stylized acanthus leaves</note>.

--- Page 96 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page marks a transition from Palladio’s contemporary city designs (such as the Palazzo Barbarano mentioned on the previous page) to his theoretical reconstructions of Ancient Roman domestic architecture. He is now fulfilling his promise to describe the "Atrium," a central feature of the classical house, based on the writings of Vitruvius.</meta>

->### BOOK TWO ###<-
->#### OF THE TUSCAN ATRIUM, Chapter IV. ####<-

**SINCE I have presented** some of those buildings which I have designed in the cities, it is very fitting that, to fulfill what I promised, I should provide the designs of some principal parts of the houses of the **Ancients**. Because the **Atrium** <term>Atrio</term> <note>The central hall or reception area of a Roman house, typically open to the sky in the center to collect rainwater</note> was a most notable part of those houses, I will speak first of the Atria, and consequently of the rooms joined to them; then I shall come to the Halls. **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect of the 1st century BCE whose treatise 'De Architectura' was the primary source of knowledge for Renaissance builders like Palladio</note> says in the sixth book that there were five types of Atria among the Ancients: namely, **Tuscan**, **Four-columned**, **Corinthian**, **Testudinate** <note>From the Latin 'testudo' (tortoise), referring to a vaulted or roofed-over hall without a central opening</note>, and **Open-roofed**, of which I do not intend to speak. The following designs are of the **Tuscan Atrium**. 

The width of this Atrium is two-thirds of its length. The **Tablinum** <term>Tablino</term> <note>A formal reception room or office, traditionally located at the back of the atrium, where family records and statues were kept</note> is two-fifths as wide as the Atrium's width, and equally long. From here one passes into the **Peristyle** <term>Peristilio</term>; that is, into the courtyard with porticoes around it, which is one-third longer than it is wide. The porticoes are as wide as the columns are long. From the sides of the Atrium, one could make small sitting rooms that would overlook the gardens; and if they were made as seen in the drawing, their columns would be of the **Ionic order** twenty feet long, and the portico would be as wide as the **intercolumniations** <term>intercolunnij</term> <note>The clear space measured between two adjacent columns</note>. Above these, there would be other **Corinthian** columns, a fourth part smaller than those below, between which windows would be placed to bring in light. There would be no roof over the walkways, but they would have railings around them. Depending on the site, one could make more or fewer rooms than I have drawn, and according to the needs and convenience of those who are to live there.

<margin>CONTINUES</margin>

->## OF THE ATRIUM WITH FOUR COLUMNS. Chapter V.<-

<margin>DD 2 OF THE</margin>
The following design features the <term>Atrium with four columns</term><note>An atrium where the roof is supported by four columns at the corners of the central opening, providing more stability for larger rooms than the Tuscan style.</note>: its width is three-fifths of its length. The <term>wings</term><note>original: "ale"; these were open alcoves or side-rooms positioned at the back of the atrium, used for displaying ancestral masks or receiving guests.</note> are one-fourth of the total length. The columns are of the <term>Corinthian</term><note>The most ornate of the classical orders, characterized by slender proportions and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves.</note> order: their diameter is half the width of the wings. The <term>open space</term><note>original: "discoperto"; referring to the compluvium, the rectangular opening in the roof that allowed light in and rainwater to fall into a pool below.</note> is one-third the length of the atrium. The <term>Tablinum</term><note>A formal room, often used as an office or reception area, situated between the atrium and the peristyle.</note> is as wide as half the width of the atrium, and is of equal length. From the atrium, one passes through the Tablinum into the <term>Peristyle</term><note>An inner courtyard surrounded by columns.</note>: which is one and a half squares in length. The columns of the first order are <term>Doric</term><note>The simplest and sturdiest of the classical orders, known for its circular capitals and lack of a base in its original Greek form.</note>, and the porticoes are as wide as the height of said columns. Those above—that is, those of the second order—are <term>Ionic</term><note>An order characterized by the use of volutes (scroll-like ornaments) on the capitals.</note>, being one-fourth thinner than those of the first order; they sit upon a ledge or pedestal two and three-quarter feet high.

A, Atrium.
B, Tablinum.
C, Door of the Tablinum.
D, Portico of the Peristyle.
E, Rooms near the Atrium.
F, Loggia through which one enters the Atrium.
G, Open part of the Atrium with <term>balustrades</term><note>original: "poggiuoli"; low walls or railings surrounding the upper opening to prevent falls.</note> around it.
H, Wings of the Atrium.
I, Frieze of the Atrium's cornice.
K, The solid wall space above the columns.
L, Measure of ten feet.

## ON THE CORINTHIAN ATRIUM. Chapter VI.

The following building belongs to the **Convent of the Charity** <note>original: "Conuento della Carità"; today the site of the Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice</note>, where the **Regular Canons** <note>a community of priests living under a religious rule, specifically the Augustinians in this case</note> reside in **Venice**. I have sought to make this house resemble those of the Ancients, and therefore I have designed a **Corinthian Atrium** for it. The length of this atrium is determined by the diagonal line of the square of its width <note>a geometric method for determining pleasing proportions: if you draw a square based on the width, the atrium's total length equals the diagonal of that square</note>. The **wings** <note>original: "ale"; side alcoves or aisles</note> are one part out of three and a half of the total length. The columns are of the **Composite order** <note>a mixed style of capital combining the scrolls of the Ionic with the leaves of the Corinthian</note>, three and a half feet thick and thirty-five feet long.

The **open area** <note>original: "scoperto"; the central courtyard or impluvium area</note> in the middle is one-third the width of the Atrium. Above the columns, there is an open terrace at the same level as the floor of the third order of the **Cloister** <note>original: "Inclaustro"</note>, where the monks' cells are located. Near the Atrium on one side is the **Sacristy**, surrounded by a **Doric cornice** which supports the vault. The columns seen there support that part of the Cloister wall which, in the upper section, divides the rooms or cells from the **Loggias** <note>covered galleries or walkways open on one side</note>. This Sacristy serves as a **Tablinum** <term>Tablino: in ancient Roman houses, this was the room where family records and ancestral portraits were displayed</term>, though to suit the layout, I have placed it to one side of the Atrium. On the other side is the room for the **Chapter** <note>the meeting hall for the monks</note>, which corresponds to the Sacristy.

Near the Church, there is an **oval staircase**, hollow in the middle, which turns out to be very convenient and beautiful. From the Atrium, one enters the **Cloister**, which has three orders of columns, one above the other. The first is **Doric**; the columns project from the pillars by more than half their diameter. The second is **Ionic**; its columns are one-fifth smaller than those of the first. The third is **Corinthian**, and its columns are one-fifth smaller than those of the second. In this third order, instead of pillars, there is a continuous wall, and directly above the arches of the lower orders, there are windows that provide light to the entrance of the cells. The **vaults** of these cells are made of **reeds** <note>a traditional construction technique using woven reeds plastered over to create lightweight ceilings</note> so that they do not weigh down the walls.

Opposite the Atrium and Cloister, beyond the staircase, is the **Refectory** <note>the communal dining hall</note>, which is two squares long and as high as the floor of the third level of the Cloister. It has a Loggia on each side, and beneath it is a **Cellar** built in the manner of a **cistern** <note>waterproofed with specialized plaster</note> so that water cannot enter. At one end, it has the kitchen, ovens, poultry yard, wood storage, laundry, and a quite beautiful garden; at the other end are other utility rooms. In this building, including guest quarters and other functional spaces, there are forty-four rooms and forty-six cells.

<image-desc>A faint architectural illustration depicting the elevation of a three-story cloister (Inclauſtro). The first two levels show open arcades with classical columns (Dorico and Ionico orders), while the third level is a solid wall with windows (Corinthio order) positioned directly above the arches of the lower levels.</image-desc>

He details the proportions, the stacking of architectural orders in the cloister, and the practical layout of the monks' living and working spaces.</summary>

# ON THE TORTOISE-SHELL ATRIUM, AND THE PRIVATE HOUSE
## of the Ancient Romans. Chapter VII.

Beyond the aforementioned types of atriums, another was very much in use among the Ancients, and called by them **tortoise-shell** <note>original: *testugginata*; referring to a vaulted roof that, unlike other atrium styles, did not have a central opening for rainwater</note>. Because this part of architecture is extremely difficult due to the obscurity of **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BC Roman architect whose treatise *De architectura* is the foundation of Renaissance theory</note>, and is worthy of much attention, I will state what I believe regarding it. I will also add the arrangement of the <term>Oeci</term> <note>from the Greek *oikos*; these were large reception halls or salons</note>, or Salons, Offices, Dining Rooms, Baths, and other places, so that in the following drawing all the parts of the private house will be seen in their proper places according to Vitruvius.

The **Atrium** is as long as the diagonal of the square of its width, and its height up to the supporting beam is equal to its width. The rooms situated beside it are six feet lower in height. Upon the walls that divide them from the Atrium, there are several pillars that support the **tortoise-shell** vault, or the roof of the Atrium; the space between these pillars allows light to enter. These rooms then have an open terrace above them. Opposite the entrance is the **Tablinum** <note>the office or reception room of the master of the house</note>, which is two and a half parts of the Atrium's width. These places served, as I have said elsewhere, to house the images and statues of ancestors. Further ahead one finds the **Peristyle** <note>an inner courtyard surrounded by columns</note>, which has porticos as wide as the columns are long. The rooms are of the same width, and are as high as they are wide up to the spring of the vaults; these vaults have a curvature of one-third their width. Several types of <term>Oeci</term> are described by Vitruvius (these were Halls or Salons where banquets and feasts were held, and where women sat to work): namely the **Tetrastyle**, so called because they had four columns; the **Corinthian**, which had half-columns around them; and the **Egyptian**, which were enclosed by a wall above the first columns with half-columns aligned with those below, though one-fourth smaller. The windows were placed in the spaces between these upper columns, providing light to the central area. The height of the galleries surrounding them did not exceed the first columns, and above them was an open area and a corridor or balcony. Drawings for each of these will be placed separately. The **Square Oeci** were places to stay cool in the Summer and looked out over gardens and other greenery. They also made other halls called **Cyzicene** <note>named after the city of Cyzicus; these were large dining rooms often facing north to stay cool</note>, which served the same aforementioned comforts. The **Offices** and **Libraries** were in suitable locations facing the East; as were the <term>Triclinia</term> <note>original: *Ticlini*; formal dining rooms named for the three couches used for reclining during meals</note>, which were the places where they ate. There were also **Baths** for men and for women, which I have drawn in the final part of the house.

# ON HALLS WITH FOUR COLUMNS.

## CHAPTER VIII.

THE FOLLOWING design is of the Halls, which were called **Tetrastyle** <note>original: "Terrastili," a term derived from the Greek *tetra* (four) and *stylos* (column). This specifically refers to a room where the ceiling is supported by four pillars.</note>; because they had four columns. These were made square, and the columns were placed there to proportion the width to the height, and to make the level above secure <note>Palladio is explaining that the columns are not just decorative; they provide the structural support needed to span a large room and safely carry the weight of the floor or rooms on the story above.</note>; which I have also done in many buildings, as has been seen in the drawings placed above, and will be seen in those that follow.

## OF CORINTHIAN HALLS. Chapter IX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'L' featuring an architectural scene with several figures in a room.</image-desc>**Corinthian** Halls <note>In Palladio's time, a "Corinthian Hall" referred to a specific style of grand reception room inspired by Vitruvius's descriptions of ancient Roman houses.</note> were made in two ways; that is, either with columns that rose from the ground, as seen in the first drawing, or with columns placed upon <term>pedestals</term> <note>original: "piedestili." The decorative base or block on which a column is set to give it extra height.</note>, as in the second drawing. But in both the one and the other, the columns were placed near the wall, and the <term>architraves</term>, <term>friezes</term>, and <term>cornices</term> <note>These three elements—the beam, the decorative band, and the projecting top edge—make up the "entablature," the horizontal structure supported by columns.</note> were worked in <term>stucco</term> <note>A fine plaster used for decorative moldings.</note>, or were made of wood, and there was only a single order of columns. The vault was made either as a semi-circle <note>A standard barrel vault.</note> or <term>a schiffo</term> <note>original: "à schiffo." A type of coved vault where the sides curve up from all four walls to meet a flat rectangular central panel, resembling the hull of a ship (schifo) turned upside down.</note>; that is, it had a rise <note>original: "frezza." The vertical distance or 'depth' of the curve from the top of the wall to the highest point of the vault.</note> equal to one-third of the width of the Hall, and it was to be adorned with compartments of stuccoes and paintings. The length of these Halls would be very beautiful if it were a square and two-thirds of the width <note>Palladio suggests a proportional ratio of 5:3 for the floor plan.</note>.

## ON EGYPTIAN HALLS. Chapter X.

[Signature: FF]

The drawing that follows is of the <term>Egyptian Halls</term> <note>These are not halls from ancient Egypt, but rather a specific style of grand room described by the Roman architect Vitruvius, characterized by a second story of columns.</note>: which were very similar to <term>Basilicas</term> <note>In the Roman era, a basilica was a large public building for legal and business matters, rather than a church.</note>; that is, places where justice was administered, of which more will be said when <term>Plazas</term> <note>Referring to the Roman Forum or public squares, discussed in Palladio's Third Book.</note> are treated. In these halls, a <term>portico</term> was created by placing the <term>columns</term> on the inside, away from the <term>wall</term>, just as in Basilicas; and above the columns were the <term>Architraves</term>, <term>Friezes</term>, and <term>Cornices</term>. The space between the columns and the wall was covered by a <term>floor</term>, and this floor was open <note>meaning open to the air, or without a ceiling immediately above it at the same level as the central hall.</note>, and formed a <term>corridor</term> or <term>balcony</term> all around. Above the aforementioned columns was a continuous wall with <term>half-columns</term> on the inside, which were a fourth part smaller than those mentioned before; and between the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the technical term for the clear space between two adjacent columns.</note> there were <term>windows</term> which gave light to the <term>Hall</term>, and through which one could look into the hall from the aforementioned open floor. These Halls must have possessed a wonderful grandeur, both due to the ornamentation of the columns and their height: because the <term>ceiling</term> was placed above the Cornice of the second <term>order</term>, and they must have been very convenient for <term>festivals</term> or <term>banquets</term>.

...great beauty. These halls should be designed with a length that is one and a half times their width <note>For example, if the hall is 20 feet wide, it should be 30 feet long</note>. The columns of the lower level, including their bases and capitals, must be as tall as the width of the side aisles—the space between the wall and the columns themselves. 

The floor above these side aisles is to be left open to the sky, serving as a walkway or balcony that looks down into the central area. Directly above the lower columns, a second wall is constructed, decorated with **half-columns** <note>columns that appear partially embedded in the wall</note>. These upper columns should be one-fourth smaller than the columns on the ground floor. In the spaces between these upper columns, windows are placed to provide light to the central hall.

### OF THE PRIVATE HOUSES OF THE GREEKS.

The Greeks held a different method of building from the Latins: because (as **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose ten-volume work is the primary source for this text</note> says) they left out the **Loggias** <note>covered galleries open to the air</note> and the **Atriums** <note>central open-air halls typical of Roman houses</note>, making the entrance of the house narrow and tight; on one side they placed the horse stables, and on the other, the rooms for the **doormen**. From this first passage, one entered into the Courtyard, which had porticos on three sides. On the side facing south, they made two **Antae** <term>pilasters or square pillars at the end of a wall</term>; these supported the beams of the floors further in. Leaving some space on both sides, there were very large areas designated for the **matrons** <note>mothers of the family</note>, where they stayed with their male and female servants. Level with these antae were some rooms, which we may call the **Antechamber**, **Chamber**, and **Back-chamber**, as they were positioned one behind the other. Around the porticos were places for eating, sleeping, and other such things necessary for the family. 

To this building, they added another of greater size and ornament with more ample courtyards. In these, they either made four porticos of equal height, or one of greater height—specifically the one facing the South. A courtyard that had this taller portico was called **Rhodian** <note>original: "Rhodiaco"</note>, perhaps because the invention came from **Rhodes**. These courtyards had magnificent loggias in front and their own doors, and only the men lived there. Beside these buildings, to the right and left, they built other houses which had their own private doors and all the conveniences belonging to a residence; in these, they lodged **foreigners**. It was the custom among those people that when a foreigner arrived, they would take him to eat with them on the first day, and then they would assign him an accommodation in said houses and send him all the things necessary for living. Thus, the foreigners were free from any obligation and felt as if they were in their own home. Let this suffice for what has been said of the houses of the Greeks and of city houses.

### The parts of the houses of the Greeks.

A, Entrance passage.
B, Stables.
C, Places for the doormen.
D, First courtyard.
E, Passage through which one entered the rooms.
F, Places where the women stayed to work.
G, First large room, which we would call an Antechamber.
H, Moderate-sized chamber.
I, Small room or closet.
K, Small dining rooms.
L, Rooms.
M, Second courtyard, larger than the first.
N, Portico larger than the other three, from which the courtyard is called **Rhodian**.
O, Passage through which one went from the smaller courtyard to the larger one.
P, The three porticos that have small columns.
Q, **Cyzicene triclinia** <term>elaborate dining rooms named after the city of Cyzicus</term> and **Chanceries** <note>original: "Cancellariæ"; likely rooms for writing or archives</note>, or places for painting.
R, Hall.
S, Library.
T, Square halls, where they ate.
V, The houses for foreigners.
X, Small lanes that divided said houses from those of the master.
Y, Small open courtyards.
Z, Main street.

...specifically the one facing the midday sun <note>original: "mezo giorno," the South</note>. Such a courtyard, which has one portico higher than the others, is called **Rhodian**. These buildings have magnificent entrance halls and their own ornate gates; the porticos are decorated with stone or marble and have coffered ceilings. In the porticos that face the North, they placed the **Libraries**; and in those facing the East, the **Dining Rooms** <note>original: "triclinij," referring to the three-couch dining arrangement of antiquity</note>. They also built large halls <note>term: "Oeci" — spacious halls used for social gatherings or as workrooms for women</note> of such size that there was ample space for weavers to do their work.

To the right and left of these larger buildings are the **Guest Quarters** <note>original: "Hospitalia"</note>. These are separate suites with their own small courtyards and dining rooms, so that guests arriving from elsewhere were not housed in the private family quarters, but in these apartments where they could live with freedom and privacy.

These Greek houses also included **Walkways** <note>original: "Xysti"</note>, which were very long porticos where athletes exercised. Between the pillars of these porticos, the Greeks created groves of trees and pleasant paths. Nearby were the **Palaestrae** <note>wrestling schools or gymnasiums</note>, built with such grandeur that they often seemed like small cities themselves.

# ON THE SITE TO BE CHOSEN FOR VILLA BUILDINGS
### Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap letter 'L' featuring a landscape with a classical building and trees.</image-desc>
City houses are truly a source of great splendor and convenience for a gentleman, as he must live in them for as long as is necessary for the administration of the State <note>original: "Republica"</note> and the management of his own affairs. But perhaps no less utility and consolation will be drawn from country houses <note>term: "Villa" — a rural estate including both the owner's residence and functional farm buildings</note>, where the rest of his time will be spent overseeing and decorating his possessions, and increasing his wealth through the industry and art of agriculture. There, through the exercise usually taken in the villa on foot and on horseback, the body will more easily preserve its health and strength; and there, finally, the mind—tired by the agitations of the city—will find great restoration and consolation, and can quietly attend to the study of letters and contemplation. For this reason, the ancient Sages used to retire frequently to such places where, visited by their virtuous friends and relatives, and possessing houses, gardens, fountains, and similar delightful spots—and above all, their own Virtue—they could easily achieve that blessed life which can be obtained here below. Therefore, having with the help of the Lord God finished treating city houses, it is right that we pass to those of the villa, in which private and family business principally consists. But before coming to the designs of these, it seems very appropriate to me to speak of the site or location to be chosen for these buildings, and of their arrangement. Because we are not enclosed within certain and determined boundaries by public or neighbor’s walls (as usually happens in cities), it is the duty of a wise Architect to investigate and seek out a convenient and healthy place with all diligence and effort, since one stays in the villa mostly during the summer time, when even in very healthy places our bodies are weakened and sickened by the heat.

First, then, a site shall be chosen that is as convenient as possible to the possessions, and in the middle of them, so that the master, without much effort, can oversee and improve his lands all around, and the fruits of those lands can be conveniently brought by the laborer to the manor house. If it is possible to build on a river, it will be a very convenient and beautiful thing, because the produce can be carried to the city in boats at any time with little expense, and it will serve the needs of the house and the animals. Furthermore, it will bring great coolness in the summer and provide a most beautiful view; and with great utility and ornament, one can irrigate the fields, the gardens, and the orchards <note>original: "bruoli," referring to kitchen gardens or small fruit groves</note>, which are the soul and delight of the villa. But if navigable rivers cannot be had, one should seek to build near other running waters, avoiding above all dead waters that do not flow, because they generate very bad air. We will easily avoid this if we build in elevated and cheerful places—that is, where the air is moved by the continuous blowing of winds, and the earth, because of the slope, is purged of damp and evil vapors. Thus, the inhabitants may remain healthy, cheerful, and of good color, and the nuisance of mosquitoes <note>original: "Zenzale"</note> and other small animals born from the putrefaction of stagnant and marshy waters will not be felt.

And because water is most necessary for human life, and according to its various qualities produces various effects in us—where some cause issues with the spleen, some goiters <note>original: "gozzi"</note>, some the stone <note>note: kidney or bladder stones</note>, and others other ailments—the greatest diligence should be used to build near waters that have no strange taste and share in no color, but are clear, bright, and light, and which, when spread over a white cloth, do not stain it; for these will be signs of their goodness. Many ways to test if waters are good are taught to us by Vitruvius <note>a famous Roman architect and author whose work was the foundation of Renaissance architectural theory</note>: for that water is held to be perfect which makes good bread, in which legumes cook quickly, and which, when boiled, leaves no dregs at the bottom of the vessel. It will be an excellent sign of the water's goodness if, where it passes, no moss is seen, nor do reeds grow there, but it makes the place clean and beautiful with sand or gravel at the bottom, and not dirty or muddy. Animals accustomed to drinking there will also give a sign of the water's goodness and healthfulness if they are vigorous, strong, robust, and fat, and not gaunt and weak. 

As for the healthfulness of the air, besides the things said above, ancient buildings will give a sign if they are not corroded and ruined; if the trees are well-nourished, beautiful, and not bent in any direction by the winds, and are not of the kind that grow in marshy places. Also, if the rocks or stones native to those places do not appear decayed on their upper side; and if the color of the people is natural and shows a good temperament. One must not build in valleys closed between mountains, because buildings hidden among valleys—besides being deprived of seeing from afar and being seen, and being without any dignity or majesty—are entirely contrary to health. This is because the earth, made pregnant by the rains that run there, sends out vapors pestiferous to minds and bodies, weakening the spirits and wasting away the joints and the nerves:

<summary>Palladio discusses the virtues of country life and provides practical criteria for selecting a villa site, emphasizing health, water quality, and environmental factors like air flow and topography.</summary>

<header>BOOK 2</header>
<meta>catchword: OF THE</meta>

nerves <note>original: "nerui" — referring to physical vigor and health</note>: and whatever is stored in the granaries will be corrupted by excessive moisture. Furthermore, if the Sun enters by the reflection of its rays, it will create excessive heat; and if it does not enter due to continuous shade, the inhabitants will become listless <note>original: "stupide"</note> and of a sickly color. The winds also, if they enter such valleys, will bring too much fury as if through narrow channels; and if they do not blow there, the air gathered there will become dense and unhealthy. When it is necessary to build on a mountain, choose a site facing a temperate region of the Sky, which neither has continuous shade from larger mountains, nor feels the heat of nearly two Suns due to the Sun's striking a nearby cliff; for in either case, living there will be very bad. And finally, in choosing the site for the building of a Villa, all those considerations must be had that are taken in choosing the site for Cities: since a city is nothing but a certain large house, and conversely, a house is a small city.

### ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF HOUSES
->of the Villa. Chapter XIII.<-

Having found a site that is cheerful, pleasant, convenient, and healthy, one will attend to its elegant and convenient arrangement. Two types of buildings are required in the Villa: one for the habitation of the Master and his family; the other for managing and guarding the produce <note>original: "entrate"</note> and the animals of the Villa. However, the site must be divided in such a way that neither of these is an impediment to the other. The master's habitation must be made with regard to his family and condition, and is done as is customary in Cities, which we have treated above. The covered areas for the villa houses will be made with respect to the produce and animals, and joined to the master's house in such a way that one can go everywhere under cover; so that neither the rains nor the burning Summer Suns are a nuisance when going to oversee one’s business. This will also be of great utility for storing timber and infinite other villa items under cover, which would be spoiled by rain and Sun; besides, these porticos add much ornament. Care will be taken to lodge the men employed for the Villa's use, the animals, the produce, and the tools comfortably and without any crowding. The rooms of the <term>Fattore</term> <note>The farm manager who oversees the estate's business</note>, of the <term>Gastaldo</term> <note>The steward or bailiff in charge of agricultural labor and livestock</note>, and of the laborers should be in a convenient place, near the gates and ready for the guarding of all other parts. The stables for working animals, such as oxen and horses, should be distant from the Master's habitation, so that manure is kept far from it; and they shall be placed in very warm and bright places. The places for productive animals, such as pigs, sheep, pigeons, poultry, and the like, will be located according to their qualities and natures; and in this, one must observe what is customary in different countries. The Cellars <note>original: "Cantine"</note> must be made underground, enclosed, far from all noise and from all moisture and stench, and they must have light from the East or from the North; for by having it from another side where the Sun can heat them, the wines placed there, heated by the warmth, will become weak and spoil. They shall be made somewhat sloping toward the middle, and have a floor of *terrazzo* <note>a durable flooring made of lime and ground brick or stone</note>, or be paved in such a way that if wine is spilled, it can be collected. The <term>tinacci</term> <note>Large fermenting vats</note> where the wine boils <note>referring to the fermentation process</note> will be kept under the covered areas built near said cellars, and elevated so high that their taps are somewhat higher than the upper hole of the barrel; so that the wine from the vats can easily be sent into the barrels through leather hoses or wooden channels. The <term>Granaries</term> <note>original: "Granari"</note> must have light toward the North: because in this way the grain cannot heat up so quickly; but cooled by the wind, it will be preserved for a long time, and those little animals <note>weevils or pests</note> that cause great harm will not be born there. Their floor or pavement must be of *terrazzo*, if possible, or at least of boards: because the grain is spoiled by touching lime. Other storerooms should also face the same part of the Sky for the same reasons. The <term>Teggie</term> <note>Open-sided sheds or haylofts</note> for hay shall face the South or the West: because, dried by the heat of the Sun, there will be no danger of them overheating and catching fire. The tools needed by the Farmers should be in convenient places under cover to the South. The <term>Ara</term> <note>A threshing floor</note> where the grain is threshed must be exposed to the Sun, spacious and wide, beaten down, and somewhat raised in the middle, and have porticos around it or at least on one side; so that in sudden rains the grain can be quickly brought under cover; and it shall not be too close to the Master's house because of the dust, nor so far that it cannot be seen. And let this suffice for what has been said in general about the choice of sites and their arrangement. It remains that (as I have promised) I set down the designs of some buildings that I have ordered in the Villa according to various inventions.

## ON THE DESIGNS OF THE VILLA HOUSES OF SOME
### Venetian Nobles. Chapter XIII.

The building that follows is in Bagnolo, a place two miles away from Lonigo, a town in the Vicenza district, and it belongs to the Magnificent Lords Count Vittore, Marco, and Daniele, brothers of the Pisani family. On either side of the courtyard there are stables, cellars, granaries, and other similar places for the use of the Villa. The columns of the porticos are of the Doric order. The central part of this building is for the Master's residence: the floor of the main rooms is seven feet above the ground; underneath are the kitchens and other similar places for the staff <note>original: "famiglia" — in this context, it refers to the domestic servants and household workers rather than the nuclear family</note>. The Hall is vaulted, as high as it is wide and half as much again <note>i.e., the height is 1.5 times the width</note>; the vault of the Loggias also reaches this height. The rooms have flat ceilings <note>original: "in solaro" — meaning with exposed wooden beams rather than masonry vaults</note> and are as high as they are wide: the larger ones are one-and-two-thirds squares long; the others are a square and a half. And it should be noted that not much consideration was given to placing the smaller staircases in a position where they would have direct light <note>original: "lume viuo"</note> (as we mentioned in the first book), because since they only serve the lower areas and the upper ones—which are used for granaries or mezzanines—priority was given to properly arranging the principal floor <note>original: "ordine di mezzo"</note>, which is for the residence of the Master and guests. And the stairs that lead to this floor are placed in a very suitable location, as seen in the drawings. This is also said as a warning to the prudent reader for all the other following buildings of a single order <note>term: "order" — here referring to a formal architectural story or level</note>: because in those that have two beautiful and decorated levels, I have taken care that the stairs are well-lit and placed in convenient locations. I say "two" because the level underground for cellars and similar uses, and the upper level used for granaries and <term>mezzanines</term> <note>original: "mezati" — low-ceilinged floors between main stories</note>, I do not call a principal "order," as they are not dedicated to the residence of Gentlemen.

THE following building belongs to the Magnificent Signor Francesco Badoero in the Polesine at a place called La Fratta, on a site somewhat elevated and washed by a branch of the Adige, where there was anciently a castle belonging to Salinguerra da Este, brother-in-law of Ezzelino da Romano <note>Ezzelino III da Romano (1194–1259) was a powerful and notoriously cruel ruler in the Veneto; Salinguerra was his ally</note>. A pedestal five feet high serves as a base for the whole building: at this height is the floor of the rooms, all of which have flat ceilings <note>original: "in solaro" — referring to timber-framed ceilings rather than masonry vaults</note>, and they have been decorated with grotesques <note>fanciful wall paintings featuring intertwined foliage and mythical figures</note> of most beautiful invention by Giallo Fiorentino. Above them is the granary, and below are the kitchen, the cellars, and other spaces pertaining to convenience. The columns of the loggias of the master's house are Ionic: the cornice, like a crown, surrounds the entire house. The pediment <note>original: "frontespicio"</note> over the loggias creates a very beautiful sight, because it makes the middle part more prominent than the sides. Descending then to the ground level, one finds spaces for the Steward <note>original: "Fattore"</note>, the Bailiff <note>original: "Gastaldo"</note>, stables, and other facilities suitable for a Villa.

**THE MAGNIFICENT** Signor Marco Zeno has built according to the following design in Cessalto <note>original: "Cefalto"</note>, a place near Motta di Livenza, a town in the territory of Treviso. Upon a basement <note>original: "basamento" — a raised platform or pedestal that elevates the main living floor above the damp ground</note> which surrounds the entire building, is the floor of the rooms, all of which are vaulted <note>original: "fatte in volto" — constructed with masonry arches rather than flat timber ceilings</note>. The height of the vaults of the larger rooms is determined according to the second method for the heights of vaults <note>In Book I, Palladio defines three mathematical methods for setting vault heights; the "second method" calculates the height as the arithmetic mean of the room's length and width</note>. The square rooms have lunettes <note>crescent-shaped arched openings in the vaulting</note> in the corners, aligned with the windows. The small rooms <note>original: "camerini"</note> next to the loggia have banded vaults <note>original: "volti a fascia" — coved or flat-topped vaults characterized by a wide central band</note>, as does the hall; the vault of the loggia is as high as that of the hall, and both exceed the height of the other rooms. This building has gardens, a courtyard, a dovecote <note>original: "colombara" — a structure for housing pigeons, which provided both food and valuable fertilizer for the estate</note>, and everything else necessary for the use of a Villa.

**NOT VERY** far from Gambarare <note>a village in the municipality of Mira, near Venice</note> on the [river] Brenta is the following building belonging to the Magnificent Signors Nicolò and Luigi Foscari. This building is raised eleven feet from the ground <note>original: "undeci piedi" — Venetian feet, which were slightly larger than the modern English foot</note>, and underneath are kitchens, dining rooms <term>tinelli: specifically rooms where servants and household staff ate</term>, and similar functional spaces; the structure is vaulted both on the lower and upper levels. The larger rooms have vaults whose height is determined according to the first method for vault heights <note>In Book I, Palladio defines the "first method" as making the vault's height equal to the width of the room</note>. The square rooms have cupola <term>cupola: a dome-shaped vault</term> vaults; above the small rooms <note>original: "camerini"</note> there are mezzanines <term>mezati: low-ceilinged floors typically used for storage or servant quarters, tucked between main levels</term>. The vault of the Hall is a semi-circular cross vault <term>cross vault: a vault formed by the perpendicular intersection of two barrel vaults</term>; its springing line <note>original: "imposta" — the point where the curve of the arch begins to rise from the wall</note> is as high from the floor as the hall is wide. This hall has been decorated with most excellent paintings by Mr. Battista Venetiano <note>Giovanni Battista Zelotti (c. 1526–1578), a frequent collaborator of Palladio known for his grand fresco cycles</note>.

Mr. Battista Franco <note>Battista Franco, also known as Il Semolei (c. 1510–1561), a prominent Mannerist painter and draftsman</note>, a very great draftsman of our times, had also begun to paint one of the large rooms; but overtaken by death, he left the work unfinished. The loggia is of the Ionic order. The cornice runs all the way around the house and forms a pediment <note>original: "frontepicio"</note> over the loggia and on the opposite side. Under the eaves, there is another cornice that runs above the pediments. The upper rooms are like mezzanines because of their low height, as they are only eight feet high.

**THE FOLLOWING** building is at Maser, a village near Asolo, a town in the territory of Treviso. It belongs to the Most Reverend Monsignor, Elect [Patriarch] of Aquileia <note>Daniele Barbaro (1514–1570), a humanist scholar and diplomat who provided the commentary for a famous edition of Vitruvius’s "De Architectura" illustrated by Palladio</note>, and the Magnificent Signor Marc’Antonio, brothers of the Barbaro family. That part of the building which projects slightly forward has two levels of rooms; the floor of the upper rooms is level with the rear courtyard, where a fountain has been carved into the hillside facing the house, decorated with countless ornaments in stucco and painting <note>This refers to the famous Nymphaeum, which features intricate sculptures by Alessandro Vittoria and frescos that integrate the architecture with the natural spring</note>. This fountain forms a small pool that serves as a fishpond; from there, the water flows into the kitchen, and after having irrigated the gardens on the right and left sides of the road—which, ascending gradually, leads to the building—it forms two ponds with their watering troughs above the public road. Leaving there, it waters the orchard <term>bruolo: a traditional Venetian term for a large, productive enclosed garden or orchard</term>, which is very large and filled with excellent fruits and various game animals. The facade of the master’s house has four columns of the Ionic order; the capitals of the corner columns face two sides. I will explain how these capitals are made in the book on Temples <note>Palladio refers here to Book IV of this treatise, where he details the reconstruction of ancient Roman temples and their specific architectural orders</note>. On either side there are loggias, which have two dovecotes <term>colombare: pigeon towers; in Palladian villas, these functional agricultural structures were often integrated into the ends of the wings to provide visual symmetry</term> at their ends; beneath these are spaces for winemaking, stables, and other areas for villa use.
