<header>BOOK FOUR.</header>

# ON THE SITE WHICH MUST BE CHOSEN
## to build Temples upon. Chapter One.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'L' depicting a scene with several human figures, possibly a religious or mythological motif, including a figure kneeling before another.</image-desc>
Tuscany was not only the first to receive Architecture as a foreign guest in Italy—from which the order we call Tuscan <term>The Tuscan order is the simplest of the five classical orders of architecture, characterized by plain columns and simple capitals, originating from ancient Etruscan practice.</term> took its measurements—but it was also a teacher to neighboring peoples regarding the affairs of the Gods, whom the greater part of the world once worshipped while wandering in blind error. Tuscany demonstrated what sort of Temples, in what locations, and with what ornaments they ought to be built, according to the quality of the specific Gods. Although one can see that these observations have not been taken into consideration in many Temples, I will nonetheless recount them briefly as they have been left to us by the writers. I do this so that those who delight in Antiquities may be satisfied, and so that the mind of every person may be awakened and inflamed to take every suitable care in building Churches; for it is a very ugly and blameworthy thing that we, who possess the true Worship, should be surpassed in this by those who had no light of truth.

And because the locations in which sacred Temples are to be placed are the first thing that must be considered, I will speak of them in this first chapter. I say, then, that the ancient Tuscans ordained that Temples to Venus, Mars, and Vulcan should be built outside the City, as these were deities who moved spirits toward lusts, wars, and fires. Conversely, within the City, they built for those who presided over Chastity, Peace, and the fine arts. For those Gods under whose special protection the City was placed—namely Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, whom they held to be the defenders of Cities—they built Temples in the highest places, in the center of the land, and within the citadel <note>original: "rocca"</note>.

To Pallas <note>The Greek goddess Athena.</note>, Mercury, and Isis, because they presided over craftsmen and trade, they built Temples near the Squares, and sometimes upon the Squares themselves. To Apollo and Bacchus, they built near the Theater; to Hercules, near the Circus and the Amphitheater.

To Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine and healing.</note>, to Health <note>original: "Salute", referring to the goddess Salus.</note>, and to those Gods by whose medicines they believed many men were healed, they built in highly healthy places and near healing waters; this was so that by moving from bad and pestilential air to good and healthy air, and by drinking those waters, the sick might recover more quickly and with less difficulty, whereby the zeal of religion would increase.

And so, for the rest of the other Gods, they thought it appropriate to find locations to build their Temples according to the properties attributed to them and the manner of their sacrifices.

But we, who by the special grace of God are delivered from that darkness, having left behind their vain and false superstition, shall choose those sites for Temples that are in the most noble and celebrated part of the City, far from dishonorable places and upon beautiful and adorned squares where many streets meet. In this way, every part of the Temple can be seen with its proper dignity, bringing devotion and wonder to whoever sees and looks upon it.

And if there are hills in the City, the highest part of them shall be chosen.

But where there are no elevated places, the floor of the Temple shall be raised above the rest of the City as much as is suitable, and one shall ascend to the Temple by steps; for ascending to a Temple brings with it greater devotion and Majesty.

The fronts <note>referring to the facades or main entrances.</note> of the Temples shall be made to look over a very great part of the City, so that Religion may seem placed as a guardian and protectress of the Citizens.

But if Temples are built outside the City, then their fronts shall be made to look over the public roads, or over rivers if they are built near them, so that travelers may see them and offer their salutations and reverence before the front of the Temple.

# BOOK OF THE FORMS OF TEMPLES, AND OF THE DECORUM THAT MUST BE OBSERVED IN THEM.

### Chapter II

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' (replacing the 'I' in the Italian text) featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or saint, holding a book within a rectangular frame decorated with floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>TEMPLES are made round, quadrangular, six-sided, eight-sided, or with even more corners, all of which should fit within the capacity of a circle; they are also made in the shape of a Cross, and in many other forms and figures, according to the various inventions of men. Whenever these are designed with beautiful and suitable proportions, and distinguished by elegant and ornate Architecture, they deserve to be praised. But the most beautiful and most regular forms, from which the others receive their measurements, are the Round and the Quadrangular; and therefore Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio was a Roman architect and engineer whose 1st-century BCE treatise "On Architecture" became the foundational text for Renaissance architects like Palladio.</note> speaks only of these two, and teaches us how they should be partitioned, as will be discussed when we treat the partitioning of Temples. In Temples that are not round, one must diligently observe that all the angles are equal, whether the Temple has four, six, or more angles and sides. 

The Ancients took care to consider what was appropriate for each of their Gods, not only in choosing the locations where the Temples should be built, as was said above, but also in choosing the form. Hence, for the Sun and the Moon—because they continually revolve around the World, and through this turning produce effects manifest to everyone—they made the Temples round in shape, or at least approaching roundness. They did the same for Vesta, whom they said was the Goddess of the Earth, an element we know to be round. For Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note>, as the patron of the Air and the Sky, they made the Temples open in the middle with porticos around them, as I will describe further below. 

In the ornaments, they also gave great consideration to which God they were building for. For this reason, for Minerva, Mars, and Hercules, they made the Temples in the Doric order <note>The simplest and sturdiest of the classical Greek orders, associated with strength and lack of ornament.</note>; for they said that for such Gods, who presided over military service, buildings without delicacies or tenderness were appropriate. But for Venus, Flora, the Muses, and the Nymphs, and for the more delicate Goddesses, they said Temples should be made that suited a flowery and tender virginal age; therefore, they gave them the Corinthian order <note>The most ornate of the classical orders, characterized by slender columns and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves.</note>, appearing to them that slender and florid works, adorned with leaves and volutes <term>Volutes are the spiral, scroll-like ornaments found on the capitals of Ionic and Corinthian columns.</term>, were suitable to such an age. But to Juno, Diana, Bacchus, and other Gods for whom neither the gravity of the first nor the delicacy of the second seemed appropriate, they attributed Ionic works, which hold the middle place between the Doric and the Corinthian. Thus we read that the Ancients, in building Temples, strove to preserve decorum <term>In architecture, 'decorum' (or propriety) refers to the suitability of a building's style and ornament to its function and the status of the person or deity it honors.</term>, in which consists a very beautiful part of Architecture. 

And therefore we also, who do not have false Gods, in order to preserve decorum regarding the form of Temples, will choose the most perfect and excellent. And since the Round form is such—because it alone among all figures is simple, uniform, equal, strong, and spacious—we will make Temples round. This figure is most especially suited to them because, being enclosed by a single boundary in which one can find neither beginning nor end, nor distinguish one from the other, and having its parts similar to one another, and all participating in the figure of the whole—and finally, finding in every part the extreme equally distant from the middle—it is most fit to demonstrate the Unity, the infinite Essence, the Uniformity, and the Justice of **GOD**. 

Beyond this, it cannot be denied that strength and perpetuity are sought more in Temples than in all other buildings, since they are dedicated to **GOD O. M.** <note>original: "D I O O. M." abbreviating "Deo Optimo Maximo," meaning "To God, the Best and Greatest."</note> and the most celebrated and worthy memories of the City are preserved within them; hence, for this reason as well, one must say that the round figure, in which there is no angle, is supremely suited to Temples. Temples must also be very spacious, so that many people can comfortably stay there for the Divine offices; and among all figures enclosed by an equal circumference, none is more spacious than the Round. 

Also very praiseworthy are those Churches made in the shape of a Cross, which have the entrance in the part that would be the foot of the Cross, and opposite it the high altar and the Choir; and in the two branches that extend on either side, like arms, two other entrances or two other altars; because, being shaped with the form of the Cross, they represent to the eyes of the onlookers that wood from which hung our salvation. And in this form, I have made the Church of **San Giorgio Maggiore** in **Venice**.

<meta>This page continues Chapter II's discussion on the "decorum" or suitability of temple architecture, specifically emphasizing the emotional and spiritual effect of the building on the worshiper. It then transitions into Chapter III, which defines the various "aspects" or outward forms of temples based on the arrangements of their columns, citing the Roman authority Vitruvius.</meta>

FOURTH BOOK. 7

Temples must have wide porticoes and larger columns than those required by other buildings; it is appropriate that they be large and magnificent (though not larger than the size of the City requires) and built with great and beautiful proportions. Indeed, for the Divine Worship for which they are made, every degree of magnificence and grandeur is required. They must be constructed with the most beautiful orders of columns, and each order must be given its own proper and suitable ornaments. They shall be made of the most excellent and precious materials, so that through their form, ornaments, and substance, the Divinity may be honored as much as possible. If it were possible, they should be made with such beauty that one could not imagine anything more lovely; and they should be so arranged in every part that those who enter may be filled with wonder and held in a state of spiritual suspense, contemplating their grace and elegance. Among all colors, none is more suitable for Temples than whiteness, since the purity of color—as in life—is supremely pleasing to GOD. But if they are to be painted, those pictures that distract the mind from the contemplation of Divine things by their subject matter would not be appropriate; for in Temples we must not depart from gravity, nor from those things which, when seen by us, render our souls more inflamed toward Divine Worship and toward doing good.

->ON THE ASPECTS OF<-

->TEMPLES. Chapter III.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative initial letter A at the beginning of the chapter, featuring a detailed landscape woodcut within the square frame of the letter, showing classical-style buildings and trees.</image-desc>
By ASPECT is meant that first appearance the Temple presents to those who approach it. There are seven most regulated and well-understood Aspects of Temples, of which it seemed necessary to me to set down here as much as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of "De Architectura."</note> says in the first chapter of the first book; <note>Palladio cites the first book here, though in modern editions of Vitruvius, the descriptions of temple types appear in Book III.</note> so that this subject—which, due to the lack of observation of Antiquity, has been considered difficult by many and understood by few until now—may be rendered easy and clear by what I shall say and by the drawings that follow, which will serve as examples of what he teaches us. I have also chosen to use the names he employs, so that those who set themselves to reading the aforementioned Vitruvius (an endeavor to which I exhort everyone) may recognize the same names in his work and not feel they are reading about different things. To come, then, to our purpose, Temples are made either with porticoes or without porticoes. Those made without porticoes can have three aspects: one is called <term>in Antis</term> <note>original: "in Antis"; a Greek architectural term meaning "between the pilasters."</note>, which means "face in pilasters," because <term>Antae</term> is the name given to the pilasters made at the angles or corners of buildings. Of the other two, one is called <term>Prostylos</term> <note>original: "Prostilos"; from the Greek "pro" (before) and "stylos" (column).</note>, meaning "face in columns," and the other <term>Amphiprostylos</term> <note>original: "Amphiprostilos"; meaning "columns at both ends."</note>. That which is named <term>in Antis</term> will have two pilasters at the corners, which also turn along the sides of the Temple, and between said pilasters, in the middle of the front, two columns that project outward and support the pediment <note>The triangular gable at the top of a temple front.</note> above the entrance. The other, called <term>Prostyle</term>, will have—in addition to what the first has—columns at the corners corresponding to the pilasters, and on the right and left as the corners turn, two other columns, one on each side. But if the same arrangement of columns and pediment is maintained at the back, the result will be the aspect called <term>Amphiprostyle</term>. Of the first two aspects of Temples, no remains are found in our day, and therefore there will be no examples of them in this book. Nor did I think it necessary to make drawings of them, as the floor plan and elevation of each of these aspects are illustrated in the Vitruvius commented upon by the Most Reverend Monsignor Barbaro <note>Daniele Barbaro (1514–1570), a Venetian humanist and Palladio's patron, who published an influential translation and commentary of Vitruvius in 1556.</note>. But if porticoes are added to Temples, they are then either made around the entire Temple or on the front only. Those that have porticoes only on the front facade can be said to also have the aspect called <term>Prostyle</term>. But those made with porticoes all around can be made in four aspects. For they are made with six columns on the front facade and on the back, and with eleven columns on the sides, counting the corner ones; and this Aspect is called <term>Peripteral</term> <note>original: "Peripteros"; meaning "winged all around."</note>, and the porticoes around the Cell <note>The "Cella," or the main enclosed chamber of the temple.</note> come to be as wide as one <term>intercolumniation</term> <note>The space between two columns.</note>. Ancient Temples can be seen that have six columns on the facade and yet do not have porticoes all around; instead, on the walls of the Cell, on the outside, there are half-columns that match those of the portico and have the same ornaments, as in Nîmes in Provence. Of this sort, one can say, is the Temple of the Ionic order in Rome, which is now the Church of Santa Maria Egittiaca <note>Known today as the Temple of Portunus; it was converted into the church of Santa Maria Egiziaca in the 9th century.</note>. This the Architects did to make the Cell wider and to reduce the expense, while nevertheless maintaining the same peripteral appearance for whoever viewed the Temple from the side. Or, Temples are given eight columns across the front and fifteen on the

sides including the corner ones: these come to have double porticoes around them, and therefore their aspect is called *Dipteros*, that is, <term>Double-Winged</term> <note>original: "Dipteros", referring to a double row of columns surrounding the temple</note>. Or Temples are well made that have, like the aforementioned, eight columns in front and fifteen on the sides, but the porticoes around are not made double, because one row of columns is removed; thus these porticoes come to be as wide as two intercolumniations and one column thickness; and their aspect is called *Pseudodipteros*; that is, <term>False Double-Winged</term> <note>original: "Pseudodipteros"</note>. This Aspect was the invention of Hermogenes, a most ancient Architect, who in this way made the porticoes around the Temple wide and convenient, lightened the labor and the expense, and took nothing away from the appearance. Or finally they are made so that on both facades there are ten columns, and the porticoes around are double, as in those that have the *Dipteros* aspect. These Temples on the inside had other porticoes with two orders of columns one above the other, and these columns were smaller than those on the outside; the roof went from the outer columns to the inner ones, and all the space surrounded by the inner columns was uncovered; hence the aspect of these Temples was called *Hipethros*; that is, <term>Uncovered</term> <note>original: "Hipethros", now commonly spelled Hypaethral</note>. These Temples were dedicated to Jove as Patron of the Sky and the Air; and in the middle of the Courtyard the Altar was placed. Of this sort I believe was the Temple of which a few remains are seen in Rome on <term>Monte Cavallo</term> <note>The Quirinal Hill, named for the "Horse Tamers" statues located there</note>, and that it was dedicated to Jove Quirinus and built by the Emperors: because in the time of Vitruvius (as he says) there were none.

# OF FIVE SPECIES OF TEMPLES.
### Cap. IIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring ornate Renaissance-style scrolling foliage and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
THE ancients used (as has been said above) to make porticoes for their Temples for the convenience of the people; so that they would have a place to stay and walk outside the Cella <note>The inner chamber of a temple where the statue of the deity was kept</note>, in which sacrifices were made: and to give greater Majesty and grandeur to those buildings. Hence, because the intervals between column and column can be made of five sizes, according to those, Vitruvius distinguishes five species or manners of Temples: the names of which are *Picnostilos*; that is, of <term>thick columns</term> <note>Pycnostyle, with very close spacing</note>: *Sistilos*, wider: *Diastilos*, even more distant: *Areostilos*, further apart than is fitting: and *Eustilos*, which has reasonable and convenient intervals. Of all these intercolumniations—how they are and what proportion they should have with the length of the columns—it was spoken of above in the first book, and the drawings were provided: therefore I do not need to say anything else here, except that the first four manners are defective. The first two, because the intercolumniations being of one and a half diameters, or two column diameters, are very small and narrow; hence two people cannot enter the porticoes side by side; but they must go in a row, one behind the other: and the doors and their ornaments cannot be seen from afar: and finally because the narrowness of the spaces prevents walking around the Temple. However, these two manners are tolerable when the columns are made large, as is seen in almost all ancient Temples. The third, because three column diameters can be placed between the columns, the intercolumniations come to be very wide; hence the <term>Architraves</term> <note>The horizontal beams resting directly on the columns</note> break because of the size of the spaces. But this defect can be provided for by making Arches above the Architrave, at the height of the Frieze, or <term>Relieving Arches</term> <note>original: "Reuienati", structural arches built into the wall to shift weight off a lintel</note> that support the load and leave the Architrave free. The fourth manner, although it does not suffer the defect of the aforementioned (because stone or marble Architraves are not used, but wooden beams are placed over the columns), can nonetheless still be called defective; because it is low, wide, and humble, and is proper to the <term>Tuscan order</term>. So that the most beautiful and elegant manner of temples is that which is called *Eustilos*: which is when the intercolumniations are of two and a quarter column diameters; for it serves excellently for use, beauty, and stability. I have named the manners of Temples with those same names that Vitruvius uses, as I have also done for the aspects, both for the reason said above, and also because such names seem already to have been received into our language and are understood by everyone; and therefore I will also use them in the drawings of the Temples that follow.

# ON THE DESIGN AND DIVISION OF TEMPLES. Chapter V.

Although in all buildings it is required that their parts correspond with one another and have such proportion that there is no single part by which the whole and the other parts cannot be measured, this must nonetheless be observed with extreme care in Temples. This is because they are consecrated to the Divinity; to honor and observe Him, one must work with as much beauty and rarity as possible. Since the most regular forms for Temples are the Circular and the Quadrangular, I will describe how each of these should be divided, and I will also include some matters pertaining to the Temples that we Christians use. Circular Temples were sometimes made open in ancient times—that is, without a <term>cella</term> <note>the inner chamber of a temple where the statue of the deity was kept</note>, having columns that supported the dome, like those dedicated to Juno Lacinia. In the middle of these, the altar was placed, and upon it the fire, which was never extinguished. These are divided in the following manner:

The diameter of the entire space that the Temple is to occupy is divided into three equal parts. One part is given to the steps—that is, the ascent to the floor of the Temple—and two remain for the Temple and the columns. These columns are placed upon pedestals and are as high, including the base and capital, as the diameter of the smallest circle of the steps. Their thickness is one-tenth of their height. The architrave, the frieze, and the other ornaments are made according to what was stated in the first book, both in this and in all other sorts of Temples.

But those that are made closed—that is, with a cella—are made either with wings <note>side aisles or colonnades</note> around them, or with a portico only at the front. For those that have wings around them, the proportions are these: first, two steps are made all the way around, and above them the pedestals are placed, upon which the columns stand. The wings are as wide as one-fifth of the diameter of the Temple, taking the diameter from the inside of the pedestals. The columns are as long as the cella is wide, and they are as thick as one-tenth of their length. The <term>tribuna</term> <note>a vaulted or domed ceiling</note>, or the dome, is made above the architrave, frieze, and cornice of the wings, and its height is half of the entire work. In this way, Vitruvius divides circular Temples.

However, in Ancient Temples, pedestals are not seen; rather, the columns begin from the floor of the Temple. This pleases me much more, both because pedestals greatly hinder entry into the Temple, and also because columns that begin from the ground convey greater size and magnificence.

But if only a portico is placed at the front of circular Temples, it shall be as long as the width of the cella, or one-eighth less. It can also be made shorter, but never less than three-quarters of the width of the Temple; and it shall not be wider than one-third of its length.

In Quadrangular Temples, the porticoes at the fronts shall be as long as the width of these Temples. And if they are made in the <term>Eustyle</term> <note>original: "Eustilos", a Greek term for the "well-styled" or ideally proportioned spacing between columns</note> manner, which is beautiful and elegant, they shall be divided in this way: if the facade has four columns, the entire front of the Temple (excluding the projections of the column bases at the corners) shall be divided into eleven and a half parts. One of these parts shall be called a <term>module</term> <note>original: "modulo", a basic unit of measurement in classical architecture based on the diameter of a column</note>, which is the measure by which the other parts will be measured. Since the columns are made one <term>module</term> thick, four modules are given to them; three to the middle <term>intercolumniation</term> <note>original: "intercolunnio", the space between two columns</note>; and four and a half to the other two intercolumniations—that is, two and a quarter for each. If the front has six columns, it will be divided into eighteen parts; if eight, into twenty-four and a half; and if ten, into thirty-one. Always give one of these parts to the thickness of the columns, three to the middle opening, and two and a quarter to each of the other openings. The height of the columns shall be determined according to whether they are Ionic or Corinthian.

How the facades of the other manners of Temples should be regulated—namely the <term>Pycnostyle</term> <note>original: "Picnostilos", columns placed very close together</note>, <term>Systyle</term> <note>original: "Sistilos", columns placed somewhat close</note>, <term>Diastyle</term> <note>original: "Diastilos", columns placed far apart</note>, and <term>Araeostyle</term> <note>original: "Areostilos", columns placed very far apart</note>—was stated fully in the first book when we treated intercolumniations. Beyond the portico, one finds the <term>Pronaos</term> <note>original: "Antitempio", the inner porch or forecourt</note>, and then the <term>Cella</term>. The width is divided into four parts, and the length of the Temple is made equal to eight of those parts. Of these, five are given to the length of the <term>Cella</term>, including the walls containing the doors, and the other three remain for the <term>Pronaos</term>. This area has two side walls that continue from the walls of the cella, at the ends of which are two <term>antae</term> <note>original: "anti", square pillars at the end of a wall</note>—that is, two pillars as thick as the columns of the portico. Because there may be either a little or a lot of space between those walls, if the width is greater than twenty feet, two columns should be placed between the said pillars, and even more as necessity requires, aligned with the columns of the portico. Their function will be to separate the <term>Pronaos</term> from the portico. Those three or more openings between the pillars shall be closed with panels or marble parapets, leaving openings through which one can enter the <term>Pronaos</term>. And if the width is greater than forty feet, it will be necessary to place other columns on the inside opposite those placed between the pillars, and they shall be made of the...

the height of the exterior ones, but somewhat thinner, because the open air will take away some of the thickness from those outside, and the enclosed space will not allow the thinness of those inside to be discerned, and so they will appear equal. And although the said division works exactly in Temples of four columns, the same proportion does not occur in other aspects and styles, because the walls of the <term>cella</term> <note>the inner chamber of a temple</note> must meet the columns on the outside and be in a single row, so the cells of those Temples will be somewhat larger than what has been described. This is how the Ancients divided their Temples, as <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect whose 1st-century BC treatise was the foundational text for Renaissance architecture</note> teaches us; and they intended for porches to be made, under which in bad weather men could avoid the sun, rain, hail, and snow, and on solemn days linger until the hour of sacrifice. But we, having left behind the porches on the outside, build Temples that closely resemble <term>Basilicas</term> <note>large, roofed halls that in Roman times were used for law courts and public assemblies, rather than religious rites</note>, in which, as has been said, the porches were made on the inside, as we do now in Temples. This happened because the first people who gave themselves to our religion, illuminated by the truth, were accustomed for fear of the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>meaning the non-Christian pagans of the Roman Empire</note> to gather in the Basilicas of private men. Therefore, seeing that this form turned out to be very convenient—since the altar could be placed with great dignity in the place of the <term>Tribunal</term> <note>the raised platform where judges sat in a Roman basilica</note>, and the Choir was suitably positioned around the altar, and the remainder was free for the people—it has not been changed since. Therefore, in the division of the aisles that we make in Temples, one shall take note of what was said when we treated Basilicas. 

Added to our Churches is a place separate from the rest of the Temple, which we call a <term>Sacristy</term>, where the priestly vestments, the vessels, the sacred books, and other things necessary for Divine worship are kept, and where the Priests prepare themselves. Nearby are built the towers in which the bells are hung to call the people to the divine offices, which are used by none other than Christians. Near the Temple, dwellings are made for the Priests, which should be comfortable with spacious cloisters and beautiful gardens; and especially the places for the sacred Virgins <note>nuns</note> must be secure, high, and far from the noise and the sight of people. Let this be enough to have said regarding the decorum, the aspects, the styles, and the division of Temples. Now I will present the drawings of many Ancient Temples, in which I will observe this order: first I will present the drawings of those Temples that are in Rome; then of those that are outside of Rome and throughout Italy; and finally of those that are outside of Italy. For easier understanding, and to avoid the length and the tedium I might bring to the Readers if I wished to state the measurements of each part in detail, I have placed them all with numbers in the drawings.

# ON THE DESIGNS OF SOME ANCIENT TEMPLES WHICH ARE
## in Rome, and first of that of Peace. Chap. VI.

We shall therefore begin under a good omen with the designs of the Temple formerly dedicated to Peace, the remains of which are seen near the Church of *Santa Maria Nuova* <note>Now known as the Church of Santa Francesca Romana</note>, on the *Via Sacra* <note>original: "via Sacra"; the "Sacred Way," the main street of ancient Rome</note>. Writers say that it stands on the very spot where once stood the <term>Curia</term> <note>the senate house</note> of Romulus and Hostilius; then the house of Maenius, the <term>Basilica Porcia</term> <note>the first civil basilica in Rome, built in 184 BC</note>, the house of Caesar, and the portico that Augustus built and named after his wife, Livia Drusilla, after tearing down Caesar’s house because it seemed to him too grand and proud a structure. This Temple was begun by the Emperor **Claudius** and brought to completion by **Vespasian** after he returned victorious from Judea; in it, he preserved all the vessels and ornaments that he carried in his triumph from the Temple of Jerusalem <note>Vespasian used the spoils from the Sack of Jerusalem in 70 AD to fund this "Forum of Peace"</note>. We read that this Temple was the largest, most magnificent, and richest in the City, and truly its ruins, even as dilapidated as they are, represent such greatness that one can very well judge what it was like when it was whole.

In front of the entrance there was a <term>loggia</term> <note>a gallery or arcade open to the air on one side</note> of three bays, made of <term>terracotta</term> <note>original: "pietra cotta," literally "cooked stone," referring to brickwork</note>, and the rest was a continuous wall for the entire width of the facade. On the pillars of the loggia’s arches, on the outside, there were columns placed for ornament, the order of which also continued along the continuous wall. Above this first loggia was another open one, with its balcony, and directly above each column, a statue must have been placed. In the interior part of the Temple, there were eight marble columns of the **Corinthian** order, five feet and four inches thick, and fifty-three feet long including the base and capital. The <term>Architrave</term>, <term>Frieze</term>, and <term>Cornice</term> <note>the three parts of the entablature that sit atop the columns</note> were ten and a half feet high, and they supported the vault of the middle nave. The base of these columns was taller than half the column's diameter, and its rim was thicker than a third part of its height—which they perhaps did because it seemed to them it could better support the weight placed upon it. Its projection was one-sixth of the column's diameter.

The Architrave, Frieze, and Cornice were carved with quite beautiful invention. The <term>cymatium</term> <note>the uppermost molding of a cornice</note> of the Architrave is worthy of notice for being different from others and very gracefully made. The Cornice has <term>modillions</term> <note>ornamental brackets</note> instead of a <term>dripstone</term> <note>original: "Gocciolatoio"; the projecting part of a cornice that throws off rain</note>. The coffers for the roses between the modillions are square, and they should be made this way, as I have observed in all ancient buildings. Writers say that this Temple burned in the time of the Emperor **Commodus**, which I do not see how it could be true, as there is no part made of wood; but it could easily be that it was ruined by an earthquake or some other similar accident, and then restored at another time when matters of Architecture were not so well understood as in the time of Vespasian. I am led to believe this by seeing that the carvings are not as well made, nor worked with that diligence seen in those of the Arch of Titus and other buildings made in the good times. The walls of this Temple were adorned with statues and paintings, and all the vaults were decorated with <term>stucco</term> compartments; nor was there any part that was not highly ornate. I have made three Plates of this Temple.

In the first, the plan is drawn.

In the second, the elevation of the exterior and interior of the facade, and the interior of the side.

In the third are the particular members.

### FOURTH [BOOK]. 151 / THE TEMPLE OF MARS THE AVENGER. Chap. VII.

Near the Conti Tower, one sees the ruins of the Temple formerly built by Augustus to <term>Mars the Avenger</term> <note>original: "Marte Vendicatore"; the temple was dedicated to Mars to celebrate the vengeance taken against the assassins of Julius Caesar.</note>, following the vow he made when he was at <term>Philippi</term> <note>original: "Farfaglia"; the author likely refers to the Battle of Philippi (42 BCE) where Augustus and Mark Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius, though the text uses a corrupted spelling.</note> with Mark Antony against Brutus and Cassius to seek vengeance for the death of Caesar, where he engaged in battle and won. From the parts that remain, one understands that this was a most ornate and marvelous building, and it must have been rendered much more admirable by the forum that stood before it. In this forum, we read that those who returned to the City as victors and triumphants would carry the standards of victory and triumph. Augustus placed two panels in its most beautiful part, on which were painted the methods of waging battle and triumphing; there were also two other panels by the hand of <term>Apelles</term> <note>A famous Greek painter of the 4th century BCE, highly prized by Roman collectors.</note>, in one of which were Castor and Pollux, the Goddess of Victory, and Alexander the Great; in the other was a representation of a battle and an Alexander. There were two porticos in which Augustus himself dedicated the statues of all those who had returned to Rome in triumph. Now, no trace of this forum is seen, unless those sections of wall on the sides of the Temple were part of it, which is very likely given the many niches for statues located there. The aspect of the Temple is <term>Peripteral</term> <note>original: "Peripteros"; a Greek term used by the ancient writer Vitruvius to describe a temple surrounded by a single row of columns on all sides.</note>; and because the width of the <term>cella</term> <note>the inner chamber of a temple where the cult statue was housed</note> exceeds twenty feet, columns are placed between the two <term>antae</term> <note>original: "anti"; square pillars at the ends of the walls</note> or pillars of the <term>Antetemple</term> <note>original: "Antitempio"; the porch or entrance hall (pronaos) of the temple</note> corresponding to those of the portico, as was stated above should be done in such cases. The portico does not continue around the entire Temple. Also, in the wings of the walls added on either side, the same order is not observed on the outside, although all parts correspond on the inside. From this, it is understood that there must have been a public street behind and alongside it, and that Augustus wished to accommodate the site so as not to cause inconvenience nor take away the houses neighboring the owners. The style of this Temple is <term>Pycnostyle</term> <note>original: "Picnoftilos"; an architectural arrangement where the space between columns is very narrow—specifically 1.5 times the diameter of a column.</note>; the porticos are as wide as the spaces between the columns. On the inside—that is, in the cella—no sign or trace is seen, nor are there even sockets in the walls from which one could firmly say that there were ornaments and tabernacles; nevertheless, because it is very likely that there were some, I have created them from my own invention. The columns of the porticos are of the <term>Corinthian order</term>. The capitals are carved with olive leaves and have an <term>abacus</term> <note>the flat slab on top of a capital</note> much larger than what is seen in others of that order, relative to the size of the whole capital. The first leaves are seen to swell somewhat near where they emerge, which gives them great grace. These porticos have beautiful ceilings, or what we call <term>coffers</term> <note>original: "lacunari"</note>; and therefore I have drawn their profile and their plan view. Around this Temple were very high walls of <term>Peperino</term> <note>a grey volcanic stone flecked with black, resembling peppercorns.</note>, which on the outside were of <term>rustic work</term> <note>rough-hewn masonry</note>, and on the inside had many tabernacles and places for placing statues. And so that everything may be seen perfectly, I have made seven plates of it.

-> * * * * * * * <-

In the First, there is the entire plan in small form, and the full elevation of as much as is seen of this building, both on the outside and the inside.

In the Second is the elevation of the side of the portico and the cella.

In the Third is the elevation of half the facade, with part of the walls that are at the sides of the Temple.

In the Fourth is the elevation of the interior part of the portico and the cella, with the ornaments that I have added.

In the Fifth are the ornaments of the Portico.
G, Is the Capital.
H, The Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.
I, The coffers of the portico, that is, the ceilings.

In the Sixth is drawn the ceiling of the portico, and how it turns at the antae or pillars of the Antetemple.
M, The ceiling of the Architrave between the columns.

### Details of the Corinthian Order

<note>This plate provides a detailed architectural breakdown of the Corinthian order from the Temple of Mars the Avenger. It focuses on the entablature—the horizontal structure supporting the roof—and the ornate capital of the column.</note>

**[Architectural Illustration]**

At the top left, we see a cross-section of the **cornice** <term>the projecting top edge of the entablature</term> and the **frieze** <term>the middle section of the entablature, often decorated</term>. The ornamentation includes **egg-and-dart** moldings <term>an alternating pattern of oval and pointed shapes</term>, **dentils** <term>small, rectangular blocks resembling teeth</term>, and **rosettes** <term>floral carvings</term> set within the recessed coffers of the overhang.*

A central flower adorns the top edge of the capital, just below the **abacus** <term>the flat slab at the very top of a capital</term>. The column shaft below is **fluted** <term>carved with vertical grooves</term>.*

### Detailed Proportions of the Corinthian Order

<note>This plate provides a rigorous architectural study of the Corinthian order as found in the Temple of Mars the Avenger. It focuses on the mathematical "parts" that determine the height and projection of each decorative element, ensuring classical harmony.</note>

**[Architectural Illustration]**

*This engraving provides a comprehensive breakdown of the temple's column components. The drawing is divided into specialized sections to show both the aesthetic carvings and the underlying geometry.*

*The top section, marked **F**, illustrates the **cornice** <term>the uppermost projecting section of the entablature</term>. The profile on the left shows the depth of the overhang, while the frontal view shows the spacing of the **modillions** <term>decorative brackets</term> and the **frieze**. The various numbers (such as 30 and 40½) represent modular units used by architects to scale the building regardless of its actual size.*

*The middle section, marked **E**, features the most famous element of this temple: the **Corinthian capital**. This specific design is renowned for its use of **Pegasi** <term>mythological winged horses</term> or griffins at the corners in place of standard **volutes** <term>scroll-like ornaments</term>. These figures emerge from layers of finely carved **acanthus leaves** <term>stylized foliage modeled after a Mediterranean plant</term>. The **abacus** <term>the flat slab at the very top of the capital</term> is topped with a central floral rosette. Below the capital, the **fluted** column shaft <term>carved with vertical grooves</term> begins.*

*The lower section, marked **D**, illustrates the **pedestal** <term>the block that supports the column</term>. A notable feature here is the decorative band labeled **B**, which showcases a "running dog" or **Vitruvian wave** pattern <term>a repeating scroll-like motif resembling a breaking wave</term>.*

*The vertical stack of measurements on the left edge provides the exact height of each molding in the base, labeled in parts and minutes to maintain the strict proportions required by the Roman style.*

# ON THE TEMPLE OF NERVA TRAJAN. Chapter VIII.

NEAR the aforementioned Temple built by Augustus, one sees the remains of the Temple of Nerva Trajan <note>This likely refers to the Temple of Trajan or the structures within the Forum of Trajan/Nerva</note>. Its design is **Prostyle** <term>Prostyle: a temple with a row of columns across the front only</term>, and its style is of closely spaced columns. The portico, together with the **cella** <term>cella: the inner chamber of a classical temple</term>, is a little less than two squares long. The floor of this Temple is raised from the ground by a **basement** <term>basement: a high podium or platform supporting a building</term> that runs around the entire structure and forms a side-wall for the steps used to ascend to the portico. At the ends of these side-walls, there were two statues—one at each head of the basement. The base of the columns is **Attic** <term>Attic base: a popular Roman column base consisting of two large rings (tori) separated by a concave groove (scotia)</term>, differing in this from the one taught to us by **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura'</note> and which I included in the first book, in that it has two additional **astragals** <term>astragals: small, rounded moldings often called beads</term>: one below the **cavetto** <term>cavetto: a hollow, concave molding</term> and the other below the **cincture** <term>cincture: a ring-like molding at the base of the column shaft</term>. The "tongues" of the capitals are carved into olive leaves, and these leaves are arranged in groups of five, like the fingers on a human hand; I have observed that all ancient capitals of this type are made this way, and they turn out better and with more grace than those where the leaves are grouped in fours. On the **architrave** <term>architrave: the lowest part of the entablature, resting directly on the column capitals</term> are beautiful carvings that divide one band from another, and these carvings and divisions are only on the sides of the Temple. This is because, on the front, the architrave and the **frieze** <term>frieze: the middle part of the entablature, often decorated with reliefs</term> were made into a single flat surface to conveniently hold the inscription, of which a few letters can still be seen, though they are truncated and worn by time.

->EMPEROR NERVA CAESAR AUGUSTUS, SUPREME PONTIFF,<-
->HOLDER OF TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE SECOND TIME, ACCLAIMED EMPEROR TWICE, PROCONSUL.<-
<note>Original Latin inscription: IMPERATOR NERVA CAESAR AVG. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. II. IMPERATOR II. PROCOS.</note>

The **cornice** <term>cornice: the uppermost projecting section of the entablature</term> is very finely carved and has beautiful and highly appropriate projections. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice together equal one-fourth of the length of the columns. The walls are built of **Peperino** <term>Peperino: a grey volcanic tuff stone used in Roman construction</term> and were once clad in marble. Inside the cella, along the walls, I have placed tabernacles with statues, as the ruins suggest they were once there. Before this Temple was a square, in the middle of which stood the statue of the said Emperor. Writers say that its ornaments were so many and so marvelous that they struck those who looked upon them with awe, judging them the work not of men, but of giants. Thus, when the Emperor **Constantius** <note>Constantius II, who visited Rome in 357 AD</note> came to Rome, he was first amazed by the rare structure of this building; then, turning to his architect, he said he wished to make a horse in Constantinople similar to that of Nerva in his memory. To this, **Hormisdas** (for that was the architect’s name) replied that it would first be necessary to build him a stable like this one, referring to this square. The columns surrounding it do not have pedestals but rise from the ground, as it was very reasonable that the Temple should be more prominent than the other parts. These too are of the **Corinthian** order, and directly above the cornice there were small pilasters on which statues must have been placed. No one should wonder that I place such an abundance of statues in these buildings, for we read that there were so many in Rome that they seemed like a second population. I have made six plates of this building.

In the first is half of the Temple's facade.
**T** is the side entrance.

In the second is the internal elevation, and nearby is the plan of the Temple and the square together.
**S** is the place where the statue of Trajan stood.

In the third is the side elevation of the portico, and through the spaces between columns, one can see the order of columns that surrounded the square.

In the fourth is half of the facade of the square facing the Temple.

In the fifth are the ornaments of the Temple portico. **A** is the basement of the whole structure.
**B** is the Base. **C** is the Architrave. **D** is the Frieze. **E** is the Cornice.
**F** is the ceiling of the architrave between the columns.

In the sixth are the ornaments surrounding the square. **G** is the Base. **H** is the Architrave.
**I** is the Frieze, which was carved with figures in low relief. **K** is the Cornice.
**L** are the small pilasters upon which statues were placed. **M** are the ornaments of the square doors located in the facade of the square opposite the Temple portico.

<summary>Palladio provides an architectural reconstruction and description of the Temple of Nerva Trajan, detailing its unique Attic base, its Corinthian ornaments, and the massive scale of the surrounding forum. He emphasizes the grandeur of the complex through a historical anecdote about Emperor Constantius and the architect Hormisdas.</summary>

<keywords>Temple of Nerva Trajan, Forum of Trajan, Corinthian order, Attic base, Roman engineering, Peperino stone, classical proportions, Emperor Constantius, Hormisdas, architectural plates</keywords>

The drawings use a system of modular measurements, indicated by the letter **P** <note>original: "P," likely standing for "Parti" (Parts) or "Palmi" (Palms), a standard unit of architectural measurement during the Renaissance</note>, to ensure mathematical harmony between every element of the structure.

The upper portion of the drawing provides a detailed section of the **entablature** <term>the set of horizontal mouldings supported by the columns</term>.

*   **E - The Cornice:** The uppermost element, featuring a series of **modillions** <term>ornamental brackets found under the corona of a cornice</term> and **dentils** <term>small, tooth-like rectangular blocks</term>. The measurements here (such as 27, 30, and 33) define the projection and height of each individual curve and flat surface.
*   **D - The Architrave:** The main beam that rests directly upon the capitals. It is divided into horizontal bands, providing a sturdy visual base for the decoration above.
*   **C - The Frieze:** The middle section of the entablature. In this specific temple, the frieze is notable for its relief carvings, though here it is shown in profile to highlight its depth and relationship to the other parts.

### The Corinthian Capital and Shaft
The lower half of the plate focuses on the column itself, particularly the iconic **Corinthian capital** <term>the decorated top of the column shaft</term>.

*   **The Capital:** This is the most complex element of the order. It is decorated with two tiers of **acanthus leaves** <term>stylized representations of the Mediterranean acanthus plant</term>. Above the leaves, the **volutes** <term>spiral, scroll-like ornaments</term> curl outward to support the corners of the **abacus** <term>the flat slab at the very top of the capital</term>. The measurements (P I 1/4 through P I 4) denote the vertical proportions of the leaf-rows and scrolls.
*   **A - The Column Shaft:** Only the top and bottom of the shaft are shown. The lower segment illustrates the **fluting** <term>the vertical grooves carved into the column shaft</term>, which adds a sense of rhythm and slender elegance to the stone.
*   **B - The Column Base:** The column sits upon a **base** consisting of a series of rings and cushions. The profile on the left shows how the base transitions from the vertical shaft to the horizontal **plinth** <term>the square block at the very bottom of the column</term>.

# BOOK FOURTH
## OF THE TEMPLE OF ANTONINUS AND FAUSTINA. Chapter IX.

Near the Temple of Peace described above, one sees the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina; thus, it is the opinion of some that Antoninus was placed by the Ancients among the number of their Gods, because he had this Temple, and had the Salii priests and the Antonine priests dedicated to him. The façade of this Temple is made of columns, and its style is the **Pycnostyle** <term>an architectural arrangement where columns are placed very close together, specifically one and a half diameters apart</term>. The floor, or ground, of the Temple is raised from the earth by one-third of the height of the portico columns; and one ascends to it by steps, which are flanked by two pedestals that continue in their order around the entire Temple. The base of these pedestals is thicker than half of the **cimacia** <term>the uppermost molding or "crown" of a pedestal or cornice</term>, and it is made more simply; I have observed that the ancients made all such pedestals similarly, even in the pedestals placed under columns, and with good reason, as all parts of a building should be more solid the closer they are to the ground. At the extreme end of these, aligned with the corner columns of the portico, there were two statues; that is, one for each pedestal head. The base of the columns is **Attic** <term>a popular column base consisting of two large rounded moldings separated by a hollow groove</term>. The capital is carved with olive leaves. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice together measure one-fourth and one-third of that fourth part of the height of the columns. On the architrave, these words can still be read:

->TO THE DIVINE ANTONINUS AND<-
->TO THE DIVINE FAUSTINA BY DECREE OF THE SENATE<-
<note>original: "DIVO ANTONINO, ET DIVAE FAVSTINAE EX S. C." The "S. C." stands for *Senatus Consulto*, meaning the temple was dedicated by official decree of the Roman Senate.</note>

In the frieze are carved Griffins which face one another, placing their front paws upon candelabra of the form they used in sacrifices. The cornice does not have carved **dentils** <term>small, block-like tooth-like moldings</term> and is without modillions; but between the dentil and the drip-edge, it has a quite large **ovolo** <term>a rounded, convex molding, often decorated with an egg-and-dart pattern</term>. It is not apparent that there was any ornament on the inside of this Temple; yet, considering the magnificence of those Emperors, I am led to believe there must have been some, and therefore I have placed statues there in my drawings. This Temple had a courtyard in front of it, which was made of **Peperino** <term>a grey volcanic tuff stone containing fragments of "peppers" or black minerals, commonly used in Rome</term>. At its entrance, opposite the portico of the Temple, there were beautiful arches, and all around there were columns and many ornaments, of which no trace is seen today; I myself saw a part of it that was still standing being demolished while I was in Rome. From the sides of the Temple, there were two other open entrances; that is, without arches. In the middle of this courtyard was the bronze equestrian statue of Antoninus, which is now in the Piazza del Campidoglio.
<note>Palladio identifies the famous bronze equestrian statue as Antoninus Pius; today it is known to represent his successor, Marcus Aurelius. It was moved to the Capitoline Hill (Campidoglio) by Michelangelo.</note>

Of this Temple, I have made five plates.

In the **First** is the side elevation of the exterior: through the spaces between the portico columns, one sees the arrangement of the columns and the ornaments that were around the courtyard.

In the **Second** is the drawing of half the façade of the Temple, and the vaulted part of the courtyard.

In the **Third** is the elevation of the portico and the **cella** <term>the inner chamber of a temple where the cult statue stood</term> on the inside.
**B** is the wall that divides the portico from the cella. Beside it is drawn the plan of the Temple and the courtyard.
**A** is the place where the statue of Antoninus stood.
**Q** is the side entrance of the Temple.
**R** is the entrance opposite the portico of the Temple.

In the **Fourth** is the elevation of half the entrance that faced the front of the Temple.

In the **Fifth** are the ornaments of the portico of the Temple.
**A** is the pedestal.
**B** is the base.
**C** is the capital.
**D** is the architrave where the inscription is located.
**E** is the frieze.
**F** is the uncarved dentil.
**G** is a small cornice placed on the sides of the Temple on the exterior.

->**Technical Details and Proportions**<-

<note>The letters Q and R found on the plan correspond to specific structural alignments and the spacing between columns, which was a primary concern for architects studying the "Perfect Order" of antiquity.</note>

### Architectural Elevation of a Multi-Tiered Monument

The illustration on this page provides a comprehensive technical drawing of a monumental facade, focusing on the integration of sculpture and structural elements.

**Upper Level: The Statuary Attic**
The uppermost section of the structure features a row of ten classical statues.
*   **Figures 1–10:** These figures represent a variety of subjects in both draped and nude forms, following the Roman tradition of placing statues atop a building's <term>attic</term> <note>the story or low wall situated above the main cornice of a building</note>. These figures would typically represent deities, virtues, or historical personages.

**Middle Level: The Balustrade**
Below the main row of statues sits a decorative railing or balustrade.
*   **Pedestal Figures:** Four smaller statues are positioned here. Two are winged figures—likely <term>putti</term> <note>cherub-like representations of infants, common in Renaissance and Classical art</note>—and two are adult male figures standing on pedestals.
*   **Relief Work:** To the right, a framed <term>relief sculpture</term> <note>a carved work where the figures remain attached to a solid background</note> is integrated into the wall section.

**Lower Level: The Triple Arcade**
The base of the visible structure consists of a grand <term>arcade</term> <note>a succession of arches supported by columns or piers</note>.
*   **Arches:** Three large arches form a portico or entrance.
*   **Columns:** These arches are supported by columns topped with highly decorative <term>capitals</term> <note>the crowning member of a column that provides a transition to the weight it supports</note>.
*   **Statuary Base:** On the far right, a separate statue stands upon a large, ornate pedestal, flanking the main entrance.

**Measurement and Scale:**
The drawing is densely annotated with numbers (1 through 39) and technical abbreviations to indicate precise proportions.
*   **Measurement Units:** The labels **P**, **I**, and **S** likely refer to the units of measurement used by the architect <note>original: "P-I-S"; likely standing for Piedi (Feet), Pollici (Inches), and Secondi or Scrupoli (smaller divisions or "grains")</note>.
*   **Reference Point R:** The letter **R** is used as a specific reference point for the vertical calculations of the structure’s height.

### Proportions of the Corinthian Entablature and Capital

This plate provides a detailed technical breakdown of the <term>Corinthian order</term> <note>the most ornate of the three main classical orders of ancient Greek and Roman architecture, characterized by slender fluted columns and elaborate capitals decorated with acanthus leaves</note>, specifically focusing on the upper elements of a building's facade.

**The Entablature (Sections B, F, E, and D)**
The upper portion of the diagram details the <term>entablature</term> <note>the superstructure of moldings and bands which lie horizontally above columns</note>. The architect has provided specific fractional measurements to ensure the "perfect" classical profile.

*   **The Cornice (B):** This is the uppermost projecting section. The diagram lists various heights for the <term>moldings</term> <note>the contoured decorative strips</note> using fractions such as 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 1/4, 1/3, 2/5, 3/5, and 4/5. These ratios ensure that the shadows and depth of the stone carvings appear balanced to the eye from below.
*   **The Decorative Frieze (F & E):** The middle section of the entablature, known as the <term>frieze</term>, is depicted with a "zoomorphic" or animal-based motif. It shows a relief of a winged lion or <term>griffin</term> <note>a legendary creature with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle</note> with its paw resting upon an ornate <term>candelabrum</term> <note>a decorative stand for lamps or candles, frequently used as a vertical ornament in Roman wall carvings</note>.
*   **The Architrave (D):** The lowest part of the entablature, which rests directly on the capitals. The drawing shows the division of this beam into horizontal bands.

**The Corinthian Capital (C)**
The lower section of the plate illustrates a highly decorative <term>capital</term> <note>the crowning member of a column providing structural support for the architrave</note>.

*   **Acanthus Leaves:** The capital is wrapped in two distinct rows of <term>acanthus</term> leaves <note>a motif based on the leaves of the Mediterranean Acanthus plant, a staple of Corinthian decoration</note>.
*   **Volutes and Abacus:** At the corners, spiraling <term>volutes</term> <note>scroll-like ornaments</note> emerge from the foliage to support the <term>abacus</term> <note>the flat slab forming the top of a capital</note>. In the center of the abacus is a carved flower, a standard feature of this architectural style.

**The Column Shaft (A)**
*   To the left, a section of the <term>shaft</term> <note>the long, cylindrical part of the column between the base and the capital</note> is shown with its base molding, demonstrating how the vertical column transitions into the ornate capital above.

# BOOK OF THE TEMPLES OF THE SUN AND THE MOON. Chapter X.

Near the Arch of Titus, in the garden of Santa Maria Nova <note>now known as the site of the Basilica of Santa Francesca Romana, located between the Roman Forum and the Colosseum</note>, one can see two temples of the same form and with the same ornaments. The one situated toward the East is believed to have been the Temple of the Sun, while the other, facing toward the West, the Temple of the Moon. These temples were built and dedicated by <term>T. Tatius</term> <note>Titus Tatius, the legendary King of the Sabines who, according to tradition, ruled alongside Romulus</note>, King of the Romans. They approach a circular form because they are as wide as they are long; this was done out of respect for the path of the said planets, which is circular around the Heavens.

The <term>loggias</term> <note>covered galleries or porches supported by columns</note> that once stood before the entrances of these temples are completely ruined. No other ornaments are visible except for those on the <term>vaults</term> <note>the arched ceilings</note>, which feature <term>stucco</term> compartments worked with great diligence and beautiful invention. The walls of these temples are extremely thick; and between one temple and the other, alongside the large <term>chapels</term> <note>the recessed niches or apses</note> which face the entrance, one can see the remains of some stairs that must have led to the roof. I have reconstructed the loggias in front and the interior ornaments as I imagined they must have been, taking into consideration what is visible today above ground and the little that could be seen of the foundations. I have made two plates regarding these Temples.

In the First Plate, there are the plans of both temples as they are joined together; one can see where the stairs are located, which I mentioned led above the roof. Beside these plans are the exterior and interior <term>elevations</term> <note>flat drawings of the vertical sides of the building</note>.

In the Second Plate are the ornaments: specifically those of the vaults, as the others are ruined and no trace of them remains, along with the interior side elevations.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**A**, These are the compartments of the chapels facing the doors; there are twelve squares for each.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**C**, This is the <term>profile</term> and <term>sacoma</term> <note>a full-scale template or contour of a molding</note> of said squares.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**B**, These are the compartments of the large <term>nave</term> <note>the central main body of the temple</note>, which is divided into nine squares.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**D**, This is the profile and <term>modano</term> <note>an architectural term for a mold or the specific curvature of a decorative molding</note> of the said squares.

# FOURTH BOOK

->**Decorative Details and Wall Elevations**<-

This plate illustrates the refined ornamental vocabulary used to decorate the interior surfaces of the temple. These details provided the Roman builders with both structural lightness and aesthetic richness.

### Ornamental Bands
The upper portion of the drawing isolates three distinct decorative patterns used throughout the structure:
*   **Frieze D**: The uppermost band depicts a <term>frieze</term> <note>a decorative horizontal band typically found above columns</note> adorned with stylized <term>acanthus</term> <note>a plant with thick, scalloped leaves used as a standard classical motif</note> and shell-like motifs.
*   **Coffered Ceiling B**: Below the frieze is a detail of the <term>coffers</term> <note>sunken decorative panels in a ceiling, also called lacunaria</note>. Each square coffer is deep-set with concentric borders and features a central **rosette** <note>a stylized flower ornament</note>. They are separated by a vertical twisted cable or "rope" pattern.
*   **Geometric Mosaic C**: A third band illustrates a complex geometric pattern composed of interlocking diamonds and triangles, likely representing a <term>mosaic</term> <note>a floor or wall covering made of small colored pieces of stone or glass</note> or an inlaid marble floor.

### Wall Elevation and Statuary
The lower half of the plate shows the reconstruction of a wall section or facade, demonstrating how the decorative elements were integrated with the architecture.
- **Niches and Statues (1-5)**: A series of five arched <term>niches</term> <note>recesses in a wall specifically designed to hold a statue or urn</note> are shown. Each contains a standing figure, numbered **1 through 5**, framed by elegant <term>pilasters</term> <note>shallow rectangular columns attached to a wall</note>.
- **Structural Arches**: To the right, two large arched openings are visible. The arch labeled **A** and the one marked with the number **32** show the transition from the decorated wall to the larger structural voids of the building.
- **Entrance G**: On the far left, a smaller arched entrance is labeled **G**, providing a sense of scale for the human figures depicted nearby.
- **Scale O**: At the bottom center, a linear scale bar marked **0, 1, 2** allows for the calculation of the proportions of these decorative elements in relation to the whole.

# BOOK FOUR

# ON THE TEMPLE COMMONLY CALLED THE GALLUCE
### Chapter XI.

Near the Trophies of Marius <note>A monumental fountain built under Emperor Alexander Severus, though long misidentified as a monument to the Roman general Gaius Marius</note>, one sees the following building of a round shape. After the "machine" of the <term>Pantheon</term> <note>the famous circular Roman temple with its massive dome</note>, this is the largest structure of a circular design in Rome. This place is commonly called "the Galluce" <note>original: "le Galluce"; a name historically given to the Nymphaeum of Licinius, once mistakenly called the Temple of Minerva Medica</note>, which has led some to claim that this was the Basilica of Gaius and Lucius. This <term>basilica</term> <note>a large public building used for legal and business matters</note>, together with a beautiful portico, was commissioned by Augustus in the name of Gaius and Lucius, his grandsons. I do not believe this to be true, however, because this building lacks any of the features required of a basilica. I have already explained how those were constructed in my third book, where I divided the areas of the public squares according to the descriptions of **Vitruvius** <note>the primary Roman authority on architecture whose writings guided the Renaissance</note>. Therefore, I believe it was a Temple.

This building is constructed entirely of <term>fired brick</term> <note>original: "pietra cotta"</note> and must have been clad in marble, though it is now completely stripped. The central **cella** <note>the inner chamber of a temple</note>, which is a perfect circle, is divided into ten faces; in each face, there is a chapel recessed into the thickness of the walls, except for the face where the entrance is located. The two chambers <note>original: "celle"</note> on the sides must have been highly decorated, as many <term>niches</term> <note>recesses for statues</note> can be seen there. It is likely there were columns and other ornaments which, accompanying said niches, would have created a most beautiful effect.

Those who designed the Emperor's chapel and the chapel of the King of France at Saint Peter's <note>referring to two ancient circular structures, the rotunda of St. Andrew and St. Petronilla, which were repurposed as chapels for the Holy Roman Emperor and the French monarchy before being demolished</note>, which have since been ruined, took their example from this building. Because it has structural members on all its sides that act as **buttresses** <note>original: "contraforti"; structural supports that push back against the weight of the roof</note>, it is very strong and has remained standing for a long time. Because no ornamentation is visible in this temple (as I have mentioned), I have produced only one plate, which contains the plan and the interior elevation.

# BOOK FOUR. OF THE TEMPLE OF JUPITER. Chapter XII.

On the Quirinal Hill, today called Monte Cavallo <note>Italian: 'Horse Hill', named after the giant statues of the Dioscuri mentioned later in the text</note>, behind the houses of the Colonna lords, one can see the remains of the following building, which is called the Frontispiece of Nero. Some maintain that the Tower of Maecenas was located here, and that from this place Nero watched the city of Rome burn with great delight; however, they are quite mistaken, because the Tower of Maecenas was on the Esquiline Hill, not far from the Baths of Diocletian. Others have said that the houses of the Cornelii family were here. For my part, I believe this was a temple dedicated to Jupiter: because while I was in Rome, I saw excavations where the main body of the temple stood, and several Ionic capitals were found which served the interior of the temple. These belonged to the corners of the loggias, because the middle part, in my opinion, was open to the sky.

The layout of this temple was the "false-winged" style called by Vitruvius <term>Pseudodipteros</term> <note>A temple design that appears to have a double row of columns, but the inner row is omitted to create a wider portico</note>. Its style consisted of closely spaced columns. The columns of the exterior porticos were of the Corinthian order. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice were one-fourth the height of the columns. The architrave had its <term>cyma</term> <note>the uppermost molding of a cornice</note> of a very beautiful design. The frieze on the sides was carved with foliage, but on the front, which is now ruined, there must have been the letters of the inscription. The cornice has squared <term>modillions</term> <note>ornamental brackets supporting the weight of the roof's overhang</note>, and one of them aligns directly with the center of the column. The modillions in the cornice of the pediment are set vertically, as they should be. In the interior of the temple, there must have been porticos, as I have drawn. 

Around this temple, there was a courtyard decorated with columns and statues, and in front were the two horses seen today in the public street, from which the hill took its name, Monte Cavallo; one was made by Praxiteles and the other by Phidias <note>Famous Greek sculptors; the statues are actually Roman copies of Greek originals</note>. There were very convenient stairs that ascended to the temple, and in my opinion, this must have been the largest and most decorated temple in Rome. I have made six plates of it.

In the first is the plan of the entire building with the rear part, where the stairs were located; these, rising one above the other, led into the courtyards that were at the sides of the temple. The elevation of this style of stairs, with a larger-scale plan, was placed by me above in the first book, where I treat the different styles of stairs.

In the second is the exterior side of the temple.

In the third is half of the exterior facade of the temple.

In the fourth is the interior part; and in both of these plates, one can see a small portion of the courtyard decorations.

In the fifth is the side of the interior part.

In the sixth are the decorations.

**A**, The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice.
**C**, The base.
**E**, The capital of the portico columns.
**D**, The base of the pilasters that correspond to the columns.
**B**, The cornice that goes around the courtyards.
**F**, The <term>Acroterion</term> <note>original: 'Acroteria'; pedestals at the corners or peak of a roof, often supporting statues</note>.

# BOOK FOUR.
# OF THE TEMPLE OF JUPITER.
## Chapter 12.

On the Quirinal Hill, today called Monte Cavallo <note>The hill is now the site of the Quirinal Palace, the official residence of the President of the Italian Republic. It was called Monte Cavallo due to the colossal statues of the "Horse Tamers" located there.</note>, behind the houses of the Colonna lords <note>The Colonna family were powerful Roman nobles whose palace remains nearby.</note>, one can see the remains of the following building, which is called the "Frontispiece of Nero" <note>Historically known as the Temple of Serapis, this massive ruin was a prominent landmark in the 16th century before its eventual destruction.</note>. Some claim that the Tower of Maecenas <note>Maecenas was the wealthy cultural advisor to Emperor Augustus; his gardens and tower were legendary symbols of Roman luxury.</note> was located here, and that from this place Nero watched the city of Rome burn with such great delight; in this they are much mistaken, because the Tower of Maecenas was on the Esquiline Hill, not far from the Baths of Diocletian <note>The largest of the imperial bath complexes, built around 300 AD.</note>. 

There have been others who said that the houses of the Cornelii <note>A prestigious ancient Roman family (the gens Cornelia) that included famous figures like Scipio Africanus.</note> were here. For my part, I believe that this was a temple dedicated to Jupiter; for while I was in Rome, I saw excavations where the body of the temple was, and some <term>Ionic capitals</term> <note>The decorative tops of columns identified by their spiral, scroll-like "volutes."</note> were found which served the interior part of the temple, and they were those from the corners of the loggias, because the middle part, in my opinion, was open to the sky. 

The appearance of this temple was the "false-winged" style called <term>Pseudodipteros</term> <note>original: "Pseudodipteros"; a Greek architectural term describing a temple that looks like it has a double row of columns (dipteral), but the inner row is omitted to create a wider covered walkway.</note> by Vitru... <note>The text cuts off, likely referring to Vitruvius, the 1st-century BC Roman architect whose treatise 'De architectura' was the standard authority for Renaissance builders.</note>
