# BOOK ON THE TEMPLE OF FORTUNA VIRILIS. Chapter XIII.

->[THE TEMPLE OF MANLY FORTUNE]<-

Near the Senatorial Bridge, today called the Bridge of Santa Maria, one can see the following temple almost entirely intact; it is currently the Church of Saint Mary of Egypt. It is not known for certain what it was called in ancient times. Some say it was the **Temple of Fortuna Virilis** <note>Manly Fortune</note>, of which one reads a marvelous thing: that when it burned down with everything inside, only the gilded wooden statue of **Servius Tullius** <note>The legendary sixth king of Rome</note> that was within was found safe, completely unharmed by the fire.

But because temples to Fortune were regularly built in a round shape, others have said that it was not a temple at all, but the **Basilica of C. Lucius** <note>The Basilica of Gaius and Lucius</note>, basing this opinion on certain inscriptions found there. In my judgment, this cannot be true: first, because this building is small, and **basilicas** <term>basilica: in Roman times, a large public hall for law courts and business</term> were necessarily large buildings due to the quantity of people who did business in them; and second, because in basilicas, the porticos were built on the inside, while in this temple there is no trace of an internal portico. Therefore, I believe for certain that it was a temple.

Its form is **Prostyle** <term>prostyle: a temple with a row of columns across the front but not on the sides or back</term>, and it has half-columns set into the walls of the **cella** <term>cella: the inner chamber of a temple where the cult statue was kept</term> on the outside. These align with the columns of the portico and have the same ornaments; thus, to those who see it from the side, it gives the appearance of being winged all around <note>original: "alato a torno"; this refers to a pseudo-peripteral style, where engaged columns mimic a free-standing colonnade</note>. The **intercolumniations** <term>intercolumniation: the space between two columns</term> are two and a quarter diameters wide, so its style is **Systyle** <note>A tight spacing of columns defined by Vitruvius</note>. The floor of the temple is raised six and a half feet from the ground, and one ascends to it by steps, which are flanked by the **pedestals** <note>the supportive bases of the entire structure</note>.

The columns are of the **Ionic order**. The base is **Attic**, despite the fact that it seems it should also be Ionic, just like the capital. However, one does not find any building where the Ancients used the Ionic base exactly as described by **Vitruvius** <note>The Roman architect whose 1st-century BCE treatise defined the "rules" of classical architecture</note>. The columns are fluted and have twenty-four channels. The **volutes** <term>volute: the spiral, scroll-like ornament of an Ionic capital</term> of the capitals are oval. The capitals located at the corners of the portico and the temple face two sides; I do not know if I have seen this elsewhere. Because it seemed to me a beautiful and graceful invention, I have used it in many buildings, and how it is made will appear in the drawing. The ornaments of the temple door are very beautiful and well-proportioned. This entire temple is made of **Peperino** <term>peperino: a gray volcanic tuff stone containing fragments of basalt and limestone</term> and is covered in stucco. I have made three plates of it.

### [Plate One: The Plan and Base Details]

In the first plate is the plan with some ornaments.

H, is the base }
I, the die. } of the pedestal, which supports the entire building.
K, the cymatium. } <note>the crowning molding of the pedestal</note>
L, is the base of the columns above the pedestal.
F, the ornaments of the door.
G, the bracket of said door in front view.

### [Plate Two: The Facade]

In the second plate is the facade of the temple.

M, is the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice.
O, the pediment.
P, the plan. }
Q, the side view. } of the capital.
R, the core without the volute.

### [Plate Three: The Side View]

In the third plate is the side of the temple.

M, is part of the frieze, which circles around the whole temple with such carvings.
S, is the plan of the corner capitals, by which one easily understands how they are made.

### BOOK OF THE TEMPLE OF VESTA. Chapter 14.

Following along the bank of the Tiber near the aforementioned Temple <note>The author refers to the Temple of Portunus, historically called the Temple of Virile Fortune, discussed in the previous chapter.</note> one finds another round temple, which today is called Santo Stefano <note>This building is the Temple of Hercules Victor, though in the Renaissance it was frequently misidentified as the Temple of Vesta or the Church of Santo Stefano alle Carrozze.</note>. They say it was built by Numa Pompilio <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious institutions.</note> and dedicated to the Goddess Vesta. He intended it to be of a round shape to resemble the element of the earth, by which human life is sustained, and of which they said Vesta was the Goddess. This Temple is of the Corinthian order. The <term>intercolumniations: the space between two adjacent columns</term> are one and a half diameters. The columns, including the base and capital, are eleven "heads" long ("head" refers, as I have said elsewhere, to the diameter of the column at its base). The bases are without a <term>plinth: the square slab or "zoccolo" that usually sits beneath the base of a column</term> or pedestal; instead, the step where they rest serves that purpose. The Architect who designed it did this so that entry into the portico would be less obstructed, as the style uses closely spaced columns. 

The <term>cella: the inner chamber of a temple</term>, including the thickness of the walls, has a diameter equal to the length of the columns. The capitals are carved with olive leaves <note>While Corinthian capitals typically use acanthus leaves, the author notes the use of olive leaves here, a specific detail of this building's decoration.</note>. The <term>cornice: the crowning molding of an entablature</term> is not visible; however, it has been added by me in the drawing. Under the ceiling of the portico, there are very beautiful <term>lacunaria: sunken ornamental panels, also known as coffers</term>. The door and the windows have very beautiful and clean ornaments. Under the portico, and on the inside of the Temple, there are <term>cymas: moldings with a double-curve profile</term> that support the windows and run all the way around, creating the appearance of a <term>basement: the lower part of a wall or structure, acting as a continuous pedestal</term> upon which the wall is founded and upon which the <term>tribune: a vaulted or domed ceiling</term> rests. This wall, on the outside (that is, under the porticoes), is divided into square panels from the said cornice up to the ceiling; on the inside, it is smooth and has a cornice equal to that of the porticoes, which supports the tribune. I have made three plates of this Temple.

**[Architectural Floor Plan: Temple of Vesta]**

*This architectural diagram illustrates the floor plan of the circular temple. The structure consists of an outer ring of twenty Corinthian columns surrounding a central circular room (the cella). The plan includes specific measurements in "P" (Palmi or feet) and "m" (minuti or minutes).*

| :--- | :--- |

| Distance between the cella wall and the outer columns | P 6 1/2 m 1/4 |

### BOOK FOUR.

In the first plate, which precedes this one, the <term>floor plan: a drawing showing the horizontal arrangement of the building's walls and columns</term> is shown.

In the second, the <term>elevation: a scale drawing of the vertical side of a building</term> is presented, showing both the exterior view and the interior section.

In the third, the individual <term>elements: the specific parts or components of the architectural design</term> are illustrated.

**A.** The base of the columns.
**B.** The <term>capital: the decorative top of a column</term>.
**C.** The <term>entablature: the upper section of a classical order</term> consisting of the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice.
**D.** The ornaments of the doorway.
**E.** The ornaments of the windows.
**F.** The small exterior cornice around the <term>cella: the inner chamber of the temple</term>, which serves as the starting point for the decorative wall panels.
**G.** The small interior cornice, upon which the sills of the windows rest.
**H.** The ceiling of the <term>portico: a porch or walkway supported by columns</term>.

# FOURTH BOOK. ON THE TEMPLE OF MARS, Chapter XV.

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative woodcut initial 'A' at the beginning of the text, depicting figures in a classical landscape with architectural ruins.</image-desc>

At the square commonly called the Piazza dei Preti <note>now known as Piazza di Pietra</note>, which is found when going from the Rotunda <note>the Pantheon</note> to the Column of Antoninus <note>the Column of Marcus Aurelius</note>, one sees the remains of the following temple. According to some, it was built by Emperor Antoninus and dedicated to the God Mars <note>modern archeology identifies these ruins as the Temple of Hadrian, built by his successor Antoninus Pius</note>. Its appearance is winged all around <note>original: "lo alato a torno"; this refers to a peripteral temple, surrounded by a colonnade</note>. Its manner is of closely spaced columns. The <term>intercolumniations: the space between two adjacent columns</term> are one diameter and a half. The porticos around it are wider than a single intercolumniation by as much as the <term>antae: square pillars at the end of a wall</term> project from the rest of the walls. The columns are of the Corinthian order.

The base is Attic; and it has a small bead <note>original: "bastoncino"</note> under the cincture of the column; the cincture, or fillet, is very thin, and thus appears very graceful. It is made so thin whenever it is joined with a small bead above the <term>torus: the large, rounded molding at the base of a column</term>—also called a bead—because there is no danger of it breaking. The capital is carved with olive leaves and is very well designed. The architrave, in place of a flat molding, has a half-ovolo <term>ovolo: a rounded, convex molding</term>, and above that a cavetto <term>cavetto: a hollow, concave molding</term>. This cavetto has very beautiful carvings, different from those of the Temple of Peace and the temple we mentioned earlier on the Quirinal Hill dedicated to Jupiter. The frieze leans outward by one-eighth of its height and is swollen in the middle <note>this is known as a pulvinated frieze</note>. The cornice has squared modillions <term>modillions: decorative brackets placed under a cornice</term>, and above those the corona; it does not have dentils, as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect and author of 'De Architectura'</note> says should be done whenever modillions are used, though this rule is seen to have been observed in few ancient buildings. Above the cornice on the sides of the temple, there is a small cornice which aligns its face with the face of the modillions; this was made to place statues upon, so that they could be seen entirely, and their feet and legs would not be hidden by the projection of the cornice. On the inner part of the portico, there is an architrave of the same height as the one on the outside; but it differs in that it has three <term>fasciae: the flat, horizontal bands that make up an architrave</term>. The members that divide one fascia from another are small moldings carved with leaves and little arches, and the smallest fascia is also carved with leaves. Furthermore, in place of a flat molding, this one has an astragal <term>astragal: a small molding shaped like a string of beads</term> above a cyma recta <term>cyma recta: an S-shaped molding, concave at the top and convex at the bottom</term> worked very delicately with leaves. This architrave supports the vaults of the porticos. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice together make up one out of five and a half parts of the length of the columns; and although they are less than a fifth part, they nevertheless turn out admirably and with much grace. The walls on the outside are made of Peperino <note>a grey volcanic tuff stone</note>, and inside the temple there are other walls of brick <note>original: "pietra cotta," literally "baked stone"</note> so that they might be better suited to support the vault, which was made with beautiful panels worked in stucco. These walls were clad in marble, and there were niches and columns around them for ornament. Nearly an entire side of this temple can be seen; nonetheless, I have endeavored to show it in its entirety as best as I could determine from its ruins and from what Vitruvius teaches us. Therefore, I have made five plates of it.

# BOOK FOURTH. 61

## ON THE BAPTISTERY OF CONSTANTINE. Chapter 16.

The drawings that follow are of the **Baptistery of Constantine**, which is located at **Saint John Lateran**. In my opinion, this temple is a modern work <note>original: "opera moderna"; Palladio correctly suspects the building was heavily remodeled or reconstructed using older parts rather than being a pure "ancient" structure from Constantine's era.</note> constructed from the <term>spolia: repurposed materials taken from ancient ruins</term> of older buildings. However, because it is a beautiful invention and possesses very well-carved ornaments in various styles—from which an architect may find use on many occasions—it seemed necessary to me to include it alongside the ancient works, especially since it is widely regarded by everyone as being ancient.

The columns are made of <term>porphyry: a hard, purple-red stone highly prized in antiquity</term> and are of the **Composite order**. The base is a mixture of the **Attic** and **Ionic** styles: it features the two "bastoni" <note>original: "bastoni"; these are the convex, rope-like moldings known as tori.</note> of the Attic base and the two <term>scotiae: concave, recessed moldings</term> of the Ionic. However, instead of the two <term>astragals: small, rounded bead-like moldings</term> usually placed between the scotiae in the Ionic style, this base has only one, which occupies the same space that the two would have. All these members are expertly crafted and feature beautiful carvings.

Above the bases of the <term>loggia: a gallery or room with one or more open sides</term>, there are leaves that support the shafts of the columns. This detail is worthy of notice, and the judgment of that architect is to be praised; he knew how to adapt so well when the column shafts were not as long as was required, adding this decoration without stripping the work of any of its beauty or majesty. I have made use of this same invention myself for the columns I placed as ornaments for the door of the **Church of Saint Giorgio Maggiore in Venice**; those columns did not reach the necessary height, yet they were made of such beautiful marble that they did not deserve to be left out of the work.

The **Capitals** are a composition of **Ionic** and **Corinthian**—the method for making these was described in the first book—and they feature <term>acanthus: a Mediterranean plant with jagged leaves used as a classic decorative motif</term>. The **Architrave** is very finely carved; its <term>cymatium: the crowning molding</term> features a <term>bead-molding: a small, circular decorative strip</term> in place of a <term>cyma reversa: an S-shaped molding that curves inward at the top</term>, and above that, a half-<term>ovolo: a rounded, egg-shaped molding</term>. The **Frieze** is plain. The **Cornice** has two <term>cyma recta: moldings that curve outward at the top</term> placed one above the other—a thing rarely seen, as it is unusual for two members of the same sort to be placed together without some other member, besides a listel or a small step, in between. Above these curves is the **Dentil** <note>original: "Dentello"; small rectangular blocks resembling teeth</note>, followed by the **Corona** <note>original: "Gocciolatoio"; the projecting part of the cornice designed to shed water</note> with the soffit, and finally the top-most cyma recta. In this cornice, the architect observed the rule of not using <term>modillions: ornamental brackets</term> when using dentils.

->Of this Temple I have made two plates.<-

In the **First**, the plan and the elevation are drawn, showing both the exterior and the interior.

In the **Second**, the specific members are shown:
*   **A, E** — The Base.
*   **B** — The Capital.
*   **C** — The Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.
*   **D** — The Soffit of the Architrave between one column and the next.
*   **E** — The foot divided into twelve inches.

# BOOK FOUR

64

### THE BOOK OF BRAMANTE’S TEMPLE. Chapter XVII.

<meta>Pencil mark 'GA' next to page number.</meta>

**P**oice the greatness of the Roman Empire began to decline because of the continual invasions of the Barbarians, Architecture—as happened then to all other arts and sciences—abandoned its former beauty and grace. It grew steadily worse until, with all knowledge of beautiful proportions and the ornate manner of building lost, it was reduced to such a state that it could fall no lower. But because all human things are in perpetual motion, it happens that they sometimes rise to the height of their perfection and sometimes descend to the extreme of their imperfection. Thus Architecture, in the time of our fathers, having emerged from those shadows in which it had long been buried, began to reveal itself once more in the light of the world. Under the Papacy of Julius II <note>Pope Julius II, reigned 1503–1513, a great patron of the High Renaissance.</note>, the most excellent Bramante <note>Donato Bramante, the architect who first designed the new St. Peter's Basilica.</note>, a diligent observer of ancient buildings, created most beautiful structures in Rome. Behind him followed Michelangelo Buonarroti, Jacopo Sansovino, Baldassare of Siena <note>Baldassare Peruzzi.</note>, Antonio da Sangallo, Michele Sanmicheli, Sebastiano Serlio, Giorgio Vasari, Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, and the Knight Lione <note>Leone Leoni, a famous sculptor and goldsmith.</note>; whose marvelous buildings are seen in Rome, Florence, Venice, Milan, and other cities of Italy. Furthermore, most of them were excellent painters, sculptors, and writers at the same time; some of these are still living today, along with others whom I will not name now to avoid being overly long. Since, therefore (to return to our subject), Bramante was the first to bring back to light the good and beautiful Architecture which had been hidden from the time of the Ancients until that day, it seemed right to me to grant his works a place among the ancient ones. I have therefore included in this book the following Temple, designed by him upon the Janiculum Hill <note>One of the hills of Rome, offering a commanding view of the city.</note>. Because it was built in commemoration of Saint Peter the Apostle, who is said to have been crucified there, it is named San Pietro in Montorio <note>Specifically the 'Tempietto', a small, circular commemorative tomb-like chapel.</note>. This Temple is of the <term>Doric order</term> <note>The most sturdy and simple of the three Greek architectural orders.</note> both inside and out. The columns are made of granite, the bases and capitals of marble, and the rest is all of <term>travertine</term> <note>Original: "pietra Tiburtina". A light-colored limestone sourced from Tivoli, used extensively in Rome.</note>.
I have made two plates of it.

->In the First is the Floor Plan.<-

->In the Second is the Elevation of the exterior and the interior.<-

# BOOK FOUR. ON THE TEMPLE OF JUPITER STATOR. Chapter XVIII.

Between the Capitoline and the Palatine hills near the Roman Forum, three columns of the Corinthian order are visible. According to some, these belonged to one side of the Temple of Vulcan, while others believe they were part of the Temple of Romulus. There are also those who say they belonged to the Temple of Jupiter Stator <note>original: "Gioue Statore"; this title, meaning "Jupiter the Stayer," refers to the god stopping the Roman retreat in battle.</note>, and I believe it was so named and vowed by Romulus when the Sabines—having taken the Capitoline and the Citadel through treachery—were advancing victoriously toward the Palatine. Others have claimed that these columns, along with those found beneath the Capitoline, were part of a bridge that Caligula <note>The Roman Emperor known for his grand and often eccentric building projects.</note> ordered to be built to cross from the Palatine to the Capitoline. This opinion is clearly far from the truth because the ornamentation shows these columns belonged to two different buildings, and because the bridge built by Caligula was made of wood and crossed over the Roman Forum. But to return to our subject: regardless of which temple these columns belonged to, I have never seen any work better or more delicately crafted; all the members have a very beautiful form and are extremely well conceived. I believe the style of this temple was the <term>Peripteros</term> <note>A temple design where the central cella is surrounded by a single row of columns on all sides.</note>; that is, "winged" all around, and the arrangement was the <term>Pycnostyle</term> <note>An architectural arrangement where the space between columns is very narrow, specifically one and a half times the diameter of a column.</note>. It had eight columns across the front and fifteen on the sides, counting those at the corners. The bases are composed of both the Attic and Ionic styles. The capitals are worthy of consideration for the beautiful invention of the carvings made in the <term>Abacus</term> <note>The flat slab forming the uppermost part of the capital of a column.</note>. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice together make up one-fourth of the length of the columns. The cornice alone is nearly as high as the architrave and frieze combined, a feature I have not seen in other temples.

I have made three plates of this temple.

# BOOK [ON] THE TEMPLE OF JUPITER THE THUNDERER. Chapter XIX.

At the base of the <term>Capitoline Hill</term> <note>Italian: "Campidoglio"; one of the seven hills of Rome, the site of the most important ancient temples</note> some remains of the following temple are visible. Some say this was dedicated to **Jupiter the Thunderer** <note>original: "Gioue Tonante"</note> and that it was built by **Augustus** because of a danger he escaped during the Cantabrian War. While he was traveling by night, the litter he was inside was struck by a bolt of lightning, which killed a servant walking ahead of him without doing any harm to the person of Augustus himself. 

I doubt this somewhat, because the ornaments seen there are worked most delicately with beautiful carvings, and it is manifest that in the time of Augustus, works were made more robust, as seen in the portico of **Saint Mary Rotunda** <note>the Pantheon; original: "Santa Maria Ritonda"</note>, built by **Marcus Agrippa**, which is very simple, and in other buildings as well. Some maintain that the columns found here belonged to the bridge that **Caligula** ordered to be built, an opinion which I have shown below to be entirely false. 

The arrangement of this Temple was what is called <term>double-winged</term> <note>original: "Dipteros"; a temple design featuring a double row of columns surrounding the central chamber</note>; it is true, however, that on the side facing the Capitoline Hill there was no portico. But from what I have observed in other buildings constructed near mountains, I am led to believe that in this part it was made as the **Plan** shows: that is, it had a very thick wall which enclosed the <term>Cella</term> <note>the inner chamber of a temple which housed the cult statue</note> and the porticos, and leaving some space, another wall with <term>buttresses</term> <note>original: "contraforti"</note> that entered into the mountainside. 

In such cases, the Ancients made the first wall very thick so that humidity would not penetrate the interior of the building, and they made the other wall with buttresses so that it would be capable of supporting the continuous weight of the mountain. They left the aforementioned space between one wall and the other so that the waters descending from the mountain, gathered there, would have a free course and in this way would not cause any damage to the structure. 

The style of this Temple was <term>Pycnostyle</term> <note>original: "Picnostilos"; an architectural term for columns spaced very closely together</note>. The **Architrave** and the **Frieze** on the front were on a single plane so that they could accommodate the carving of the inscription, and some letters are still visible there. The <term>ovolo</term> <note>an egg-and-dart molding</note> of the cornice above the frieze is different from any I have yet seen, and this variety—there being two rows of ovolos in this cornice—is handled very judiciously. The <term>modillions</term> <note>ornamental brackets</note> of this cornice are arranged so that a blank space, rather than a modillion, falls directly over the columns, as also seen in some other cornices; although regularly it should be done so that a modillion falls directly over the center of the columns. And because the details of this temple can be understood from the drawings of the preceding temples, I have made only two plates for it.

In the First [Plate] is the plan.
**A, E** the space between the two walls.
**B,** The buttresses that enter into the Mountain.
**C,** The spaces between the buttresses.

In the Second [Plate] are the particular members of the portico.
**A, E** the **Base**.
**B,** The **Capital**.
**C,** The **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice**.
**H,** The **Soffit** <note>the decorated underside</note> of the Architrave between the columns.

### DETAILS OF THE ENTABLATURE AND ORNAMENTS

<image-desc>
This plate illustrates the highly decorative elements of the temple’s upper structure. The Temple of Jupiter the Thunderer was renowned in the Renaissance for the exquisite quality of its stone carving.

**Key Architectural Components:**
*   **A, B, C, D, E**: These labels correspond to specific details of the **entablature** <term>the collective name for the architrave, frieze, and cornice</term> and the **capital** <term>the crowning member of a column</term>.
*   The drawings highlight the **modillions** <term>ornamental brackets under the cornice</term> and the **egg-and-dart** moldings, which are characteristic of the Corinthian order.

**Technical Measurements and Proportions:**
The measurements indicate the precise height and projection of each molding to ensure perfect harmony when viewed from the ground.
*   **Vertical Measurements (Left side):** **26 ⅔**, **30 ⅔**, and **45 ½**. These figures represent the proportions of the different layers of the entablature.
*   **P I G 1/2**: This shorthand refers to Feet, Inches, and Minutes <note>original: "P" for Piedi, "I" for Incia, and "G" for Grani or Grossezza—units of measurement used to achieve mathematical precision</note>.
*   **Vertical Measurements (Right side):** A series of numbers (**16, 18, 10, 22, 26 ½...**) providing the exact thickness of each individual "member" or lip of the stone moldings.
</image-desc>

The ornaments of this temple are exceptionally beautiful and executed with great mastery <note>Palladio often used this temple as a prime example of how to handle the Corinthian order's complexity</note>. The **frieze** <term>the middle section of the entablature</term> was famously decorated with the instruments of sacrifice, as this was a sacred space.

The height of the **architrave** <term>the lintel or beam that rests directly on the columns</term>, the **frieze**, and the **cornice** <term>the projecting top edge</term> are all calculated in relation to the diameter of the columns to maintain the "Symmetry" or proper proportion required by the ancients.

# ON THE PANTHEON, TODAY CALLED THE ROTONDA. Ch. XX.

Among all the Temples to be seen in Rome, none is more celebrated than the Pantheon—today called the Rotonda—nor has any remained more intact; it is seen almost in its original state regarding the structure, though stripped of its statues and other ornaments. It was built, according to the opinion of some, by Marcus Agrippa around the year 14 AD <note>modern scholarship dates the current structure primarily to the reign of Hadrian, though it incorporates Agrippa's earlier site</note>, but I believe the body of the Temple was made during the time of the Republic, and that **M. Agrippa** only added the portico; this is understood from the two pediments <term>the triangular gable found above the porch</term> on the facade. This Temple was called the Pantheon because, after Jupiter, it was consecrated to all the Gods; or else (as others would have it) because it is shaped like the World—that is, Round. Its height from the pavement to the opening from which it receives light <term>the oculus, or the circular opening at the top of the dome</term> is exactly equal to its diameter from one wall to the other. And just as one now descends to the floor or pavement, in ancient times one ascended to it by several steps. Among the most famous things read to have been inside the Temple was a statue of Minerva made of Ivory by Phidias, and another of Venus, who wore as an earring half of that pearl which Cleopatra drank at a dinner to surpass the generosity of Mark Antony. This half of the pearl alone is said to have been valued at 250,000 gold ducats. This entire Temple is of the Corinthian order <term>the most decorative of the classical orders, using acanthus leaf motifs</term> both on the outside and the inside. The bases are composed of Attic and Ionic styles. The capitals are carved with olive leaves; the architraves, friezes, and cornices have very beautiful profiles or moldings and are made with few carvings. Within the thickness of the wall that surrounds the Temple, there are some hollow spaces made so that earthquakes might do less harm to this structure, and to save on expense and material. This Temple has a very beautiful portico on the front, on the frieze of which these words are read:

->MARCUS AGRIPPA, SON OF LUCIUS, CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME, BUILT THIS.<-
<note>original: "M. AGRIPPA L. F. COS. III. FECIT."</note>

Below these, on the bands of the architrave in smaller letters, are these other words which show how the Emperors Septimius Severus and Marcus Aurelius restored it after it was consumed by time:

->EMPEROR CAESAR SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS PIIUS PERTINAX<-
->ARABICUS PARTHICUS, SUPREME PONTIFF, WITH TRIBUNICIAN POWER<-
->FOR THE 11TH TIME, CONSUL 3 TIMES, FATHER OF THE COUNTRY, PROCONSUL, AND EMPEROR CAESAR MARCUS<-
->AURELIUS ANTONINVS PIIUS FELIX AUGUSTUS, WITH TRIBUNICIAN<-
->POWER FOR THE 5TH TIME, CONSUL, PROCONSUL, RESTORED THE PANTHEON, WORN BY AGE,<-
->WITH EVERY REFINEMENT.<-
<note>original: "IMP. CÆS. SEPTIMIVS SEVERVS... PANTHEVM VETVSTATE CVM OMNI CVLTV RESTITVERVNT." Note that Marcus Aurelius Antoninus here refers to the emperor commonly known as Caracalla.</note>

Inside the Temple, within the thickness of the wall, there are seven chapels with niches in which there must have been statues; and between one chapel and another, there is a tabernacle <term>a decorative frame or shrine</term>, such that there come to be eight tabernacles. It is the opinion of many that the middle chapel, which is opposite the entrance, is not ancient, because its arch breaks some columns of the second order; they believe that in the time of the Christians, after Pope Boniface—who first dedicated this Temple to Divine worship <note>Pope Boniface IV consecrated it as Santa Maria ad Martyres in 609 AD</note>—it was enlarged as is fitting for Christian Temples to have a principal and greater altar than the others. But because I see that it fits perfectly with all the rest of the work, and that all its members are very well crafted, I hold for certain that it was made at the same time as the rest of this building. This chapel has two columns, one on each side, which create a projection, and they are fluted; the space between one flute and the other is carved with beads very elegantly. And because all parts of this Temple are most notable, I have made ten plates so that all may be seen.

In the First plate is the ground plan. The stairs seen on either side of the entrance lead above the chapels into a secret passage that goes all around the Temple, through which one goes out to the steps to climb to the top of the building by several stairs located there. That part of the building seen behind the Temple, marked M, is part of the Baths of Agrippa.

In the Second plate is half of the front facade.

<sig>K K K K</sig>
<meta>catchword: In the [Nella]</meta>

In the Third [plate] is the half of the facade under the portico. As seen in these two plates, this Temple has two pediments <term>the triangular gable-ends of a roof</term>; one for the portico, and the other on the wall of the Temple.

Where the letter T is, there are some stones that protrude slightly outward, for which I cannot imagine what purpose they served.

The beams of the portico are all made of bronze plates. <note>This refers to the original bronze trusses of the Pantheon's portico, which were famously removed in the 17th century by Pope Urban VIII to cast the Baldacchino in St. Peter’s and cannons for Castel Sant'Angelo.</note>

In the Fourth plate is the side elevation of the exterior.
X, is the second cornice <term>the decorative molding that crowns a wall</term>, which runs all the way around the Temple.

In the Fifth is the side elevation of the interior.

In the Sixth are the ornaments of the portico:
A, is the Base.
B, is the Capital.
C, the Architrave, the Frieze, and the cornice.
D, is the profile <term>original: "facoma," the outline or cross-section</term> of the ornaments made above the columns and the pillars in the interior part of the portico.
T, the pillars of the portico, which correspond to the columns.
V, the scrolls of the *caulicoli* <term>the small stalks or stems from which the volutes of a Corinthian capital emerge</term> of the capitals.
X, the soffit <term>the underside of an architectural feature</term> of the architrave between one column and the other.

In the Seventh is part of the interior elevation facing the entrance, where one sees how the chapels and the tabernacles are arranged and with what ornaments, and how the coffers in the vault <term>the recessed panels in the dome</term> are divided. It is very likely that these were once adorned with silver plates, based on certain remains found there; for if such ornaments had been made of bronze, there is no doubt they would have been taken just as those bronzes were—which, as I have mentioned, are in the portico. <note>The author argues that because the bronze in the portico remained, the missing ornaments inside must have been a more precious metal like silver, which would have been stolen sooner.</note>

In the Eighth, shown in a somewhat larger size, is a drawing of one of the tabernacles in full view, with part of the chapels that are at its sides.

In the Nona are the ornaments of the columns and the pillars of the interior.
L, is the Base.
M, the Capital.
N, the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.
O, the scrolls of the *caulicoli* of the capitals.
P, the fluting of the pillars.

In the Tenth are the ornaments of the Tabernacles located between the chapels. Here one should note the fine judgment of the Architect: in framing the architrave, frieze, and cornice of these Tabernacles—since the pillars of the chapels did not project far enough from the wall to accommodate the full depth of that cornice—he made only the "straight cyma" <term>a S-shaped molding</term> and converted the remaining members into a flat band.
E, is the profile of the door ornaments.
F, the design of the festoons <term>carved garlands of fruit or flowers</term> that are on either side of said door.

->AND WITH this Temple, let there be an end to the drawings of the Temples that are in Rome.<-

# BOOK FOUR

-> **[Plate of the Interior Section of the Pantheon]** <-

This engraving presents a masterfully detailed vertical cross-section of the Pantheon’s interior, demonstrating how the Corinthian order is scaled to support one of antiquity's greatest structural achievements.

### The Structure of the Dome

The upper portion of the plate reveals the ingenious construction of the dome.
<margin>P. 3. 4.</margin>
The interior is lined with five tiers of receding coffers—sunken decorative panels—which serve a dual purpose: they create a stunning visual rhythm and significantly reduce the weight of the concrete vault. On the exterior, a series of stepped rings provide the necessary weight to counteract the outward "thrust" or pressure of the massive dome.
<note>The label "P. 3. 4." likely refers to the height or thickness of specific masonry layers measured in architectural "Parts."</note>

### The Attic and Intermediate Levels

Between the main floor and the base of the dome lies the attic story.
<margin>min. 20. 0. 5.</margin>
This level is articulated with small pilasters <term>shallow, rectangular columns attached to a wall</term> and alternating rectangular openings.
<note>The measurements "min." (Minutes) represent the finest level of detail in the modular system of proportion used by Renaissance architects to ensure every element of a building remained in harmony with the whole.</note>

### The Main Order and Aedicules

The lower level showcases the primary Corinthian order that defines the Pantheon's majesty.

*   **The Aedicula (K):** The engraving highlights a prominent shrine or altar-frame, labeled **K**. It features a sharp triangular pediment <term>the triangular gable found above an entry or niche</term> supported by delicate columns.
*   **The Statues (I, H):** Within these niches, standing figures represent the deities to whom the temple was originally dedicated.
*   **The Large Order (N, M):** The labels **N** and **M** mark the primary entablature and the capital of the massive freestanding columns that ring the interior.

### Structural Proportions

The various letters (**K, I, H, N, M**) and numbers serve as a guide for the architect to understand the relationship between the height of the floor, the placement of the shrines, and the start of the dome’s curvature. This ensures that even in a space as vast as the Pantheon, the human eye perceives a perfect, balanced geometry.

# DRAWINGS OF SEVERAL TEMPLES OUTSIDE OF ROME AND THROUGHOUT ITALY; AND FIRST, THE TEMPLE OF BACCHUS. Chapter XXI.

Outside the gate known today as Saint Agnes, and called the Viminal Gate by the ancients after the name of the hill upon which it is situated, one sees the following Temple, which is quite intact and dedicated to Saint Agnes <note>The author is describing the building now known as the Mausoleum of Santa Costanza, built in the 4th century for the daughter of Emperor Constantine. It is located next to the Basilica of Sant'Agnese fuori le mura.</note>. I believe that it was originally a tomb, because a very large sarcophagus <term>original: "cassone," literally a large chest, here referring to a funerary container</term> made of porphyry <term>a prestigious, hard purple stone reserved for imperial use</term> was found there. This sarcophagus was very well carved with grapevines and children gathering grapes, which has led some to believe that it was a Temple of Bacchus <note>Bacchus was the Roman god of wine; the grape motifs are actually Christian allegories for the Eucharist, but were often misinterpreted by Renaissance antiquarians as pagan symbols</note>. Because this is the common opinion, and because the building now serves as a church, I have placed it here among the Temples. 

In front of its portico, one can see the remains of an oval-shaped courtyard, which I believe was adorned with columns. In the spaces between these columns <term>intercolumniations</term>, there were niches that must have once held statues.

# BOOK FOUR

The portico of the Temple, as far as can be seen, was constructed with pillars and consisted of three bays. Inside the temple, the columns are arranged in pairs to support the dome <term>original: "cuba," a term used here for a cupola or vaulted dome</term>. All these columns are made of granite, while the bases, capitals, and cornices are made of marble. The bases are in the Attic style <note>The Attic base is a common classical form consisting of two large circular moldings (tori) separated by a hollow groove (scotia)</note>; the capitals are very beautiful and belong to the Composite order <note>The Composite order is a Roman architectural style that combines the scrolls of the Ionic order with the acanthus leaves of the Corinthian order</note>. They feature certain leaves emerging from the "Rose" <note>the central decorative flower on the capital</note>, from which the volutes <term>spiral, scroll-like ornaments</term> seem to sprout very gracefully. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice are not particularly well-crafted, which leads me to believe that this temple was not built during the "good times" <note>The author refers to the peak of classical Roman architecture (the 1st and 2nd centuries AD). He correctly identifies that this 4th-century building dates from the later Empire, when classical standards were changing</note>, but rather during the time of the Emperors closer to our own age. It is very richly decorated with various patterns and workmanship, partly in fine stone and partly in mosaic, found on the floor as well as on the walls and the vaults. <image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'F' featuring a figure on a chariot, surrounded by clouds and putti.</image-desc> OUTSIDE the Gate of St. Sebastian, which in ancient times was called the Appian Gate, named after the most famous road built with admirable skill and expense by Appius Claudius <note>The Roman censor who began construction of the Appian Way in 312 BCE</note>, one sees the remains of the following building near the said Church of St. Sebastian. # BOOK / OF THE TEMPLE OF VESTA, Chap. XXIII.

IN TIVOLI, sixteen miles from Rome above the falls of the river Aniene—today called the Teverone—one sees the following round Temple. The inhabitants of those places say that it was the home of the Tiburtine Sibyl <note>The Tiburtine Sibyl was a female prophet in Roman mythology said to reside in Tivoli; her prophecies were often associated with the coming of Christ in later Christian interpretations.</note>; however, this opinion is without any foundation. Therefore, I believe, for the reasons mentioned above, that it was a temple dedicated to the Goddess Vesta <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; her temples were traditionally circular in imitation of the primitive round huts of early Rome.</note>. This temple is of the Corinthian order. The intercolumniations <term>intercolunnij (the clear space between two adjacent columns)</term> are two diameters wide. Its floor is raised from the ground by a third of the length of the columns. The bases have no plinth <term>zoccolo (the square block forming the lowest part of a column base)</term>, so that the area for walking under the portico would be more unobstructed and spacious. The columns are exactly as long as the cella <term>cella (the inner chamber of a temple where the cult statue was kept)</term> is wide; they lean inward toward the wall of the cella, so that the upper face of the column is perfectly plumb with the inner face of the column base. The capitals are very well made and are carved with olive leaves, which leads me to believe it was built during the good eras <note>The "good eras" refers to the height of the Roman Empire (1st and 2nd centuries CE), known for the highest quality of stone carving.</note>. Its door and windows are narrower at the top than at the bottom, just as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio was a 1st-century BCE Roman architect whose treatise *De Architectura* became the foundational "bible" for Renaissance architects like Palladio.</note> teaches us they should be made in Chapter 6 of the 4th Book. This entire Temple is made of Tiburtine stone <note>original: "pietra Tiburtina," now commonly known as travertine, a light-colored limestone deposited by mineral springs and frequently used in Roman construction.</note> covered with very fine stucco, so that it appears to be made entirely of marble. I have made four plates of this temple.

In the First, the Plan is drawn.

In the Second is the Elevation.

In the Third are the members of the portico:
A, E: The Basement <term>Basamento (the continuous pedestal or foundation wall)</term> that goes all around the Temple.
B: The base of the columns.
C: The Capital.
D: The Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.

In the Fourth are drawn the ornaments of the door and windows:
A: The ornaments of the door.
B: The ornaments of the windows on the outside.
C: The ornaments of the windows on the inside.

The bands of the ornaments for the door and windows are different from those usually made. The astragals <term>Astragali (small, semi-circular moldings, often resembling a string of beads)</term> located under the moldings project beyond the said moldings—a feature I have never seen before in other ornaments.

<note>The illustration on this page provides a dual view of the temple: the left half shows the exterior elevation (how the building appears from the outside), while the right half shows a cross-section (a "cut-through" view revealing the interior and the thickness of the walls and dome).</note>

**Architectural Dimensions and Labels:**

*   **Center of the Cella:** 20 Palms, 13 minutes <note>original: "-P. 20 C 1 m 3"; this indicates the internal diameter of the cella <term>cella (the inner chamber of a temple where the statue of the deity was kept)</term> is 20 palms and 13 minutes. In this architectural system, a palm is a unit of measurement (approx. 22.3 cm), which is further divided into minutes for precision.</note>
*   **Upper Measurement:** 4 Palms, 1/4 minute <note>This likely refers to the diameter of the column at its thinnest point, near the capital.</note>
*   **Lower Measurement:** 4 Palms, 1/4 minute
*   **Total Diameter of the Base:** 46 1/2 Palms <note>original: "F 46 7/2"; The 'F' is an OCR error for 'P' (Palms). This measurement represents the full width of the temple's circular platform.</note>
*   **Intercolumniation:** 4 Palms, 7 1/2 minutes <note>original: "Palms 4, 7 1/2"; this indicates the space between the columns, known as <term>intercolumniation (the clear distance between two adjacent columns)</term>.</note>

*   **The Left (Elevation):** Displays the exterior Corinthian columns and the stepped profile of the outer dome.

<header># BOOK FOUR. THE TEMPLE OF CASTOR AND POLLUX. Chapter XXIV.</header>

In Naples, in a very beautiful part of the city between the castle square and the Vicaria <note>The Vicaria refers to the Castel Capuano, which served as the royal palace and later the central courts of Naples.</note>, one can see the portico of a temple built and consecrated to Castor and Pollux by Tiberius Julius Tarsus and by Pelagon, a freedman of Augustus, as appears in its inscription written with these Greek letters:

-><note>original Greek: "ΤΙΒΕΡΙΟΣ ΙΟΥΛΙΟΣ ΤΑΡΣΟΣ ΔΙΟΣ ΚΟΥΡΟΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΙ ΠΟΛΕΙ ΤΟΝ ΝΑΟΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΝΑΩΙ ;"</note> TIBERIUS JULIUS TARSUS, TO THE SONS OF JUPITER AND TO THE CITY, THE TEMPLE AND THE THINGS WITHIN THE TEMPLE;<-

-><note>original Greek: "ΠΕΛΑΓΩΝ ΣΕΒΑΣΤΟΥ ΑΠΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΠΙΤΡΟΠΟΣ ΣΥΝΤΕΛΕΣΑΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΚΑΘΙΕΡΟΣΕΝ"</note> PELAGON, FREEDMAN AND PROCURATOR OF AUGUSTUS, HAVING COMPLETED IT FROM HIS OWN FUNDS, CONSECRATED IT. That is:<-

-><note>original Latin: "TIBERIVS IVLIVS TARSVS IOVIS FILIIS, ET VRBI, TEMPLVM, ET QVÆ IN TEMPLO,"</note> TIBERIUS JULIUS TARSUS, TO THE SONS OF JUPITER, AND THE CITY, THE TEMPLE, AND THE THINGS IN THE TEMPLE,<-

-><note>original Latin: "PELAGON AVGVSTI LIBERTVS, ET PROCVRATOR PERFICIENS EX PROPRIIS CONSECRAVIT."</note> PELAGON, FREEDMAN OF AUGUSTUS, AND PROCURATOR, COMPLETING IT FROM HIS OWN FUNDS, CONSECRATED IT.<-

**Which signify that Tiberius Julius Tarsus began to build this temple—and those things that are inside—for the sons of Jupiter (that is, for Castor and Pollux) and for the city; and that Pelagon, freedman and commissioner of Augustus, finished it with his own money and consecrated it. This portico is of the <term>Corinthian order (the most ornate of the classical orders, characterized by slender columns and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves)</term>. The <term>intercolumniation (the space between columns)</term> is more than one and a half diameters, but does not reach two diameters. The bases are made in the <term>Attic style (a specific base consisting of two large rings called tori separated by a hollow molding)</term>. The capitals are carved with olive leaves and are worked with the utmost diligence. Very beautiful is the invention of the <term>caulicoli (the stalks or stems from which the volutes of a Corinthian capital spring)</term> that are beneath the rose; these are tied together and seem to grow out of the leaves that clothe the upper part of the other stalks, which support the horns of the Capital. Thus, from this and from many other examples scattered throughout this book, it is known that the Architect is not forbidden from departing sometimes from common usage, provided that such variation is graceful and has a natural quality. In the <term>frontispiece (the pediment or triangular gable above the portico)</term>, a sacrifice is sculpted in low relief by the hand of a most excellent sculptor. Some say that there were two temples here, one round and the other rectangular: no trace of the round one is seen, and the rectangular one, in my opinion, is modern. Therefore, leaving aside the main body of the temple, I have placed only the elevation of the portico's facade in the First plate, and its individual members in the Second.**

> A, Is the Base.
> B, The Capital.
> C, The <term>Architrave (the main beam resting on the columns)</term>, the <term>Frieze (the decorative middle band)</term>, and the <term>Cornice (the crowning top molding)</term>.
> D, The foot divided into twelve inches, with which the said members are measured.

### Detailed Study of the Entablature

This plate provides a technical architectural rendering of the upper sections of the classical order used in the temple, specifically focusing on the <term>entablature</term> <note>The collective term for the horizontal moldings and bands supported by the columns, consisting of the architrave, frieze, and cornice.</note>. 

The drawing utilizes a system of modular measurements to ensure mathematical harmony. These measurements are expressed in <term>Parts</term> <note>A proportional unit of measure used by Renaissance architects to ensure a building's elements remained in scale regardless of the structure's actual size.</note>.

The uppermost part of the structure, the <term>cornice</term>, is depicted with elaborate ornamentation:
*   A <term>cyma recta</term> <note>An S-shaped molding that curves outward at the bottom and inward at the top.</note> featuring leaf-like decorations.
*   An <term>ovolo</term> molding carved with a classic egg-and-dart pattern.
*   A series of <term>modillions</term> <note>Ornate brackets or blocks placed under the corona of a cornice.</note> decorated with acanthus leaf details.
*   A row of <term>dentils</term> <note>Small, rectangular blocks used as a repeating ornament, resembling a row of teeth.</note> below the modillions.

*   **The Frieze:** This section is shown as a plain, unadorned band.

# BOOK OF THE TEMPLE WHICH IS BELOW TREVI. Chapter XXV.

Between Foligno and Spoleto, below Trevi, one finds the small temple <note>Known today as the Tempietto del Clitunno, a unique structure that incorporates both classical Roman elements and early Christian adaptations.</note> of which the following drawings are made. The basement that supports it is eight and a half feet high; one ascends to this height by the stairs placed at the sides of the portico, which lead into two small porticoes that project out from the rest of the Temple. The appearance of this Temple is <term>Prostyle</term> <note>From the Greek *prostylos*, meaning a temple with a row of columns across the front but not on the sides or rear.</note>. Its style consists of closely spaced columns. The Chapel facing the entrance into the <term>cella</term> <note>The inner chamber of a classical temple.</note> has beautiful ornaments, and the columns have twisted fluting; both these and those of the porticoes are of the <term>Corinthian</term> order, delicately worked and with a beautiful variety of carvings. Thus, in this temple, as in all others, one clearly recognizes the truth of what I said in the first book: that the Ancients, in this sort of building—and especially in small ones—placed the greatest diligence in polishing every part and giving them all possible ornaments that were appropriate. However, in large structures such as Amphitheaters and the like, they polished only some small parts, leaving the rest rough to avoid the expense and the time that would have been required to polish them all, as will be seen in the book on Amphitheaters, which I hope to publish soon.

I have made four plates of this small Temple.

In the First, there is the Plan of the floor of the Temple, marked **A**.
**B, E** the Plan of the portico below the said floor.
**C, The Base.** } of the basement that surrounds and supports the whole Temple.
**D, The Cymatium.** } <note>The crowning molding of a pedestal or cornice.</note>
**E, The Base** of the columns of the front facade.
**F, The Base.** } of the columns and pilasters of the small porticoes, where the
**G, The Capital, and** } stairs reach the top.
**the Cornice.** }

In the Second, there is the elevation of the center of the facade on the outside.
**H, And the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.**

In the Third, there is the elevation of half of the interior part.
**L, The Capital of the portico.**

In the Fourth is the side Elevation.

# BOOK FOUR
## THE TEMPLE OF ASSISI. <note>original: "Scisi"; the author uses this archaic name for the city of Assisi in Umbria.</note> Chapter XXVI.

**I**he Temple that follows is situated upon the square of Assisi, a city in Umbria, and is of the **Corinthian order**. In this temple, the <term>pedestals</term> <note>The supporting blocks or bases found under the columns.</note> placed beneath the columns of the <term>portico</term> <note>A porch leading to the entrance of a building, supported by columns.</note> are worthy of notice; because, as I have mentioned above, in all other ancient temples, the columns of the porticoes are seen to reach all the way to the ground. I have not seen any other temple that possesses such pedestals. Between one pedestal and another are the steps that ascend from the square to the portico. The pedestals are as high as the central <term>intercolumniation</term> <note>The space between two adjacent columns.</note> is wide, which is two inches wider than the others.

The style of this temple is what **Vitruvius** <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer whose writings serve as the foundation for classical architecture.</note> calls **Systyle**, <note>original: "Sistilos"; a Greek term used by Vitruvius to describe a building where the columns are spaced exactly two diameters apart.</note> that is, a spacing of two diameters. The <term>architrave</term>, the <term>frieze</term>, and the <term>cornice</term> <note>These three elements together form the "entablature," the horizontal superstructure supported by the columns.</note> together are one-fifth of the height of the columns, and a little more. The cornice that forms the <term>pediment</term> <note>original: "frontespicio"; the triangular gable at the top of the temple front.</note> has some carved leaves in place of <term>modillions</term>, <note>Ornate brackets or blocks used to support the upper part of a cornice.</note> and in all other respects, it is entirely similar to the cornice that runs straight above the columns. The <term>cella</term> <note>The inner chamber of the temple where the cult statue would traditionally be kept.</note> of the temple is one-fourth longer than its width.

I have made three plates of it.

**In the First is the Plan.**

**In the Second is the Elevation of the front facade.**

**In the Third are the ornaments.**
**A, E The Capital, the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.**
**B, The pedestal and the base of the columns.**
**C, The cornice that forms the pediment.**
**D, The foot divided into twelve inches.** <note>The "oncia" or inch was a standard unit of architectural measurement.</note>

### The Entablature and Capital

**C** — <gloss>The Entablature</gloss> <note>This section shows the horizontal "sandwich" of decoration that sits atop the columns. It consists of three parts: the cornice (top), the frieze (middle), and the architrave (bottom).</note>

*   **The Cornice:** The uppermost projecting part, designed to throw rainwater away from the building. It features <term>dentils</term> <note>small, rectangular blocks resembling teeth</note> which provide a rhythmic shadow line.
*   **The Frieze:** The central band. <note>The image description mentions a pattern of triglyphs and metopes; while these are usually found in the Doric order, the architect here records the specific decorative rhythm used in this unique Corinthian variation.</note>
*   **The Architrave:** The lowest part of the entablature that rests directly on the column capitals.

**D** — <gloss>The Capital and Column Shaft</gloss> <note>This shows the top of a column. The capital is adorned with acanthus leaves, a hallmark of the Corinthian order.</note>

### Proportions of the Column Shaft
<note>The fluted column (featuring vertical grooves) is measured at various points to show its "entasis"—the slight swelling in the middle of a column that makes it appear perfectly straight to the human eye, rather than thin or "waisted."</note>

*   **Vertical Fluting:** The drawing indicates the precise spacing between the grooves (flutes) and the flat edges (fillets) between them.
*   **Scaling:** The repeating sequences of **1 2 3** and **1 2 4** in the margins refer to the mathematical modules used to ensure every part of the temple remains in harmony with the whole.

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

## DRAWINGS OF CERTAIN TEMPLES LOCATED OUTSIDE OF ITALY, and first, the two Temples of Pola. Chapter XXVII.

IN POLA, a city of Istria, besides the Theater, the Amphitheater, and an Arch, there are most beautiful buildings. I shall discuss each of these and provide the drawings in their proper places. There are two Temples of the same size and with the same ornaments located on the Square <note>The Roman Forum of Pula</note> on the same side, separated from one another by fifty-eight feet and four inches. The drawings that follow are of these temples. Their form is <term>Prostyle</term> <note>A temple with a porch of columns only on the front</note>. The style is that which, according to Vitruvius, I have called <term>Systyle</term> <note>A spacing of columns where the gap between them is exactly twice the diameter of a column</note> above, which has intercolumniations of two diameters; the middle intercolumniation is two diameters and a quarter wide. A basement <note>A podium</note> runs around these temples, at the height of which they have their floor or pavement, and one ascends to them by steps placed on the front facade, as has been seen in many other Temples.

The bases of the columns are of the Attic order, and they have a <term>torus</term> <note>The thick, rounded molding at the base</note> as thick as the entire rest of the base. The Capitals are carved with olive leaves very elegantly. The <term>caulicoli</term> <note>The small stalks or stems from which the volutes or "scrolls" of a Corinthian capital emerge</note> are clothed in oak leaves; this variety is seen in few other buildings and is worthy of notice. The Architrave is also different from most others because its first <term>fascia</term> <note>The horizontal bands that make up an architrave</note> is large, the second is smaller, and the third, beneath the <term>cymatium</term> <note>The topmost molding of the architrave</note>, is even smaller. These bands project outward at the lower part, which was done so that the Architrave would have little projection and thus would not obscure the letters that are in the frieze on the front, which are these:

->TO ROME AND TO AUGUSTUS, SON OF THE DIVINE CAESAR, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY.<-
<note>Original Latin: "ROMÆ ET AVGVSTO CÆSARIS DIVI. F. PAT. PATRIÆ."</note>

And there are foliated designs carved in the said frieze around the other parts of the Temple. The Cornice has few members and is worked with the usual carvings. The ornaments of the Door are not visible; nevertheless, I have drawn them in the manner that seemed to me they ought to have been. The <term>Cella</term> <note>The enclosed inner chamber of the temple</note> is a quarter longer than its width. The entire temple, including the portico, exceeds two squares in length <note>A 2:1 length-to-width ratio</note>. I have made three plates of it:

In the First, the Floor Plan is drawn.
**B** is the pedestal upon which the base of the columns sits.

In the Second is the Elevation of the front facade.
**E** is the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice above the columns.
**P** are the ornaments of the door made from my own invention.

In the third is the Side Elevation.
**D** is the "bell" of the Capital.
**F** is the plan of said Capital.

<page-num>III</page-num>
<header>FOURTH. III</header>

# OF TWO TEMPLES IN NÎMES, AND FIRST OF THAT,
## which is called the Maison Carrée. Chap. XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' containing an illustration of a classical landscape with buildings and a bridge.</image-desc>

In Nîmes, a city in Provence <note>Nîmes is a city in Southern France, famous for its well-preserved Roman monuments.</note>, which was the birthplace of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, one can see among many other beautiful antiquities the two following temples. This first one is called by the inhabitants of that city the *Maison Carrée* <note>original: "Mazon Quaree"; French for "Square House."</note>, because it is quadrangular in shape; and they say it was a <term>basilica</term> <note>In the Roman era, a basilica was a public building for legal and business matters; Palladio notes that its tall form suggests it was actually a temple.</note> (almost as if they knew what basilicas were used for and how they were made, which was discussed in the third book according to what Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BC Roman architect whose writings formed the basis of Renaissance architecture.</note> says of them); however, because it is of a tall form, I believe it was truly a temple. Its aspect and manner are quite manifest from what has been said regarding so many other temples. The floor of the temple rises ten feet and five inches from the ground; a pedestal forms a base around it, above the <term>cymatium</term> <note>The uppermost molding of a pedestal or cornice.</note> of which are two steps that support the bases of the columns. It could easily be that Vitruvius meant such steps when, at the end of the third chapter of his third book, he said that when making the platform around the temple, <term>uneven scammilli</term> <note>original: "scamili impari"; these were small blocks or leveling devices used to correct optical illusions in the platform of a temple.</note> should be made under the bases of the columns, which correspond to the level of the block of the pedestal that is beneath the columns, and are level under the base of the column and above the cymatium of the pedestal; a passage which has given many people cause for reflection. The base of this pedestal has fewer members and is thicker than the cymatium, as has been noted elsewhere that one ought to do for pedestals. 

The base of the columns is Attic, but it has some additional small <term>astragals</term> <note>original: "bastoncini"; small convex moldings.</note>, so it can be called Composite and suitable for the Corinthian order. The capitals are carved with olive leaves and have a carved <term>abacus</term> <note>The flat slab forming the topmost part of a capital.</note>. The flower placed in the middle of the face of the capital occupies the height of the abacus and the lip of the <term>bell</term> <note>original: "cāpana"; the core of the Corinthian capital around which the leaves are arranged.</note>; which I have noted has been observed in all ancient capitals of this sort. The architrave, the frieze, and the cornice are a quarter of the length of the columns, and all their members are carved with very beautiful invention. The <term>modillions</term> <note>Ornamental brackets under the cornice.</note> are different from any I have ever seen, and this diversity from the ordinary ones is very graceful; and although the capitals have olive leaves, the modillions are nonetheless carved with oak leaves. Above the <term>cyma recta</term> <note>original: "Gola diritta"; an S-shaped molding.</note>, instead of a rim, there is a carved <term>ovolo</term> <note>An egg-and-dart molding.</note>, which is seen in rare cornices. The <term>pediment</term> <note>original: "Frōtespicio".</note> is made exactly as Vitruvius teaches us in the aforementioned place. For of the nine parts of the length of the cornice, one is used for the height of the pediment under its own cornice. 

The jambs, or pilasters of the door, are thick on the face by a sixth part of the width of the opening. This door has very beautiful ornaments, very well carved. Above its cornice, level with the pilasters, there are two pieces of stone worked in the manner of architraves which project out from the said cornice, and in each of them is a square hole ten and a half inches wide in every direction, in which I believe they placed some beams that reached down to the ground. There, a temporary door was made that could be removed and set in place; this must have been made as a <term>lattice</term> <note>original: "gelosia"; a screen or grate.</note>, so that the people standing outside could see what was being done in the temple without hindering the priests. There are six plates of this temple.

# BOOK ON THE OTHER TEMPLE OF NIMES. Chapter XIX. #

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'I' featuring an ornate rectangular frame. Inside the letter is a scene depicting classical ruins and trees.</image-desc>

THE DRAWINGS that follow are of the other Temple of Nimes, which the people of that city say was the **Temple of Vesta** <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; her temples, such as the famous one in the Roman Forum, were traditionally circular to represent the earth.</note>. In my judgment, this cannot be true, both because temples to Vesta were made round in the likeness of the element of Earth (of which they said she was the Goddess), and also because this Temple had enclosed <term>walkways</term> <note>original: "anditi"</note> on three sides, shut in by continuous walls in which there were doors at the sides of the **Cella** <note>The inner chamber of a classical temple which housed the cult statue.</note>. The door of this Cella was in the front, so that it could not receive light from any side; nor can any reason be given why temples to Vesta should be made dark. For this reason, I believe instead that it was dedicated to one of their **infernal gods** <note>Gods of the underworld, such as Pluto or Proserpina.</note>.

Inside this temple there are <term>niches</term> <note>original: "tabernacoli"</note> in which statues must have stood. The interior facade opposite the door is divided into three parts; the ground, or pavement of the middle part, is on one level with the rest of the Temple. The other two parts have their floor as high as the height of the pedestals; one ascends to these by two sets of stairs that begin in the walkways which, as I have said, surround this temple.

The pedestals are a little higher than a third of the length of the columns. The bases of the columns are composed of the **Attic** and **Ionic** styles and have a most beautiful **profile** <note>original: "sacoma"; the specific outline or contour of a molding.</note>. The capitals are also of the **Composite order** <note>A Roman order that combines the volutes (scrolls) of the Ionic with the acanthus leaves of the Corinthian.</note> and are very neatly worked. The **Architrave**, the **Frieze**, and the **Cornice** are without carvings; and the ornaments placed in the niches around the Cella are similarly plain.

Behind the columns that face the entrance and form—to speak in our modern way—the **main chapel**, there are square pilasters which also have composite capitals, but different from those of the columns, and they are also different among themselves. This is because the capitals of the pilasters immediately next to the columns have different carvings than the other two; but they all have such a beautiful and graceful form, and are of such fine invention, that I do not know if I have ever seen capitals of this sort better or more judiciously made. These pilasters support the architraves of the side chapels to which one ascends, as I have said, by the stairs from the walkways. Therefore, they are wider in that direction than the columns are thick, which is a detail worthy of notice. The columns around the Cella support several arches made of squared stones, and from one of these arches to the other are placed the stones that form the main vault of the Temple. This entire building is made of squared stones and is covered with stone slabs placed so that one goes over the other, so that rain could not penetrate. I have used the greatest possible diligence in studying these two Temples, because they seemed to me buildings worthy of much consideration, from which one recognizes that in that age, the proper way of building was understood in every place. I have made five plates of this Temple.

->In the First, the **Plan** is drawn.<-

#### Dimensions and Measurements

The measurements are recorded in Feet and Units <note>Original: "p" for *piedi* (feet) and "G" likely for *gradi* (minutes/units), a standard division of the foot used in Renaissance architectural surveys.</note>:

*   **7 Feet, 2 Units** — The height of the spandrel <note>The space between the curve of an arch and the rectangular frame above it.</note>.
*   **3 Feet, 1 Unit** — The thickness or height of the lower masonry.
*   **3 Feet, 4 Units** — The height of the wall section **B**.
*   **1 Foot, 2 Units** — The width or spacing of the column.

#### The Interior Niches

The elevation reveals how the interior of the cella <note>The main inner room of the temple.</note> was decorated with "tabernacles" or niches:

*   **Left Niche:** Contains a sculpted male figure in a dynamic pose, draped in cloth. The base of this niche measures **3 Feet, 1/2 Unit**.
*   **Right Niche:** Contains a secondary draped figure. The base of this niche measures **3 Feet, 2 Units**.

The vaulting above these niches is shown in cross-section, revealing a "coffered" or ribbed interior, which served both to lighten the weight of the stone and to provide a grand decorative effect.

#### Proportional Measurements

Throughout the drawing, a series of numbers (ranging from **1** to **40**) are meticulously placed. These represent the specific measurements and modules <note>A standard unit of measurement used in classical architecture to determine the proportions of a building.</note> used to ensure the harmony of the design. # OF TWO OTHER TEMPLES IN ROME, AND FIRST
### regarding the Temple of Concord. Chapter XXX.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a pastoral landscape with figures, possibly shepherds or mythological characters, seated beneath trees.</image-desc>

BEYOND the Temples described above, when discussing those located in Rome, one can see at the foot of the Capitoline Hill <note>original: "Cápidoglio"</note>, near the Arch of Septimius <note>The Arch of Septimius Severus, located in the Roman Forum.</note>, where the Roman Forum formerly began, the columns of the portico of the temple that follows. This temple was built as a result of a vow made by Furius Camillus <note>Marcus Furius Camillus, a celebrated Roman general and statesman of the 4th century BCE.</note>, and dedicated, according to some, to Concord. In this Temple, the cares and business of the public were often conducted, from which it is understood that it was consecrated; for the priests only permitted the Senate to gather to discuss public affairs in consecrated temples, and only those built with an augury <term>A ritual used by ancient Roman religious officials (augurs) to interpret the will of the gods through signs.</term> were consecrated. Therefore, temples made in this manner were also called Curiae <term>Meeting houses for the Roman Senate.</term>.

Among the many statues with which it was adorned, writers mention that of Latona <note>The mother of Apollo and Diana.</note> holding her children Apollo and Diana in her arms; that of Aesculapius and his daughter Hygieia; those of Mars, Minerva, Ceres, and Mercury; and that of Victory, which was on the frontispiece <term>The pediment or triangular gable at the top of the portico.</term> of the portico, which was struck by lightning during the consulship of Marcus Marcellus and Marcus Valerius. As demonstrated by the inscription still visible on the frieze, this Temple was ruined by fire and later rebuilt by order of the Senate and the Roman people <note>original: "S. P. Q. R." — Senatus Populusque Romanus.</note>, which leads me to believe it was not restored to its former beauty and perfection. Its inscription is as follows:

-> S. P. Q. R. INCENDIO CONSUMPTUM RESTITUIT. <-
<note>original: "The Senate and People of Rome restored [this], which had been consumed by fire."</note>

That is, the Senate and Roman People have rebuilt this Temple consumed by fire. The intercolumniations <term>The space between columns, measured in column diameters.</term> are less than two diameters. The bases of the columns are a composite of the Attic and the Ionic styles; they are somewhat different from those usually made, yet they are crafted in a beautiful manner. The capitals can also be described as a mixture of Doric and Ionic, and they are very well worked. The architrave and the frieze on the outer part of the facade are all on one plane, and there is no distinction between them, which was done to allow space for the inscription. However, on the inside—that is, under the portico—they are divided and have the carvings seen in their drawing. The cornice is plain <note>original: "schietta"</note>; that is, without carvings. No ancient part of the walls of the cella <term>The inner chamber of a temple where the cult statue was kept.</term> can be seen, but they were later rebuilt, not very well; one can nonetheless recognize how it must have been.

Of this Temple, I have made three plates.

In the First, the Plan is drawn.
**G** and **E** are the Architrave and the Frieze that are under the portico.

In the Second is the Elevation of the front of the temple.

In the Third are the Architectural Members.
**A** is the basement <term>The continuous pedestal or foundation.</term> that wrapped all around the Temple.
**B** is the base of the columns.
**C** is the front.
**D** is the plan.
**E** is the profile without }
        the volutes        } of the Capital.
**F** is the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.

# THE TEMPLE OF NEPTUNE. Chapter XXXI. #

OPPOSITE the Temple of Mars the Avenger <note>original: "Marte Vindicatore"; a major temple in the Forum of Augustus in Rome.</note>, the drawings of which were provided above, in the place called "in Pantano" <note>The "swampy" area, a name historically given to the site of the Forum of Augustus due to water accumulation.</note>, which is behind Marforio <note>original: "Morſorio"; referring to the famous "talking statue" of Marforio and the surrounding area near the Roman Forum.</note>; there was in ancient times the temple that follows, whose foundations were discovered while digging to build a house; and there was also found a very great quantity of marble, all excellently worked. It is not known by whom it was built, nor to which God it was consecrated; but from its remains, which are many, it has been possible to gain knowledge of the general elements, that is, the **Plan**, and the **Elevation**; and of its particular members, which are all worked with wonderful craftsmanship. I have made five plates of it.

In the First is the **Plan**.

In the Second is the **Elevation** of half of the facade, outside the portico.
->D is the mold of the door.<-

->E is the profile of the wall of the Cella on the outside.<-

In the Fourth are the **particular Members**, that is, the ornaments.
->A is the Base.<-
->B is the Capital, above which are the Architrave, the Frieze, and the Cornice.<-

->H is the soffit <term>The underside of an architectural element, such as an arch or architrave.</term> of the Architrave between one Capital and another.<-
